cases.note: Several spaces between words collapse to one.
One word with spaces around it.

hints.text: Extra spaces anywhere must vanish in the answer. What are the real units you reorder?
Collect the words (runs of non-space characters) scanning left to right, then join them in reverse order with single spaces.

words = []
i = 0
while i < n:
  skip spaces
  read characters until a space into word
  if word is not empty: add word to words
return words in reverse order joined by ' '

cases.note: A run of 12 writes two digits.
Separate runs of the same character are compressed separately.

hints.text: Read a whole run of equal characters before writing anything. Where can you write without overwriting unread input?
Keep a read pointer and a write pointer. For each run, write the character, then the run length's digits if the length is more than 1. The write pointer never passes the read pointer.

cases.note: Different lengths are never rotations.

hints.text: Every rotation of s appears somewhere inside one particular string built from s. Which one?
If the lengths match, goal is a rotation of s exactly when goal occurs inside s + s.

if len(s) != len(goal): return false
return goal occurs inside s + s

cases.note: The match ends at the last character.
The needle is longer than the haystack.
A false start overlaps the real match.

hints.text: Try every starting index of haystack. How many characters do you need to compare at each one?
For each start i up to n - m, compare needle against haystack from i; return i on the first full match, or -1 after the loop. KMP removes the re-comparisons.

for i from 0 to n - m:
  j = 0
  while j < m and haystack[i + j] == needle[j]: j += 1
  if j == m: return i
return -1

cases.note: The largest value: MMMCMXCIX.
Uses three subtractive pairs: CM, XC and IV.

hints.text: Include the subtractive forms (CM, CD, XC, XL, IX, IV) as symbols of their own. Then is a greedy choice always right?
Walk the 13 values from 1000 down to 1. While num is at least the value, append its symbol and subtract.

values = [1000, 900, 500, 400, 100, 90, 50, 40, 10, 9, 5, 4, 1]
symbols = [M, CM, D, CD, C, XC, L, XL, X, IX, V, IV, I]
out = ""
for i from 0 to 12:
  while num >= values[i]:
    out += symbols[i]
    num -= values[i]
return out

cases.note: Starts with a letter: return 0.
Below -2^31: clamp.
Stop at the first non-digit.

hints.text: Process the string in stages: leading spaces, an optional sign, then digits. What stops the digit stage?
Skip spaces, read one '+' or '-', then accumulate digits until a non-digit. Clamp the result to [-2^31, 2^31 - 1] as you go so it never grows unbounded.

i = 0, sign = 1, result = 0
skip spaces
if s[i] is '+' or '-': set sign, i += 1
while s[i] is a digit:
  result = result * 10 + digit
  if result exceeds 2^31: stop growing it
  i += 1
result = sign * result
return result clamped to [-2^31, 2^31 - 1]
Each term describes the previous one run by run. Start from "1" and build forward.
Repeat n - 1 times: scan the current term, and for every run of equal digits append the run length followed by the digit.

term = "1"
repeat n - 1 times:
  next = ""
  for each run of equal digits d with length k in term:
    next += k as text + d
  term = next
return term

cases.note: Anything times 0 is "0", not "00".
Far beyond Number precision: no parseInt.

hints.text: Do long multiplication by hand. Where does the product of digit i of num1 and digit j of num2 land?
Use an array of length m + n. The product of num1[i] and num2[j] adds into position i + j + 1, with the carry going to i + j. Strip leading zeros at the end.

pos = array of m + n zeros
for i from m - 1 down to 0:
  for j from n - 1 down to 0:
    sum = num1[i] * num2[j] + pos[i + j + 1]
    pos[i + j + 1] = sum mod 10
    pos[i + j] += sum div 10
remove leading zeros from pos
return digits of pos, or "0" if none remain

cases.note: Everything cancels: return the empty string.
Pairs cancel; one 'a' is left over.

hints.text: Removing a pair can make two new characters adjacent. What structure lets you look at the last kept character instantly?
Use a stack of kept characters. If the next character equals the top, pop; otherwise push. The stack, bottom to top, is the answer.

stack = []
for each ch in s:
  if stack is not empty and top of stack == ch: pop
  else: push ch
return stack joined

cases.note: The star removes the last letter.
No stars: nothing changes.

hints.text: Each star deletes the closest kept character to its left. That's the most recently kept one.
Push letters onto a stack; on '*', pop. Join the stack at the end.

stack = []
for each ch in s:
  if ch == '*': pop
  else: push ch
return stack joined

cases.note: Already valid: 0 insertions.
Closers before openers: each needs its own partner.

hints.text: Scan left to right keeping the number of currently open brackets. When does a ')' force an insertion?
Track open. On '(' increment it. On ')' decrement it if it's positive, otherwise you must insert a '(' (count it). At the end, every still-open bracket needs a ')'.

open = 0, inserts = 0
for each ch in s:
  if ch == '(': open += 1
  else if open > 0: open -= 1
  else: inserts += 1
return inserts + open

cases.note: No vowels anywhere: 0.
k = n: the only window is the whole string.

hints.text: All windows have the same length k. When the window moves one step, which two characters change the count?
Count vowels in the first k characters, then slide: add 1 if the entering character is a vowel, subtract 1 if the leaving one was. Track the maximum.

count = vowels in s[0..k-1]
best = count
for i from k to n - 1:
  if s[i] is a vowel: count += 1
  if s[i - k] is a vowel: count -= 1
  best = max(best, count)
return best

cases.note: Exactly one substring: the whole string.
'c' never appears: 0.

hints.text: If s[i..j] already contains a, b and c, what about every longer substring that starts at i?
For each right end j, track the last positions of a, b and c. Every start up to the smallest of those three positions works, so add min(last) + 1.

cases.note: The whole string is a palindrome.
The longest is 'aba'; the reversed-substring trick finds the wrong answer here.

hints.text: Every palindrome mirrors around a centre. How many possible centres does a string of length n have?
Expand around each of the 2n - 1 centres (a character, or the gap between two characters) while the ends match, and keep the longest span found. Every test here has exactly one longest palindrome.

best = ""
for each centre c (each index, and each gap between indices):
  l, r = the ends of c
  while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
    l -= 1, r += 1
  if r - l - 1 > len(best): best = s[l + 1 .. r - 1]
return best

cases.note: n(n+1)/2 palindromes: every substring.

hints.text: Count by centre instead of by substring: every palindrome has exactly one centre.
Expand around each of the 2n - 1 centres; every successful expansion step is one more palindromic substring.

count = 0
for each centre c (each index, and each gap between indices):
  l, r = the ends of c
  while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
    count += 1
    l -= 1, r += 1
return count

cases.note: Nothing in common: an empty list.
A repeated common value appears once.

hints.text: Each common value appears once in the answer, however often it repeats. Which structure removes repeats for free?
Put nums1 in a Set. Walk nums2 and collect values found in that Set into a second Set, so each common value is added once.

a = set of nums1
result = empty set
for each v in nums2:
  if v in a: add v to result
return result as a list

cases.note: Nothing is missing: an empty list.

hints.text: Values are all in 1..n. A Set of what you saw makes the missing ones easy to list. Can the array itself act as that Set?
For each value v, mark index |v| - 1 by making it negative. Afterwards, every index i still holding a positive number means i + 1 never appeared.

for each v in nums:
  i = |v| - 1
  nums[i] = -|nums[i]|
result = []
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  if nums[i] > 0: add i + 1 to result
return result

cases.note: k = 0: two different indices can never be within distance 0.
Only the last two copies are close enough.

hints.text: For each value you only care about its most recent earlier position. What do you store per value?
Keep a map value -> last index. At index i, if the value was seen at j with i - j <= k, return true; then update its last index to i.

last = empty map
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  if nums[i] in last and i - last[nums[i]] <= k: return true
  last[nums[i]] = i
return false
Two hash steps: first count each value, then check something about the counts themselves.
Build value -> count, then put every count into a Set. The counts are unique exactly when the Set has as many entries as there are distinct values.

count = counts of arr
return size of set(values of count) == number of keys in count

cases.note: No 'b': zero balloons.
One 'l' and one 'o' aren't enough for a balloon.

hints.text: Each 'balloon' uses b, a, n once and l, o twice. Which letter runs out first?
Count the letters of text. The answer is the minimum of count[b], count[a], count[n], count[l] / 2 and count[o] / 2, each rounded down.

count = counts of text
return min(count[b], count[a], count[n], floor(count[l] / 2), floor(count[o] / 2))

cases.note: Two common copies of 3.

hints.text: Now a common value appears as many times as it shows up in both arrays. What should you count?
Count nums1. For each value of nums2 with a positive count, add it to the result and decrement the count.

count = counts of nums1
result = []
for each v in nums2:
  if count[v] > 0:
    add v to result
    count[v] -= 1
return result

cases.note: The whole array is needed.
Degree 1: any single element works.

hints.text: A subarray with the same degree must contain every copy of some most-frequent value. What's the shortest span containing all copies of a value?
For each value record its count, first index and last index. Among values with the maximum count, return the smallest last - first + 1.

for i from 0 to n - 1:
  v = nums[i]
  count[v] += 1
  if v not in first: first[v] = i
  last[v] = i
degree = max of count
return min of last[v] - first[v] + 1 over v with count[v] == degree

cases.note: Max - min must be exactly 1, so one value alone doesn't count.

hints.text: A harmonious subsequence uses only two values, x and x + 1. Order doesn't matter for its length.
Count every value. For each x whose x + 1 is also present, count[x] + count[x + 1] is a candidate; return the largest (0 if none).

cases.note: The same loser three times has 3 losses: in neither list.
Each lost once: nobody is unbeaten.

hints.text: Only losses matter, but a player who never lost still has to be known. What do you track per player?
Map every player to their loss count (winners get 0 if absent). Collect players with 0 and with exactly 1 loss, and sort both lists.

losses = empty map
for each [w, l] in matches:
  if w not in losses: losses[w] = 0
  losses[l] += 1
zero = sorted players with 0 losses
one = sorted players with 1 loss
return [zero, one]

cases.note: A 1x1 grid: its row equals its column.
Every row matches every column: 4 pairs.

hints.text: Comparing every row with every column is O(n^3). Can a row be turned into a key you can look up?
Count each row as a string key (e.g. joined with commas). Then build each column's key and add the count of matching rows.

rows = empty map
for each row r: rows[key(r)] += 1
pairs = 0
for each column c:
  pairs += rows[key(c)] (0 if missing)
return pairs

cases.note: An empty board is valid.
Different row and column, same 3x3 box.
Same column, far apart.

hints.text: Each filled digit belongs to one row, one column and one 3x3 box. How do you remember what each of those already holds?
Keep a Set per row, per column and per box (box index = floor(r / 3) * 3 + floor(c / 3)). A digit already in any of its three sets means invalid.

for r from 0 to 8:
  for c from 0 to 8:
    d = board[r][c]
    if d == '.': continue
    b = (r div 3) * 3 + (c div 3)
    if d in rows[r] or d in cols[c] or d in boxes[b]: return false
    add d to rows[r], cols[c], boxes[b]
return true

cases.note: Shorter than 10: no windows at all.
Two overlapping windows of the same sequence.
Exactly one window: nothing repeats.

hints.text: Every 10-letter window is a candidate. How do you know you've seen a window before?
Slide over all windows of length 10, adding each to a 'seen' Set. When a window is already in it, add it to a 'repeated' Set (so it's reported once).

seen = empty set, repeated = empty set
for i from 0 to n - 10:
  w = s[i .. i + 9]
  if w in seen: add w to repeated
  add w to seen
return repeated as a list

cases.note: All bulls, no cows.
No bulls, all cows.

hints.text: Bulls are easy: same digit, same position. Cows need counts of the leftover digits on both sides.
Count bulls in one pass. For non-bull positions, count digits of secret and of guess separately; cows = sum over digits of the smaller of the two counts.

bulls = 0
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  if secret[i] == guess[i]: bulls += 1
  else:
    s[secret[i]] += 1
    g[guess[i]] += 1
cows = sum over digits d of min(s[d], g[d])
return bulls + "A" + cows + "B"

cases.note: All squares: 3 pairs.
Width/height order matters: 1/2 isn't 2/1.

hints.text: Two rectangles are interchangeable when width/height match. How do you group ratios safely, without floating-point surprises?
Reduce each [w, h] by gcd(w, h) and use the reduced pair as a key. A group of size m contributes m * (m - 1) / 2 pairs; or add the group's current size before inserting each rectangle.

count = empty map, pairs = 0
for each [w, h] in rectangles:
  g = gcd(w, h)
  key = (w / g, h / g)
  pairs += count[key] (0 if missing)
  count[key] += 1
return pairs

cases.note: One row with an inner edge: cross 0 bricks.
No edge is shared by every row.

hints.text: A line crosses the fewest bricks where the most rows have an edge. Where are a row's edges?
For every row, walk its prefix sums (excluding the full width) and count how often each edge position appears. Answer = rows - the most common edge count.

cases.note: "00" never appears.
Only one of the two codes.
Exactly all 8 codes, each once (a de Bruijn sequence).

hints.text: There are exactly 2^k binary codes of length k. How many distinct windows of length k does s have?
Collect every length-k window into a Set. s contains all codes exactly when the Set reaches size 2^k.

seen = empty set
for i from 0 to n - k:
  add s[i .. i + k - 1] to seen
return size of seen == 2^k

cases.note: All letters different: one piece.

hints.text: Greedy: make each piece as long as possible. When must a piece end?
Keep the letters of the current piece in a Set. When the next letter is already in it, start a new piece (clear the Set). Count the pieces.

pieces = 1, seen = empty set
for each ch in s:
  if ch in seen:
    pieces += 1
    seen = empty set
  add ch to seen
return pieces

cases.note: No zeros at all: 0.
The best subarray runs to the last element.

hints.text: Treat 0 as -1. Then 'equal numbers of 0 and 1' means the subarray sums to 0.
Track a running sum and the first index each sum value appeared (sum 0 at index -1). When a sum repeats, the subarray between the two indices sums to 0.

cases.note: Two zeros sum to 0, a multiple of every k.
A single element isn't long enough.
Only the zeros form a valid subarray.

hints.text: A subarray sum is a multiple of k when two prefix sums leave the same remainder mod k.
Store the first index of each prefix remainder (remainder 0 at index -1). If a remainder repeats at least two indices later, the subarray has length >= 2 and a sum divisible by k.

first = {0: -1}, sum = 0
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  sum = (sum + nums[i]) mod k
  if sum in first:
    if i - first[sum] >= 2: return true
  else: first[sum] = i
return false

cases.note: Negative prefix sums need their remainder normalised.
Every subarray of zeros counts: 6.

hints.text: Two prefix sums with the same remainder mod k bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by k. Careful: JavaScript's % can be negative.
Count remainders of prefix sums (normalised to 0..k-1, starting with remainder 0 once). Each new prefix adds the number of earlier prefixes with the same remainder.

count = {0: 1}, sum = 0, total = 0
for each v in nums:
  sum = ((sum + v) mod k + k) mod k
  total += count[sum] (0 if missing)
  count[sum] += 1
return total

cases.note: The whole array sums to less than goal.
goal = 0 counts the runs of zeros.

hints.text: Subarray sum = goal means prefix[j] - prefix[i] = goal. How many earlier prefixes equal prefix[j] - goal?
Keep a count of prefix sums seen (prefix 0 once at the start). For each new prefix add count[prefix - goal], then record the prefix.

count = {0: 1}, sum = 0, total = 0
for each v in nums:
  sum += v
  total += count[sum - goal] (0 if missing)
  count[sum] += 1
return total

cases.note: Evens on both sides multiply the count.

hints.text: Replace each number by 1 if odd and 0 if even. Now you're counting subarrays with sum exactly k.
Use the prefix-count map: running count of odds, add count[odds - k] at each step, then record the running count.

count = {0: 1}, odds = 0, total = 0
for each v in nums:
  if v is odd: odds += 1
  total += count[odds - k] (0 if missing)
  count[odds] += 1
return total

cases.note: Fewer than four numbers: no quadruplets.
Many equal values still give one quadruplet.

hints.text: It's 3Sum with one more fixed index. Sorting is what makes skipping duplicates easy.
Sort. Fix i, then j > i, skipping repeated values for both. Use two pointers on the rest to find pairs summing to target - nums[i] - nums[j], skipping duplicates as you move.

cases.note: Every subarray has exactly one distinct value: 6.
Never 3 distinct values: 0.

hints.text: Counting 'exactly k distinct' directly is awkward. Counting 'at most k distinct' with a sliding window is easy. How do the two relate?
exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1). atMost(k): grow the window, shrink from the left while it has more than k distinct values, and add the window length at each right end.

cases.note: Shared suffixes cancel most swaps; only a and d can trade.
Swapping gives 'cb' and 'ad': both new, so 2 names.
Same suffix under both letters: no valid swap.

hints.text: Group the ideas by first letter, keeping only the suffix. Swapping letters a and b works for a pair of suffixes when neither suffix exists under the other letter.
For each pair of letters (a, b), count the suffixes they share. Valid pairs = (|A| - common) * (|B| - common), and each unordered letter pair gives two names.

groups[c] = set of suffixes of ideas starting with c
total = 0
for each letter pair a < b:
  common = size of groups[a] intersect groups[b]
  total += 2 * (size(groups[a]) - common) * (size(groups[b]) - common)
return total

cases.note: A vertical line: dx = 0 must be handled.

hints.text: Fix one point. Every other point defines a direction from it; points on the same line through the anchor share a direction.
For each anchor, count other points by reduced slope: (dy, dx) divided by their gcd with a fixed sign. The best line through the anchor has max count + 1 points.

best = 1
for each anchor p:
  slopes = empty map
  for each other point q:
    dx = q.x - p.x, dy = q.y - p.y
    g = gcd(|dx|, |dy|); normalise (dx / g, dy / g) to one sign
    slopes[(dx, dy)] += 1
  best = max(best, max of slopes + 1)
return best

cases.note: Every index matches: [0, n - 1].

hints.text: A plain binary search finds some copy of target. How do you make it keep going towards the first (or last) copy?
Run two searches: one that moves left after a match (first index) and one that moves right after a match (last index). Return [-1, -1] if the first search finds nothing.

first = -1, lo = 0, hi = n - 1
while lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  if nums[mid] >= target: hi = mid - 1; if nums[mid] == target: first = mid
  else: lo = mid + 1
last = the same search, moving lo = mid + 1 when nums[mid] <= target
return [first, last]

cases.note: 46340^2: mid * mid must not lose precision.
Just above the largest square below 2^31.

hints.text: If num is a perfect square, its root lies between 1 and num. Squares grow monotonically, so you can search that range.
Binary search x in [1, num]: if x * x equals num return true, if it's smaller move right, otherwise move left. Return false when the range empties.

lo = 1, hi = num
while lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  sq = mid * mid
  if sq == num: return true
  if sq < num: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid - 1
return false

cases.note: Exactly 3 full rows.

hints.text: k complete rows need k(k + 1) / 2 coins. That grows with k, so the largest k that fits can be binary searched.
Search k in [0, n] for the largest k with k(k + 1) / 2 <= n.

lo = 0, hi = n
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi + 1) div 2
  if mid * (mid + 1) / 2 <= n: lo = mid
  else: hi = mid - 1
return lo

cases.note: nums[lo], nums[mid] and nums[hi] are all 1: you can't tell which half is sorted.

hints.text: Without duplicates, one half around mid is always sorted. With duplicates, when can't you tell which half is sorted?
If nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi], shrink both ends by one. Otherwise decide which half is sorted, and whether target lies inside it, as in the version without duplicates.

cases.note: The single element is first.
The single element is last.

hints.text: Before the single element, pairs start at even indices. After it, pairs start at odd indices.
Binary search on even indices only: if nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1] (mid even), the single element is to the right; otherwise it's at mid or to the left.

lo = 0, hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  if mid is odd: mid -= 1
  if nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1]: lo = mid + 2
  else: hi = mid
return nums[lo]

cases.note: The peak sits right after the first element.
The peak is the second-to-last element.

hints.text: Compare arr[mid] with arr[mid + 1]. Which side of the peak are you on?
If arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1] you're on the rising slope, so the peak is to the right; otherwise it's at mid or to the left.

lo = 0, hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  if arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1]: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid
return lo

cases.note: One element is a peak by itself.
Strictly rising: the last index is the peak.
Strictly falling: index 0 is the peak.

hints.text: Treat nums[-1] and nums[n] as minus infinity. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], is there certainly a peak to the right?
Yes: walking uphill to the right must end at a peak. So move lo = mid + 1 when nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], else hi = mid. Every test here has exactly one peak.

lo = 0, hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  if nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid
return lo

cases.note: The rounded-up sum hits the threshold exactly at divisor 3.
Threshold equals the length: the divisor must be max(nums).

hints.text: A bigger divisor never makes the rounded-up sum larger. That monotonic yes/no question is what binary search on the answer needs.
Search d in [1, max(nums)]. If the sum of ceil(v / d) is within threshold, try smaller d (hi = d); otherwise lo = d + 1.

lo = 1, hi = max(nums)
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  total = sum of ceil(v / mid) over nums
  if total <= threshold: hi = mid
  else: lo = mid + 1
return lo

cases.note: One package per day: the answer is the heaviest package.
One day: carry everything at once.

hints.text: For a fixed capacity, how many days does a greedy left-to-right loading take? Does that count go up or down as capacity grows?
Binary search the capacity in [max(weights), sum(weights)]. Simulate loading greedily; if it fits in days, try smaller, else larger.

lo = max(weights), hi = sum(weights)
while lo < hi:
  cap = (lo + hi) div 2
  need = 1, load = 0
  for each w in weights:
    if load + w > cap: need += 1, load = 0
    load += w
  if need <= days: hi = cap
  else: lo = cap + 1
return lo

cases.note: Needs 4 flowers but there are only 2: -1.
Adjacency matters: day 12 is needed.

hints.text: If m * k exceeds the number of flowers it's impossible. Otherwise, if you can make m bouquets by day d, can you also by day d + 1?
Binary search the day between min and max bloomDay. For a day d, count runs of adjacent bloomed flowers and how many bouquets of k they give.

if m * k > n: return -1
lo = min(bloomDay), hi = max(bloomDay)
while lo < hi:
  d = (lo + hi) div 2
  bouquets = 0, run = 0
  for each b in bloomDay:
    run = run + 1 if b <= d else 0
    if run == k: bouquets += 1, run = 0
  if bouquets >= m: hi = d
  else: lo = d + 1
return lo

cases.note: No pair is strong enough.
Exactly reaches success: counts.

hints.text: For one spell s, a potion p works when s * p >= success. If potions were sorted, the working ones would form a suffix.
Sort potions once. For each spell, binary search the first potion with spell * potion >= success; the answer is potions.length minus that index.

sort potions
for each spell s:
  lo = 0, hi = m
  while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) div 2
    if s * potions[mid] >= success: hi = mid
    else: lo = mid + 1
  add m - lo to result
return result

cases.note: Three buses finish one trip each at t = 3.
The fast bus does almost everything.

hints.text: In t units of time, bus i completes floor(t / time[i]) trips. More time never means fewer trips.
Binary search t in [1, min(time) * totalTrips]; check whether the trips add up to at least totalTrips.

lo = 1, hi = min(time) * totalTrips
while lo < hi:
  t = (lo + hi) div 2
  trips = sum of floor(t / x) over time
  if trips >= totalTrips: hi = t
  else: lo = t + 1
return lo

cases.note: Every position is used: the gap is 1.

hints.text: This is aggressive cows: can you place m balls so every pair is at least d apart? A smaller d is always easier.
Sort positions. Binary search d for the largest value where greedy placement (put a ball as soon as the gap reaches d) places at least m balls.

sort position
lo = 1, hi = position[n - 1] - position[0]
while lo < hi:
  d = (lo + hi + 1) div 2
  placed = 1, last = position[0]
  for each p in position:
    if p - last >= d: placed += 1, last = p
  if placed >= m: lo = d
  else: hi = d - 1
return lo

cases.note: One store gets everything.

hints.text: If every store may receive at most x items, product type q needs ceil(q / x) stores. Is the total count monotonic in x?
Binary search x in [1, max(quantities)]: x works when the sum of ceil(q / x) is at most n.

lo = 1, hi = max(quantities)
while lo < hi:
  x = (lo + hi) div 2
  stores = sum of ceil(q / x) over quantities
  if stores <= n: hi = x
  else: lo = x + 1
return lo

cases.note: One number per piece: the answer is the largest number.

hints.text: Guess the answer S: can you cut the array into at most k pieces each summing to at most S? A bigger S only makes that easier.
Binary search S in [max(nums), sum(nums)]. Greedily extend the current piece until adding the next number would exceed S, then start a new piece; S works if pieces <= k.

lo = max(nums), hi = sum(nums)
while lo < hi:
  S = (lo + hi) div 2
  pieces = 1, cur = 0
  for each v in nums:
    if cur + v > S: pieces += 1, cur = 0
    cur += v
  if pieces <= k: hi = S
  else: lo = S + 1
return lo

cases.note: Found in the bottom-left corner.

hints.text: Rows and columns are sorted, but the whole matrix isn't. Which corner lets every comparison throw away a full row or column?
Start at the top-right. If the value is larger than target, move left (the column is useless); if smaller, move down (the row is useless).

r = 0, c = cols - 1
while r < rows and c >= 0:
  v = matrix[r][c]
  if v == target: return true
  if v > target: c -= 1
  else: r += 1
return false

cases.note: Equal values count separately.
k = n^2: the largest value.

hints.text: Instead of searching positions, search values: how many entries are <= x? That count grows with x.
Binary search x between matrix[0][0] and matrix[n-1][n-1]. Count entries <= x with the staircase walk from the bottom-left; the smallest x with count >= k is the answer.

lo = matrix[0][0], hi = matrix[n - 1][n - 1]
while lo < hi:
  x = (lo + hi) div 2
  count = 0, r = n - 1, c = 0
  while r >= 0 and c < n:
    if matrix[r][c] <= x: count += r + 1, c += 1
    else: r -= 1
  if count >= k: hi = x
  else: lo = x + 1
return lo

cases.note: x beyond the right end: take the last k.

hints.text: The answer is a contiguous window of length k. Can you binary search where that window starts?
Search the start i in [0, n - k]. Compare x - arr[i] with arr[i + k] - x: if the left end is farther, the window should move right; otherwise left (ties prefer the smaller elements).

lo = 0, hi = n - k
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  if x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid
return arr[lo .. lo + k - 1]

cases.note: One array is empty.

hints.text: Merging is O(m + n). The median splits the combined array into two equal halves. Can you search how many elements of the shorter array go into the left half?

Binary search i (from nums1) with j = half - i (from nums2) so that every left element is <= every right element: nums1[i-1] <= nums2[j] and nums2[j-1] <= nums1[i]. Then the median comes from the four border values.

make nums1 the shorter array
lo = 0, hi = m, half = (m + n + 1) div 2
while lo <= hi:
  i = (lo + hi) div 2, j = half - i
  L1, R1 = nums1[i - 1], nums1[i] (minus/plus infinity past the ends)
  L2, R2 = nums2[j - 1], nums2[j] (same)
  if L1 <= R2 and L2 <= R1:
    if m + n is odd: return max(L1, L2)
    return (max(L1, L2) + min(R1, R2)) / 2
  if L1 > R2: hi = i - 1
  else: lo = i + 1

cases.note: nums[mid] == nums[hi] while the minimum hides on the left.

hints.text: Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. Which outcomes tell you where the minimum is, and which tells you nothing?
nums[mid] > nums[hi]: the minimum is right of mid. nums[mid] < nums[hi]: it's at mid or left. Equal: you can only drop hi by one safely.

lo = 0, hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1
  else if nums[mid] < nums[hi]: hi = mid
  else: hi -= 1
return nums[lo]

cases.note: k is the last pair: the largest distance.

hints.text: There are n(n - 1) / 2 distances: too many to list. How many pairs have distance <= d? That count grows with d.
Sort nums and binary search d in [0, max - min]. Count pairs with distance <= d using a sliding left pointer; the smallest d with count >= k is the answer.

sort nums

  else if op == "D": push 2 * top
  else if op == "C": pop
  else: push number(op)
return sum of stack

cases.note: Exactly one bad pair: the empty string.
Removals cascade from the middle out.

hints.text: Removing a bad pair can create a new bad pair from its neighbours. That's the same shape as matching brackets.
Use a stack of characters: if the top is the same letter in the other case, pop it; otherwise push.

stack = []
for ch in s:
  if stack not empty and top != ch and lower(top) == lower(ch): pop
  else: push ch
return stack joined

cases.note: Exactly 3000 apart: both still count.
Each ping forgets everything before it.

hints.text: Pings arrive in increasing time order. Which old pings can never count again?
Keep a queue of ping times. On ping(t), add t and drop times from the front that are less than t - 3000. The queue's length is the answer.

ping(t):
  enqueue t
  while front < t - 3000: dequeue
  return size of the queue

cases.note: Popping one copy of the minimum leaves the other.

hints.text: Scanning for the minimum is O(n). What if every stack entry remembered the minimum at the time it was pushed?
Push pairs (value, min so far). getMin reads the top pair's min; popping restores the previous minimum automatically.

push(val): push (val, min(val, current min or val))
pop(): pop
top(): top value
getMin(): top min

cases.note: Going above the root stays at the root.
"..." is a valid directory name.

hints.text: Split the path on '/'. Each piece either goes deeper, stays put, or goes up one level.
Use a stack of directory names: skip empty pieces and '.', pop on '..' (if not empty), push anything else. Join with '/' and prefix '/'.

stack = []
for part in path split by "/":
  if part == "" or part == ".": skip
  else if part == "..": pop if stack not empty
  else: push part
return "/" + stack joined by "/"

cases.note: Push everything, then pop everything.
Pop right after each push.

hints.text: Just replay it. When is popping the next expected value allowed?
Push values in order; after each push, while the stack's top equals popped[j], pop and advance j. Valid if the stack ends empty.

stack = [], j = 0
for x in pushed:
  push x
  while stack not empty and top == popped[j]: pop; j += 1
return stack is empty

cases.note: Moving apart: no collisions.
The left-mover destroys one, then loses to the next.

hints.text: A collision only happens when a left-moving asteroid meets right-moving ones before it. Which earlier asteroids does it meet first?
Keep a stack of survivors. For a negative asteroid, pop smaller positive tops; if the top is equal, both explode; if the top is bigger, it dies; otherwise push it.

stack = []
for a in asteroids:
  alive = true
  while alive and a < 0 and stack top > 0:
    if top < -a: pop; continue
    if top == -a: pop
    alive = false
  if alive: push a
return stack

cases.note: Two removals: the empty string.

hints.text: Removing k equal letters can bring two runs together. Track runs, not single letters.
Keep a stack of [char, count]. Same as the top: increment, and pop when it reaches k. Different: push [ch, 1]. Rebuild the string at the end.

cases.note: Nested and side by side together.
Ten doublings: 1024.

hints.text: () is 1, AB adds, (A) doubles. A stack of partial scores per nesting level fits this naturally.
Push 0 on '('. On ')', pop v and add max(2 * v, 1) to the new top. Start with a 0 on the stack for the outer level.

stack = [0]
for ch in s:
  if ch == '(': push 0
  else:
    v = pop
    top += max(2 * v, 1)
return stack[0]

cases.note: Starts and ends in the same unit: 1.
A function calls itself.

hints.text: Calls nest like brackets. The running function is always the one on top of a call stack.
Keep a stack of ids and the previous timestamp. On start at t: credit the current top with t - prev, push, prev = t. On end at t: credit the top with t - prev + 1, pop, prev = t + 1.

cases.note: 7/2 truncates to 3, then 1 - 3 = -2.

hints.text: '*' and '/' bind tighter than '+' and '-'. What if you settle them immediately and leave the additions for the end?
Scan numbers with the operator before them: '+' pushes n, '-' pushes -n, '*' and '/' replace the top with top * n or trunc(top / n). Sum the stack.

cases.note: D acts first, twice.

hints.text: Each senator's best move is to ban the next opposing senator who would act. Order matters, so think in turns.
Put the indexes of R and D senators in two queues. Compare the fronts: the smaller index bans the other and re-enters its queue with index + n. The non-empty queue wins.

qr, qd = indexes of 'R' and 'D'
while both non-empty:
  r = dequeue qr; d = dequeue qd
  if r < d: enqueue qr with r + n
  else: enqueue qd with d + n
return "Radiant" if qr non-empty else "Dire"

cases.note: Nothing is greater: all -1.
Every answer wraps around to 5.

hints.text: The array is circular: the answer may wrap around to the start. How can one pass of a stack see the wrap?
Walk indexes 0..2n-1 using i mod n, with a stack of indexes still waiting for a greater value. Pop and fill while the current value is greater; push only in the first pass.

res = n copies of -1, stack = []
for i from 0 to 2n - 1:
  v = nums[i mod n]
  while stack not empty and nums[top] < v:
    res[pop] = v
  if i < n: push i
return res

cases.note: Rising prices: the span keeps growing.
Equal prices count (<=).

hints.text: Today's span swallows the spans of every earlier day with a price <= today's. Do you need to keep those days around?
Keep a stack of (price, span) with strictly decreasing prices. On next(price), pop every entry with price <= today's and add its span; push (price, total).

next(price):
  span = 1
  while stack not empty and top.price <= price:
    span += pop.span
  push (price, span)
  return span

cases.note: Remove everything: "0".
Leading zeros disappear after removing the 1.
Increasing digits: drop from the end.

hints.text: The leftmost digits matter most. When does dropping a digit make the number smaller?
Keep an increasing stack: while k > 0 and the top is bigger than the current digit, pop (k -= 1). Drop any remaining k from the end, strip leading zeros, return "0" if empty.

stack = []
for d in num:
  while k > 0 and stack not empty and top > d: pop; k -= 1
  push d
remove k digits from the end
strip leading zeros
return result or "0"

cases.note: All three arrive at the same moment: one fleet.
Same speed: nobody catches up.
The back car catches up exactly at the target.

hints.text: A car can only be blocked by cars ahead of it. Process cars from the one closest to the target.
Sort by position descending and compute each car's time to the target. A car whose time is larger than the slowest fleet ahead starts a new fleet; otherwise it joins.

sort cars by position, largest first
fleets = 0, slowest = 0
for each car:
  t = (target - position) / speed
  if t > slowest:
    fleets += 1
    slowest = t
return fleets

cases.note: Strict inequalities: equal values never form the pattern.

hints.text: Fix the '3' (nums[j]). You want a smaller '1' before it and a '2' after it that sits between them.
Scan from the right with a decreasing stack. Popped values are candidates for the '2' (keep the largest as third). If you meet a value smaller than third, that's the '1'.

third = minus infinity, stack = []
for i from n - 1 down to 0:
  if nums[i] < third: return true
  while stack not empty and top < nums[i]: third = pop
  push nums[i]
return false

cases.note: Ties must be counted once per subarray.
Big sums: take the modulus as you go.

hints.text: Count, for each element, how many subarrays have it as their minimum. Its contribution is value * that count.
With previous-less and next-less-or-equal boundaries (two monotonic stacks), arr[i] is the minimum of left * right subarrays. Sum modulo 1e9+7.

left[i] = distance to the previous strictly smaller element
right[i] = distance to the next smaller-or-equal element
answer = sum of arr[i] * left[i] * right[i], mod 1e9+7

cases.note: No letter repeats, so nothing can be reordered.

hints.text: You may drop an earlier letter if a smaller letter comes next and the earlier one appears again later.
Count the last index of each letter. Keep a stack and a 'used' set: skip used letters; while the top is larger than c and occurs later, pop it; push c.

last[c] = last index of c
stack = [], used = empty set
for i, c in s:
  if c in used: skip
  while stack not empty and top > c and last[top] > i:
    remove pop from used
  push c; add c to used
return stack joined

cases.note: The whole matrix.
Only single cells.

hints.text: Treat each row as the floor of a histogram: the bar height at column c is how many 1s stack up above it.
Update heights row by row (reset to 0 on '0') and run largest-rectangle-in-histogram on each row with a monotonic stack.

heights = zeros
best = 0
for each row:
  for c: heights[c] = heights[c] + 1 if row[c] == '1' else 0
  best = max(best, largest rectangle in heights)
return best

cases.note: k = n: one window.
The maximum leaves the window each step.

hints.text: When a bigger value enters the window, every smaller value before it can never be the maximum again.
Keep a deque of indexes with decreasing values. Push i after popping smaller values from the back; drop the front when it leaves the window; the front is each window's max.

dq = empty deque, res = []
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  while dq not empty and nums[back] <= nums[i]: pop back
  push i at back
  if front <= i - k: pop front
  if i >= k - 1: add nums[front] to res
return res

cases.note: Two valid runs side by side join up.
No valid run at all.

hints.text: A valid run ends where some ')' closes the run's first '('. What marks where the current run started?
Keep a stack of indexes with a base marker (-1 initially). Push on '('. On ')', pop; if the stack is empty, push i as the new base; otherwise the run length is i - top.

cases.note: A unary minus before a parenthesis.

hints.text: Only + and - (and parentheses). A minus before '(' flips the sign of everything inside.
Scan with a running result and sign. On '(' push (result, sign) and reset; on ')' finish the inner value, then result = savedResult + savedSign * inner.

result = 0, sign = 1, num = 0, stack = []
for ch in s:
  digit: num = num * 10 + ch
  '+' or '-': result += sign * num; num = 0; sign = +1 or -1
  '(': push result, push sign; result = 0; sign = 1
  ')': result += sign * num; num = 0

return result + sign * num

cases.note: All frequencies tie: plain stack order.
After one pop, 1 and 2 tie and the more recent 2 goes next.

hints.text: pop removes the most frequent value, breaking ties by recency. What if you kept one stack per frequency level?

Track freq[val] and a stack for each frequency. push increments freq and pushes onto stacks[freq]. pop takes from stacks[maxFreq], decrements that value's freq, and lowers maxFreq when that stack empties.

push(val):
  freq[val] += 1; f = freq[val]
  maxFreq = max(maxFreq, f)
  push val onto group[f]
pop():
  val = pop from group[maxFreq]
  freq[val] -= 1
  if group[maxFreq] is empty: maxFreq -= 1
  return val

cases.note: Capacity 1: every new key evicts the old one.
Updating a key overwrites its value.
get(1) made key 2 the least recent.

hints.text: You need O(1) lookup by key and O(1) 'move to most recent' plus 'evict least recent'.

A hash map from key to node of a doubly linked list ordered by recency (or a Map, which keeps insertion order): get moves the key to the end; put inserts at the end and evicts the front when over capacity.

get(key):
  if key missing: return -1
  move key to the most-recent end
  return its value
put(key, value):
  if key present: remove it
  insert key at the most-recent end
  if size > capacity: evict the least-recent key

cases.note: Capacity 1: the new key always replaces the old one.
Both keys used once: the least recent one goes.
Updating a key counts as a use.

hints.text: Evict the key with the lowest use count, and among those the least recently used. Group keys by their count.

Keep key -> (value, count), count -> ordered set of keys (a Map keeps order), and the current minimum count. Each access moves the key to count + 1; a new key starts at count 1 and resets minCount to 1.

touch(key): move key from group[count] to group[count + 1]; if group[minCount] is empty: minCount += 1
get(key): if missing: return -1; touch(key); return value
put(key, value):
  if key present: update value; touch(key); return
  if size == capacity: evict the oldest key in group[minCount]
  add key with count 1 to group[1]; minCount = 1

cases.note: Only two copies survive.

hints.text: The array is sorted, so a value already kept twice would sit exactly two slots behind the write position.
Keep a write pointer k. Copy nums[i] to nums[k] unless k >= 2 and nums[k - 2] equals nums[i].

cases.note: No 1s at all: the answer is 0.
The best run ends at the last index.

hints.text: You only care about the current run of 1s and the best run so far.
Walk once: a 1 extends the run, a 0 resets it to zero. Track the maximum after each step.

best = 0, run = 0
for x in nums:
  if x == 1: run = run + 1
  else: run = 0
  best = max(best, run)
return best

cases.note: k == n: every score is taken.

hints.text: After sorting, the best k scores are always next to each other.
Sort, then slide a window of size k: its spread is a[i + k - 1] - a[i]. Take the smallest.

sort nums
best = infinity
for i in 0 .. n - k:
  best = min(best, nums[i + k - 1] - nums[i])
return best

cases.note: One window, average exactly equal: it counts.

hints.text: Average >= threshold is the same as sum >= k * threshold, so you never need division.
Keep a running sum of the last k values: add the new one, drop the one that left, and count windows whose sum is large enough.

sum = 0, count = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 1:
  sum = sum + arr[i]
  if i >= k: sum = sum - arr[i - k]
  if i >= k - 1 and sum >= k * threshold: count = count + 1
return count

cases.note: k == n: take everything.
The big card sits in the middle and can't be reached.

hints.text: Whatever you take from the ends, the cards you leave form one contiguous block of n - k cards.
Maximising what you take means minimising the block you leave. Slide a window of size n - k and keep its smallest sum.

total = sum(cardPoints), w = n - k
window = sum of first w cards, low = window
for i in w .. n - 1:
  window = window + cardPoints[i] - cardPoints[i - w]
  low = min(low, window)
return total - low

cases.note: The best minute to rescue is the last one.

hints.text: Customers in calm minutes are happy no matter what. The technique only changes the grumpy minutes inside one window.
Add up the always-happy customers, then slide a window of length minutes summing only the grumpy-minute customers it rescues. Add the best window.

base = sum of customers[i] where grumpy[i] == 0
extra = 0, best = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 1:
  if grumpy[i]: extra = extra + customers[i]
  if i >= minutes and grumpy[i - minutes]: extra = extra - customers[i - minutes]
  best = max(best, extra)
return base + best

cases.note: The best window wraps around the end.

hints.text: If there are m ones, they must end up in some circular window of length m. Every 0 inside that window needs one swap.
Slide a window of length m around the circle (use index mod n) and find the window with the most 1s. The answer is m minus that.

m = count of 1s
if m == 0: return 0
ones = 1s in nums[0 .. m - 1], best = ones
for i in m .. n + m - 1:
  ones = ones + nums[i mod n] - nums[(i - m) mod n]
  best = max(best, ones)
return m - best

cases.note: The longest window sits in the middle.

hints.text: Reworded: find the longest subarray with at most two distinct values.
Grow a window to the right while counting each type. When a third type appears, shrink from the left until only two remain.

for right in 0 .. n - 1:
  count[fruits[right]] += 1
  while count has more than 2 keys:
    count[fruits[left]] -= 1, drop it at 0
    left = left + 1
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

cases.note: No zero to delete, but one element must still go.

hints.text: Deleting one element means the window may hold at most one 0, and you must remove one element even if there are no 0s.
Slide a window that allows at most one zero. Its length minus one is the run you get after deleting.

left = 0, zeros = 0, best = 0
for right in 0 .. n - 1:
  if nums[right] == 0: zeros = zeros + 1
  while zeros > 1:
    if nums[left] == 0: zeros = zeros - 1
    left = left + 1
  best = max(best, right - left)
return best

cases.note: Equal neighbours are never turbulent: the answer is 1.
The run starts at index 1 and reaches the end.

hints.text: Turbulent means the comparison sign flips between every adjacent pair: up, down, up, ...
Track two lengths ending at i: one whose last step went up and one whose last step went down. An up step extends the down-ending run, and vice versa. Equal values reset both.

up = 1, down = 1, best = 1
for i in 1 .. n - 1:
  if arr[i] > arr[i - 1]: up = down + 1, down = 1
  else if arr[i] < arr[i - 1]: down = up + 1, up = 1
  else: up = 1, down = 1
  best = max(best, up, down)
return best

cases.note: k = 0: only existing duplicates count.

hints.text: You can only increase values, so the target should be one of the existing values, and it is cheapest to raise the values just below it.
Sort. For a window ending at r, raising everything to nums[r] costs nums[r] * size - sum. Shrink from the left while that exceeds k.

sort nums
left = 0, sum = 0, best = 0
for right in 0 .. n - 1:
  sum = sum + nums[right]
  while nums[right] * (right - left + 1) - sum > k:
    sum = sum - nums[left], left = left + 1
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

cases.note: The whole array is already good.

hints.text: A window is good while no value appears more than k times. Adding one value can only break it for that value.
Grow right and count values. If the new value's count passes k, move left forward (decrementing counts) until it is back to k.

for right in 0 .. n - 1:
  count[nums[right]] += 1
  while count[nums[right]] > k:
    count[nums[left]] -= 1, left = left + 1
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

cases.note: Distinct powers of two never overlap: the whole array.

hints.text: Nice means no two numbers share a set bit, so the OR of the window is also the sum of its bits with no overlaps.
Keep the OR of the window in a mask. Before adding nums[r], remove numbers from the left (XOR them out) until mask & nums[r] is 0.

for right in 0 .. n - 1:

    used = used XOR nums[left], left = left + 1
  used = used OR nums[right]
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

For each right end, move left as far as possible while the window still has k copies. Every start before left works, so add left.

for right in 0 .. n - 1:
  if nums[right] == mx: seen = seen + 1
  while seen >= k:
    if nums[left] == mx: seen = seen - 1
    left = left + 1
  ans = ans + left
return ans

cases.note: Every subarray has product 1: all 6 count.
A product equal to k does not count.

hints.text: All values are positive, so extending a window only grows its product and shrinking only lowers it.
For each right end, shrink from the left until the product is below k. Then every subarray ending at right and starting in the window counts: right - left + 1 of them.

if k <= 1: return 0
product = 1, left = 0, ans = 0
for right in 0 .. n - 1:

  while product >= k:
    product = product / nums[left], left = left + 1
  ans = ans + right - left + 1
return ans

cases.note: x equals the total: remove everything.

hints.text: Removing from both ends leaves a middle block. Its sum must be total - x.
Find the longest subarray with sum total - x (all values are positive, so a sliding window works). The answer is n minus its length, or -1 if none exists.

need = sum(nums) - x
if need < 0: return -1
left = 0, sum = 0, longest = -1
for right in 0 .. n - 1:
  sum = sum + nums[right]
  while sum > need: sum = sum - nums[left], left = left + 1
  if sum == need: longest = max(longest, right - left + 1)
return -1 if longest == -1 else n - longest

cases.note: Every letter is unique: each is its own part.

hints.text: A part that contains a letter must reach that letter's last occurrence.
Record each letter's last index. Walk the string extending the current part's end to the furthest last index seen; when i reaches that end, close the part.

cases.note: Target far below: the three smallest values.
An exact match exists.

hints.text: Fix one number, then the other two come from a sorted range, which two pointers can scan in linear time.
Sort. For each i, set lo = i + 1 and hi = n - 1. Compare the sum with target: too small moves lo up, too big moves hi down. Keep the sum closest to target.

for i in 0 .. n - 3:
  lo = i + 1, hi = n - 1

    s = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi]

cases.note: Everyone weighs the limit: one person per boat.

hints.text: The heaviest person needs a boat no matter what. The best partner for them is the lightest person, if anyone fits.
Sort. Point at the lightest and heaviest. The heaviest always boards; the lightest joins if the pair fits. Count boats until the pointers cross.

i = 0, j = n - 1, boats = 0
while i <= j:

  j = j - 1
  boats = boats + 1
return boats

cases.note: Touching endpoints intersect in a single point.

hints.text: Two intervals overlap on [max(starts), min(ends)] when that range is not empty.
Walk both lists with one pointer each. Record the overlap of the current pair, then advance whichever interval ends first: it can't overlap anything later.

i = 0, j = 0, out = []
while i < len(A) and j < len(B):
  lo = max(A[i].start, B[j].start)
  hi = min(A[i].end, B[j].end)

cases.note: Every non-empty subsequence counts: 2^16 - 1.

hints.text: Only the minimum and maximum matter, and order doesn't, so sort.

With lo as the minimum and hi the furthest index where nums[lo] + nums[hi] <= target, any subset of the elements between them (with lo included) works: 2^(hi - lo) subsequences. Move two pointers and add powers of two mod 1e9+7.

lo = 0, hi = n - 1, ans = 0
while lo <= hi:

    ans = (ans + pow2[hi - lo]) mod M
    lo = lo + 1
  else: hi = hi - 1
return ans

cases.note: Equal values still need to move past the 3.

hints.text: The right end of the subarray is the last index that is smaller than the maximum seen before it. The left end is the mirror image.
Scan left to right with a running max: any value below it marks a new right end. Scan right to left with a running min: any value above it marks a new left end.

end = -1, hi = -infinity
for i in 0 .. n - 1:
  if nums[i] < hi: end = i
  else: hi = nums[i]

for i in n - 1 down to 0:

  else: lo = nums[i]
return 0 if end == -1 else end - start + 1

cases.note: Only rising, never falling: no mountain.
The whole array is one mountain.

hints.text: A mountain is a strictly rising run followed by a strictly falling run, each at least one step long.
Walk once counting up-steps and down-steps of the current mountain. Reset both on a flat step or when a rise starts after a fall. Whenever both are positive, up + down + 1 is a mountain.

up = 0, down = 0, best = 0
for i in 1 .. n - 1:
  if arr[i] == arr[i - 1] or (down > 0 and arr[i] > arr[i - 1]): up = 0, down = 0
  if arr[i] > arr[i - 1]: up = up + 1
  if arr[i] < arr[i - 1]: down = down + 1

cases.note: Even window: the average of the two middle values.
Adding the two middles can overflow a 32-bit int.

hints.text: Keep the window's values in sorted order so the median is just the middle element (or the average of the two middle ones).
Each step removes one value and adds one. With a sorted array and binary search you can find both positions quickly; two heaps with lazy deletion get it to O(log k).

window = sorted copy of nums[0 .. k - 1]
out = [median(window)]
for i in k .. n - 1:
  remove nums[i - k] from window (binary search)
  insert nums[i] into window (binary search)

return out

cases.note: Repeated words: matches overlap.
The words are longer than s.

hints.text: All words have the same length L, so a match is m consecutive chunks of length L that use each word exactly as often as it appears in words.
For each offset 0 .. L - 1, slide a window over chunks: add the next chunk, and if it is not a word, reset; if it is used too often, drop chunks from the left. A full window of m chunks is a match.
