    if w not in need: clear have, used = 0, left = right + L; continue
    have[w] += 1, used += 1
    while have[w] > need[w]: drop the chunk at left, left += L, used -= 1
    if used == m: record left, drop the chunk at left, left += L, used -= 1
return the recorded starts
Moving the first character to the end any number of times gives every rotation of s. All rotations appear as windows of length n in s + s.
Slide a window of length n over s + s, counting mismatches against "0101..." and against "1010...". The answer is the smallest count over all windows.

cases.note: 0 has no set bits: not a power of two.
Negative numbers are never powers of two.

hints.text: A power of two has exactly one set bit.
n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. For a positive power of two that leaves 0.
return n > 0 and (n AND (n - 1)) == 0

cases.note: A power of two, but not of four.
4^15, the largest power of four in range.

hints.text: Every power of four is a power of two, but not the other way round. Where does the single set bit sit?
Check it's a power of two, then check the bit is in an even position: n & 0x55555555 must be non-zero.
return n > 0 and (n AND (n - 1)) == 0 and (n AND 0x55555555) != 0

cases.note: Every one of the 31 bits differs.

hints.text: The bits where x and y differ are exactly the set bits of x ^ y.
XOR them, then count set bits. n & (n - 1) drops one set bit per step.

z = x XOR y, count = 0
while z != 0:
  z = z AND (z - 1)
  count = count + 1
return count
Each flip fixes one bit where start and goal disagree.
Count the set bits of start ^ goal.

z = start XOR goal, count = 0
while z != 0:
  z = z AND (z - 1)
  count = count + 1
return count

cases.note: The lowest bit becomes the highest: 2^31.
All 32 bits set.

hints.text: Read bits from the right end of n and push them onto the right end of the result, 32 times.
Shift the result left, OR in n & 1, then shift n right (unsigned). In JavaScript finish with >>> 0 so the answer is unsigned.

result = 0
repeat 32 times:
  result = (result << 1) OR (n AND 1)
  n = n unsigned-shift-right 1
return result as unsigned
Sort by a two-part key: the number of set bits first, then the value.
Write a popcount helper and use it in the comparator; break ties with a - b.

bits(x) = number of set bits in x
sort arr by (bits(x), x)
return arr

cases.note: The extra letter already appears in s.

hints.text: Every letter of s appears in t too. Pairs cancel under XOR.
XOR the character codes of both strings together. What's left is the added letter.

x = 0
for c in s + t:
  x = x XOR code(c)
return the character with code x

cases.note: An even count of equal values cancels to 0.

hints.text: XOR undoes itself, so prefix XORs work like prefix sums.
Build pre[i + 1] = pre[i] ^ arr[i]. The XOR of arr[l..r] is pre[r + 1] ^ pre[l].

pre[0] = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 1: pre[i + 1] = pre[i] XOR arr[i]
return [pre[r + 1] XOR pre[l] for each (l, r) in queries]

cases.note: The sign bit matters too.

hints.text: Look at one bit position: summed over the array, it's a multiple of 3 plus the single number's bit.
Either count each of the 32 bits mod 3, or keep two masks (ones, twos) that track which bits have been seen once or twice.

ones = 0, twos = 0
for x in nums:
  ones = (ones XOR x) AND NOT twos
  twos = (twos XOR x) AND NOT ones
return ones

cases.note: a ^ b is -1: the lowest set bit is still bit 0.

hints.text: XOR of everything is a ^ b for the two singles. It's non-zero, so some bit differs between them.
Pick the lowest set bit of a ^ b (x & -x). It splits the array into two groups, each with one single and only pairs otherwise. XOR each group.

x = XOR of all nums
bit = x AND -x
a = 0, b = 0
for v in nums:
  if v AND bit: a = a XOR v
  else: b = b XOR v
return [a, b]

cases.note: The carry ripples through every bit before it disappears.

hints.text: Without + you can still add one bit column at a time: XOR gives the sum bit, AND gives the carry.
Repeat: sum = a ^ b, carry = (a & b) << 1, until the carry is 0. Two's complement handles negatives for free.

while b != 0:
  carry = (a AND b) << 1
  a = a XOR b
  b = carry
return a

cases.note: left == right: the number itself.
A shared high bit survives.

hints.text: Any bit below the highest bit where left and right differ flips somewhere in the range, so it ANDs to 0.
The answer is the common binary prefix of left and right. Shift both right until they're equal, then shift back.

shift = 0
while left != right:
  left = left >> 1
  right = right >> 1
  shift = shift + 1
return left << shift

cases.note: a | b is already c.

hints.text: Bits are independent. For each position, how many flips does it take to make (a | b) match c?
If c's bit is 1, you need one flip only when both a and b are 0. If c's bit is 0, you must clear every 1 among a and b (0, 1 or 2 flips).

cases.note: Primes strictly less than 2: none.

hints.text: Testing each number separately is too slow for large n. Cross out composites instead.
Sieve of Eratosthenes: for every p with p * p < n that is still marked prime, mark p * p, p * p + p, ... as composite. Count what's left below n.
Build the answer greedily from the highest bit: can the answer have this bit set, given the bits chosen so far?

For each bit from 30 down, collect the prefixes of all numbers. Try candidate = answer | bit; it's achievable if some prefix p has p ^ candidate also in the set (a ^ b = c means a ^ c = b). A binary trie works too.

cases.note: Every cookie is too small.

hints.text: Give the least greedy child the smallest cookie that satisfies them; a bigger cookie would be wasted.
Sort both. Walk the cookies with a pointer on the children: when a cookie satisfies the current child, move to the next child.

sort g, sort s
child = 0
for cookie in s:
  if child < len(g) and cookie >= g[child]: child = child + 1
return child

cases.note: No change at all for the first customer.
The second $20 finds only one $5 left.

hints.text: You only ever hold $5 and $10 bills. Track how many of each you have.
For $10 give back a $5. For $20 prefer $10 + $5 (keeps more $5s, which are more useful), else three $5s.

five = 0, ten = 0
for b in bills:
  if b == 5: five += 1
  else if b == 10: if five == 0: return false; five -= 1, ten += 1
  else if ten > 0 and five > 0: ten -= 1, five -= 1
  else if five >= 3: five -= 3
  else: return false
return true

cases.note: The truck fits every box.

hints.text: Every box takes one slot, so a slot is best spent on the box with the most units.
Sort box types by units per box, descending, and take as many as fit from the top.

sort boxTypes by units descending
total = 0
for (count, units) in boxTypes:
  take = min(count, truckSize)
  total = total + take * units
  truckSize = truckSize - take
return total

cases.note: Both prefer A, but one must go to B.

hints.text: Imagine sending everyone to B, then moving n people to A. Moving person i changes the total by a_i - b_i.
Sort by a_i - b_i and send the first half to A, the rest to B.

sort costs by (a - b)
total = 0
for i in 0 .. 2n - 1:
  if i < n: total = total + costs[i].a
  else: total = total + costs[i].b
return total

cases.note: No power and no score: nothing can be played.

hints.text: Buy score with the cheapest tokens, and when you run out of power, sell a point for the most expensive token.
Sort, two pointers. Play the smallest face up while you can; otherwise, if you have a point and tokens remain, play the largest face down. Track the best score seen.

cases.note: Two arrive at minute 2: you only get shots at 0 and 1.

hints.text: What matters is when each monster arrives: ceil(dist / speed) minutes. Shoot the one arriving soonest first.
Sort arrival times. You fire your i-th shot at minute i, so you lose at the first i where arrival[i] <= i.

arrive = sorted [ceil(dist[i] / speed[i])]
for i in 0 .. n - 1:
  if arrive[i] <= i: return i
return n
Any profitable stretch can be split into daily rises. You can collect every one of them.
Add max(0, prices[i] - prices[i - 1]) for every day.

profit = 0
for i in 1 .. n - 1:
  if prices[i] > prices[i - 1]: profit = profit + prices[i] - prices[i - 1]
return profit

cases.note: Already at the last index: 0 jumps.
One jump covers everything.

hints.text: Think in layers: everything reachable with 1 jump, then with 2 jumps, and so on.
Track the end of the current layer and the farthest index reachable from it. When i reaches the layer's end, jump: the new end is the farthest.

jumps = 0, end = 0, far = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 2:
  far = max(far, i + nums[i])
  if i == end:
    jumps = jumps + 1
    end = far
return jumps

cases.note: Only the station with all the gas can start.

hints.text: If total gas < total cost, no start works. Otherwise exactly one does.
Drive from 0 keeping a tank. Whenever it goes negative at i, no start in [start, i] can work, so restart at i + 1 with an empty tank.

if sum(gas) < sum(cost): return -1
start = 0, tank = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 1:
  tank = tank + gas[i] - cost[i]
  if tank < 0: start = i + 1, tank = 0
return start

cases.note: Equal values aren't increasing.
The first value is replaced later and still works.

hints.text: Keep the smallest possible first value and the smallest possible second value seen so far.
For each x: if x <= first, update first; else if x <= second, update second; else x completes a triplet.

first = infinity, second = infinity
for x in nums:
  if x <= first: first = x
  else if x <= second: second = x
  else: return true
return false

cases.note: No rise or fall: length 1.

hints.text: Every peak and valley of the sequence can be kept; points in the middle of a run can't help.
Track up (longest wiggle ending with a rise) and down (ending with a fall). A rise sets up = down + 1, a fall sets down = up + 1.

cases.note: Lowering 4 or raising 2 both break something.
Raise the 1 to 7.

hints.text: Find the first drop nums[i] > nums[i + 1]. A second drop means it's impossible.
At a drop, lower nums[i] to nums[i + 1] if that keeps nums[i - 1] <= nums[i]; otherwise raise nums[i + 1] to nums[i]. Then keep scanning.

changes = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 2:
  if nums[i] > nums[i + 1]:
    changes = changes + 1
    if changes > 1: return false
    if i == 0 or nums[i - 1] <= nums[i + 1]: nums[i] = nums[i + 1]
    else: nums[i + 1] = nums[i]
return true

cases.note: Swap with the last 9, not the first.

hints.text: Swap the leftmost digit that has a larger digit somewhere to its right, with the largest such digit (its last occurrence).
Record the last index of each digit 0-9. For each position from the left, look for a bigger digit (9 down) whose last index is to the right; swap and stop.

cases.note: Only decrements help.
Ten doublings.

hints.text: Work backwards from target: the reverse moves are 'halve' (if even) and 'add 1'.
While target > startValue, halve it if even, else add 1. Then close the remaining gap with startValue - target decrements.

ops = 0
while target > startValue:
  if target is even: target = target / 2
  else: target = target + 1
  ops = ops + 1
return ops + startValue - target

cases.note: The 9 spreads across all three slots.

hints.text: Values can only move left. So the first i + 1 elements can never average below their current average.
The answer is the largest ceil(prefixSum / (i + 1)) over all prefixes: each prefix can be levelled to that, and no lower.

sum = 0, best = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 1:
  sum = sum + nums[i]
  best = max(best, ceil(sum / (i + 1)))
return best
The sum of distances |x - t| is minimised when t is a median.
Sort and pair the smallest with the largest: each pair costs their difference no matter where t sits between them.

sort nums
lo = 0, hi = n - 1, moves = 0
while lo < hi:
  moves = moves + nums[hi] - nums[lo]
  lo = lo + 1, hi = hi - 1
return moves

cases.note: A lone star can be empty.

hints.text: You don't need to decide what each * is. Track the range of possible open-bracket counts.
lo and hi bound the open count: '(' raises both, ')' lowers both, '*' lowers lo and raises hi. If hi < 0 fail; clamp lo at 0. Valid if lo == 0 at the end.

lo = 0, hi = 0
for c in s:
  if c == '(': lo += 1, hi += 1
  else if c == ')': lo -= 1, hi -= 1
  else: lo -= 1, hi += 1
  if hi < 0: return false
  lo = max(lo, 0)
return lo == 0

cases.note: 5 and 6 don't overlap: two intervals.
The new interval swallows everything.

hints.text: The list is sorted and disjoint, so it splits into three parts: entirely before the new interval, overlapping it, entirely after.
Copy intervals that end before it starts. Merge every overlapping one into it (min start, max end). Then copy the rest.

out = [], i = 0, [s, e] = newInterval
while i < n and intervals[i].end < s: append intervals[i], i += 1
while i < n and intervals[i].start <= e:
  s = min(s, intervals[i].start), e = max(e, intervals[i].end), i += 1
append [s, e]
append intervals[i ..]
return out

cases.note: Drop the one long interval, not the two short ones.

hints.text: Removing the fewest is the same as keeping the most. Which interval should you keep first?
Sort by end. Keep an interval when it starts at or after the last kept end; otherwise remove it. Ending early leaves the most room.

sort intervals by end
end = -infinity, removed = 0
for [s, e] in intervals:
  if s >= end: end = e
  else: removed = removed + 1
return removed
Shoot the balloon that ends first at its right edge: that arrow also bursts everything that started before it.
Sort by end. Fire at the first end; skip every balloon whose start is <= that position; fire again at the next unburst balloon's end.

sort points by end
arrows = 0, pos = -infinity
for [s, e] in points:
  if s > pos:
    arrows = arrows + 1
    pos = e
return arrows
This is interval scheduling with strict inequality: pick the pair that ends first.
Sort by right end. Take a pair when its left end is strictly greater than the last taken right end.

sort pairs by right end
cur = -infinity, count = 0
for [a, b] in pairs:
  if a > cur:
    count = count + 1
    cur = b
return count

cases.note: Shared endpoints still count as covered.

hints.text: Sort by start ascending, and for equal starts by end descending, so a covering interval always comes first.
Scan keeping the largest end so far. An interval whose end is <= that end is covered; otherwise it survives and raises the end.

sort by (start ascending, end descending)
maxEnd = -infinity, kept = 0
for [s, e] in intervals:
  if e > maxEnd:
    kept = kept + 1
    maxEnd = e
return kept

cases.note: Drop-off at 5 happens before the pick-up at 5.

hints.text: Passengers board at from and leave at to. Track the change in load at each location.
Add num at from and subtract it at to (a difference array, or sorted events with drop-offs first). Walk the locations; fail if the running load exceeds capacity.

delta = map of location -> change
for (num, from, to) in trips: delta[from] += num, delta[to] -= num
load = 0
for location in sorted keys of delta:
  load = load + delta[location]
  if load > capacity: return false
return true

cases.note: Free days at both ends.

hints.text: Merge the meetings into disjoint blocks; the free days are whatever the blocks don't cover.
Sort by start. Keep the end of the covered area so far; a meeting starting after it leaves a gap of start - end - 1 free days.

cases.note: Nothing covers time 0.

hints.text: This is jump game in disguise: from each covered point, how far can one more clip take you?
Record for every start the farthest end. Walk t from 0, tracking the farthest reach; when t hits the current clip's end, take another clip (fail if the reach didn't grow).

far[s] = max end among clips starting at s
count = 0, end = 0, reach = 0
for t in 0 .. time - 1:
  reach = max(reach, far[t])
  if t == end:
    if reach <= t: return -1
    count = count + 1, end = reach
return count

cases.note: All zeros: "0", not "00".

hints.text: Ordering numbers by value doesn't work (9 should beat 10). Compare a and b by which concatenation is bigger: a + b or b + a.
Sort the strings with that comparator and join. If the result starts with 0, every number was 0: return "0".

strs = nums as strings
sort strs so that a comes before b when a + b > b + a
result = join strs
if result starts with '0': return '0'
return result

cases.note: Equal heights count as 'taller or equal'.

hints.text: Shorter people are invisible to taller ones. Place the tallest first; shorter people inserted later don't change their counts.
Sort by height descending, then k ascending. Insert each person at index k of the result.

sort people by (h descending, k ascending)
queue = []
for [h, k] in people:
  insert [h, k] at position k in queue
return queue

cases.note: Two overlapping straights.

hints.text: The smallest card left must start a group; nothing smaller can contain it.
Count cards. Walk the values in sorted order; for each value with count c > 0, the next groupSize - 1 values must each have at least c cards. Subtract c from all of them.

cases.note: Each coordinate comes from a different triplet.

hints.text: Merging takes the max in each coordinate, so any triplet with a value above the target ruins it. Ignore those.
Among the safe triplets (every value <= target's), check that each of the three target values is matched by at least one of them.

cases.note: Three letters with count 1: two must go.

hints.text: Only the multiset of frequencies matters. Two letters with the same count force a deletion.

Process frequencies from largest to smallest, keeping the highest still-allowed value. Each frequency drops to min(itself, allowed); the drop is the cost, and allowed becomes that value minus 1 (not below 0).

freqs = letter counts sorted descending
allowed = infinity, deletions = 0
for f in freqs:
  keep = min(f, allowed)
  deletions = deletions + f - keep
  allowed = max(keep - 1, 0)
return deletions

cases.note: The last index is '1'.
Exact jumps of 3: 0 -> 3 -> 6.

hints.text: Index i is reachable if s[i] is '0' and some reachable j lies in [i - maxJump, i - minJump].
Keep a running count of reachable indexes inside that sliding window (add i - minJump as it enters, drop i - maxJump - 1 as it leaves).

reach[0] = true, count = 0
for i in 1 .. n - 1:
  if i - minJump >= 0 and reach[i - minJump]: count += 1
  if i - maxJump - 1 >= 0 and reach[i - maxJump - 1]: count -= 1
  reach[i] = (s[i] == '0' and count > 0)
return reach[n - 1]

cases.note: Equal neighbours need no extra candy.

hints.text: Each child has two constraints, one from each neighbour. Handle them separately.
Left-to-right: if rating rises, give one more than the left neighbour. Right-to-left: if rating rises going left, take the max with one more than the right neighbour. Sum.

cases.note: The middle tap covers everything.

hints.text: Tap i covers [i - ranges[i], i + ranges[i]]. You need the fewest intervals covering [0, n]: the video-stitching / jump-game pattern.
For each left end (clamped at 0), store the farthest right end. Then sweep: when you reach the end of the current coverage, open the tap that reaches farthest; fail if coverage stops growing.

far[l] = max right end among taps whose left end is l (clamped to [0, n])
taps = 0, end = 0, reach = 0
for x in 0 .. n - 1:
  reach = max(reach, far[x])
  if x == end:
    if reach <= x: return -1
    taps = taps + 1, end = reach
return taps

cases.note: The stream starts empty.

hints.text: You never need anything smaller than the k largest values seen so far.
Keep a min-heap of at most k values. After each add, pop while it holds more than k; the top is the k-th largest.

constructor(k, nums): heap = empty min-heap; add every x in nums
add(val):
  push val
  if heap size > k: pop
  return heap top

cases.note: Equal stones destroy each other: nothing is left.

hints.text: Every turn needs the two heaviest stones. Which structure hands you the largest value quickly, again and again?
Use a max-heap. Pop two, push their difference if it is not zero, and repeat until at most one stone is left.

heap = max-heap of stones
while heap size > 1:
  y = pop, x = pop
  if y != x: push y - x
return heap top, or 0 if empty

cases.note: k equals the number of points: return them all.

hints.text: Comparing x*x + y*y is enough; the square root never changes the order.
Keep a max-heap of size k keyed by distance. When it grows past k, drop the farthest point. What is left are the k closest.

heap = max-heap by x*x + y*y
for p in points:
  push p
  if heap size > k: pop
return every point in heap

cases.note: Duplicates count separately: the 2nd largest of [2,2,2] is 2.

hints.text: Sorting works in O(n log n). Can you avoid ordering the values you will never return?
Keep a min-heap of the k largest values seen so far; its top is the answer. (Quickselect gets average O(n).)

heap = empty min-heap
for x in nums:
  push x
  if heap size > k: pop
return heap top

cases.note: With n = 0 nothing ever waits.
One task type: idle between every pair.

hints.text: Only the counts matter, and the most frequent task decides how many idle gaps are forced.
With max count m shared by c tasks, the frame (m - 1) * (n + 1) + c is a lower bound. If there are more tasks than that, no idling is needed. (A max-heap simulation also works.)

count each task
m = max count
c = number of tasks with count m
return max(len(tasks), (m - 1) * (n + 1) + c)

cases.note: No tweets yet: an empty feed.
Only the 10 newest tweets make the feed.
Unfollowing someone you never followed does nothing.

hints.text: Stamp every tweet with a global counter. A feed is the 10 newest tweets among you and the people you follow.
Each user's tweets are already in time order. Merge those lists newest-first with a max-heap holding one tweet per user, and stop after 10.

postTweet: append (time, id) to tweets[user]; time += 1
getNewsFeed(u):
  heap = newest tweet of u and of each followee
  while heap not empty and feed has < 10:
    pop newest, add to feed, push that user's previous tweet
follow / unfollow: add / remove in follows[u]

cases.note: Every count ties, so alphabetical order decides.
k is the number of distinct words.

hints.text: Count the words first. The order is: higher count first, and for equal counts the lexicographically smaller word first.
Keep a heap of size k whose top is the worst word kept (lowest count, then the larger word). At the end pop everything and reverse.

count each word
heap = min-heap ordered by (count asc, word desc)
for each distinct word w:
  push w
  if heap size > k: pop
result = pop all, then reverse
return result

cases.note: Three a's cannot be separated.
The most frequent letter is exactly (n + 1) / 2.

hints.text: It is impossible exactly when one letter appears more than (n + 1) / 2 times. Any valid arrangement is accepted.
Greedy with a max-heap by count: place the most frequent letter that differs from the last one placed, then push it back with one less.

if max count > (n + 1) / 2: return ""
heap = max-heap of (count, letter)
out = "", held = none
while heap not empty:
  (c, ch) = pop; out += ch
  if held has count > 0: push held
  held = (c - 1, ch)
return out

cases.note: 7 is not ugly, so the 7th ugly number is 8.

hints.text: Every ugly number after 1 is a smaller ugly number times 2, 3 or 5.
Pop the smallest from a min-heap, push it times 2, 3 and 5, and skip duplicates with a set. The n-th pop is the answer. (Three pointers do it in O(n).)

cases.note: k is every possible pair.

hints.text: Picture a grid where cell (i, j) holds nums1[i] + nums2[j]. Rows and columns are sorted.
Seed a min-heap with (i, 0) for every row. Pop the smallest k times; after popping (i, j), push (i, j + 1).

heap = min-heap of (nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0) for each i
out = []
while heap not empty and len(out) < k:
  (s, i, j) = pop
  out.append([nums1[i], nums2[j]])
  if j + 1 < len(nums2): push (nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1)
return out

cases.note: No bricks and no ladders: stuck at the first climb.
Only downhill: reach the end for free.

hints.text: Ladders are worth the most on the biggest climbs. Decide that lazily as you walk.
Push every climb onto a min-heap. When the heap holds more climbs than ladders, the smallest climb must use bricks: pop it and spend. Stop when bricks go negative.

heap = empty min-heap
for i in 0 .. n - 2:
  d = heights[i + 1] - heights[i]
  if d <= 0: continue
  push d
  if heap size > ladders: bricks = bricks - pop
  if bricks < 0: return i
return n - 1

cases.note: Ties break by index.
The CPU idles until time 10.

hints.text: Sort task indexes by enqueue time and walk them with a pointer as the clock advances.
Push every task that has arrived into a min-heap keyed by (processing time, index). If the heap is empty, jump the clock to the next arrival.

order = indexes sorted by enqueue time
time = 0, p = 0, heap = empty, out = []
while len(out) < n:
  while p < n and enqueue[order[p]] <= time: push (proc, index); p += 1
  if heap empty: time = enqueue[order[p]]; continue
  (d, i) = pop; time = time + d; out.append(i)
return out

cases.note: Freed seats come back smallest first.

hints.text: reserve always wants the smallest free seat number.
Hand out seats from a counter, and keep unreserved seats in a min-heap. reserve takes from the heap if it has anything, else from the counter.

constructor(n): next = 1, heap = empty min-heap
reserve():
  if heap not empty: return pop
  next = next + 1
  return next - 1
unreserve(seat): push seat

cases.note: Equal weights: the smaller index wins.
One server: later tasks queue until it frees up.

hints.text: Two kinds of servers: free ones, wanted by (weight, index), and busy ones, wanted by the time they finish.
Keep two heaps. For task j, move every busy server that is done by time max(j, now) to the free heap; if none are free, jump the clock to the earliest finish.

free = heap of (weight, index), busy = heap of (finish, weight, index)
time = 0
for j in 0 .. m - 1:
  time = max(time, j)
  if free empty: time = max(time, busy top finish)
  move busy servers with finish <= time to free
  (w, i) = pop free; push (time + tasks[j], w, i) to busy
  ans[j] = i
return ans

cases.note: k = n: every index is taken.

hints.text: Fix which index supplies the minimum of nums2. Then you want the k - 1 largest nums1 among indexes with nums2 at least that big.
Sort pairs by nums2 descending. Walk them keeping a min-heap of the k largest nums1 and their sum; when the heap holds k, score = sum * current nums2.

pairs = zip(nums1, nums2) sorted by nums2 descending
heap = min-heap, sum = 0, best = 0
for (a, b) in pairs:
  push a; sum = sum + a
  if heap size > k: sum = sum - pop
  if heap size == k: best = max(best, sum * b)
return best

cases.note: The two windows hold one worker each, at both ends.

hints.text: Each round looks only at the first and last `candidates` workers still waiting.
Keep one min-heap for the front window and one for the back window, filled from two pointers that never cross. Take the cheaper top (front wins ties) and refill that side.

lo = 0, hi = n - 1, front = heap, back = heap
fill front from lo and back from hi, candidates each, while lo <= hi
repeat k times:
  if back empty or (front not empty and front top <= back top): take front top, refill front from lo
  else: take back top, refill back from hi
  total = total + taken cost
return total

cases.note: Adding 1 back twice puts it in the set only once.
3 was never removed, so adding it back changes nothing.

hints.text: Everything from some number `next` upward is still in the set. Only numbers below `next` that were added back need tracking.
Keep `next` plus a min-heap (and a set, to skip duplicates) of added-back numbers smaller than `next`.

next = 1, heap = empty, inHeap = empty set
popSmallest():
  if heap not empty: x = pop; remove x from inHeap; return x
  next = next + 1
  return next - 1
addBack(num):
  if num < next and num not in inHeap: push num; add to inHeap

cases.note: Too big for a number type: compare as strings.
Equal values count separately.

hints.text: The numbers can be too long for a double. Without leading zeros, a longer string is a bigger number, and equal lengths compare as strings.
Keep a min-heap of size k using that comparison; its top is the answer.

smaller(a, b) = len(a) < len(b) or (len(a) == len(b) and a < b)
heap = min-heap using smaller
for x in nums:
  push x
  if heap size > k: pop
return heap top

cases.note: Only one letter: at most two in a row.

hints.text: Always try to place the letter with the most copies left, unless that would make three in a row. Any longest happy string is accepted.
Use a max-heap by remaining count. If the top letter would make a triple, place the second one instead and push both back.
Split the numbers into a smaller half and a larger half. The median sits at the boundary.
Keep a max-heap for the low half and a min-heap for the high half, balanced so low has the same size or one more. The median is low's top, or the average of both tops.

addNum(x):
  push x to low (max-heap)
  move low top to high (min-heap)
  if high size > low size: move high top to low
findMedian():
  if low size > high size: return low top
  return (low top + high top) / 2

cases.note: Both rooms host one meeting: the lower number wins.
Meetings arrive unsorted.

hints.text: Process meetings by start time. A meeting takes the lowest-numbered free room; if none is free, it waits for the room that frees up first and keeps its length.
Keep a min-heap of free room numbers and a min-heap of (end time, room) for busy rooms. Before each meeting, release every room whose end <= start.

sort meetings by start
free = heap of 0 .. n - 1, busy = heap of (end, room)
for (s, e) in meetings:
  release busy rooms with end <= s into free
  if free not empty: r = pop free; push (e, r) to busy
  else: (end, r) = pop busy; push (end + e - s, r) to busy
  count[r] += 1
return the room with the highest count (lowest index on ties)

cases.note: Nothing is affordable at the start.
k is larger than the number of projects.

hints.text: Capital only grows, so once a project is affordable it stays affordable. Each round take the most profitable affordable project.
Sort projects by capital. Each round, push every newly affordable project's profit into a max-heap, then pop the best. Stop early if the heap is empty.

projects sorted by capital, p = 0, heap = max-heap
repeat k times:
  while p < n and capital of project p <= w: push its profit; p += 1
  if heap empty: stop
  w = w + pop
return w

cases.note: Two identical buildings draw one outline.
A tall narrow building inside a wide one.

hints.text: The outline only changes at a building's left or right edge. At each such x, the height is the tallest building covering x.
Sweep the edges left to right. A max-heap of (height, right) holds active buildings; drop tops whose right <= x. Emit [x, height] when the max height changes.

xs = sorted distinct lefts and rights
heap = max-heap of (height, right), i = 0, out = []
for x in xs:
  while i < n and left[i] <= x: push (height[i], right[i]); i += 1
  while heap not empty and heap top right <= x: pop
  h = heap top height, or 0
  if out empty or out last height != h: out.append([x, h])
return out

cases.note: Taking everyone is best when nobody lowers the efficiency.

hints.text: Fix the engineer with the lowest efficiency on the team. Everyone else must be at least as efficient, and you want their k - 1 largest speeds.
Sort by efficiency descending. Keep a min-heap of at most k speeds with their sum; at each engineer, performance = sum * their efficiency. Take the answer modulo 1e9+7 at the end.

sort engineers by efficiency descending
heap = min-heap, sum = 0, best = 0
for (s, e) in engineers:
  push s; sum = sum + s
  if heap size > k: sum = sum - pop
  best = max(best, sum * e)
return best mod 1000000007
A range covering one value from every list is [min, max] of one chosen element per list. To shrink it, the only useful move is to advance the list holding the minimum.
Put the first element of each list in a min-heap and track the current max. Pop the min, record [min, max] if it is better, then push that list's next element. Stop when a list runs out.

heap = (nums[i][0], i, 0) for each list, hi = max of those
best = none
loop:
  (lo, i, j) = pop
  if best is none or hi - lo < best width: best = [lo, hi]
  if j + 1 == len(nums[i]): return best
  push (nums[i][j + 1], i, j + 1); hi = max(hi, nums[i][j + 1])

cases.note: No stations, but the tank is exactly enough.
The first station is out of reach.
Arrive at the station with an empty tank: that still counts.

hints.text: Drive as far as you can. When you run dry, you could have stopped at any station you already passed; pretend you did, at the one with the most fuel.
Push each passed station's fuel into a max-heap. While the tank cannot reach the next point, pop the largest and count a stop; if the heap is empty, return -1.

heap = max-heap, reach = startFuel, stops = 0
for (pos, fuel) in stations + [(target, 0)]:
  while reach < pos:
    if heap empty: return -1
    reach = reach + pop; stops += 1
  push fuel
return stops

cases.note: A huge even number halves many times.

hints.text: Odd numbers can only double once; even numbers can only halve. Double every odd number first, so every value can only go down from there.
Now the only useful move is to halve the current maximum while it is even. Keep a max-heap and the current minimum; record max - min after each step.

for each x: if x is odd: x = 2x
heap = max-heap of nums, lo = min(nums), best = infinity
loop:
  hi = pop
  best = min(best, hi - lo)
  if hi is odd: return best
  lo = min(lo, hi / 2); push hi / 2

cases.note: Every cell is on the border: nothing is trapped.
The wall has a low point at 1, so the pit only fills to 1.

hints.text: Water escapes through the lowest point of the wall around it. Start with the border as the wall and always work from its lowest cell inward.
Push every border cell into a min-heap. Pop the lowest; for each unvisited neighbour, it holds max(0, wall - height) water, and enters the heap with height max(wall, its height).

heap = min-heap of border cells (height, r, c); mark them visited
water = 0
while heap not empty:
  (h, r, c) = pop
  for each unvisited neighbour (nr, nc):
    mark visited
    water = water + max(0, h - height[nr][nc])
    push (max(h, height[nr][nc]), nr, nc)
return water

cases.note: Every node has only a left child.

hints.text: The inorder (left, node, right) order is a three-line recursion. Try writing it, then try it without recursion.
Iteratively: walk left pushing every node; pop one, record it, then move to its right child and repeat.

stack = [], cur = root
while cur or stack not empty:
  while cur: push cur; cur = cur.left
  cur = pop
  out.append(cur.val)
  cur = cur.right
return out

cases.note: Every node has only a left child.

hints.text: The preorder (node, left, right) order is a three-line recursion. Try writing it, then try it without recursion.
Iteratively: pop a node from a stack, record it, push its right child and then its left child so the left comes out first.

stack = [root] if root
while stack not empty:
  node = pop
  out.append(node.val)
  push node.right if present
  push node.left if present
return out

cases.note: Every node has only a left child.

hints.text: The postorder (left, right, node) order is a three-line recursion. Try writing it, then try it without recursion.
Iteratively: run a node-right-left preorder with a stack and reverse the result.

stack = [root] if root
while stack not empty:
  node = pop
  out.append(node.val)
  push node.left if present
  push node.right if present
return reversed(out)

cases.note: An empty tree is balanced.
The root's subtrees differ by exactly 2.

hints.text: A tree is balanced when, at every node, the two subtree heights differ by at most 1.
Computing heights separately at every node is O(n^2). Return the height bottom-up instead, and use -1 to mean 'already unbalanced' so the check stops early.

height(node):
  if node is empty: return 0
  l = height(node.left); r = height(node.right)
  if l == -1 or r == -1 or |l - r| > 1: return -1
  return 1 + max(l, r)
return height(root) != -1

cases.note: The root has one child, so it is not a leaf.

hints.text: Minimum depth counts nodes down to the nearest leaf. A node with one child is not a leaf, so min(left, right) is wrong there.
BFS level by level and return the depth of the first leaf you meet; or recurse and, when one child is missing, use the other side only.

if root is empty: return 0
queue = [(root, 1)]
while queue not empty:
  (node, d) = dequeue
  if node has no children: return d
  enqueue (child, d + 1) for each child

cases.note: The match is the leaf, not the root.
Node 2 exists but has no child 3.

hints.text: A subtree is a node plus all of its descendants. So the question is: is there a node in root where the two trees are identical?
Write sameTree(a, b), then try it at every node of root.

same(a, b):
  if both empty: return true
  if one empty or a.val != b.val: return false
  return same(a.left, b.left) and same(a.right, b.right)
isSubtree(node, sub):
  if node is empty: return false
  return same(node, sub) or isSubtree(node.left, sub) or isSubtree(node.right, sub)
You need the sum and the count of every level.
BFS one level at a time: the queue length at the start of a level is its count. Divide the level sum by it.

queue = [root], out = []
while queue not empty:
  size = len(queue), total = 0
  repeat size times:
    node = dequeue; total = total + node.val
    enqueue node's children
  out.append(total / size)
return out

cases.note: Two different paths that read the same.

hints.text: Carry the path so far down the recursion; a leaf turns it into an answer. Any order is accepted.
DFS with a path string: at each node append its value; at a leaf push the string; otherwise recurse with path + '->'.

out = []
dfs(node, path):
  path = path + str(node.val)
  if node is a leaf: out.append(path); return
  if node.left: dfs(node.left, path + "->")
  if node.right: dfs(node.right, path + "->")
dfs(root, "")
return out

cases.note: A right leaf does not count.

hints.text: A left leaf is a leaf that is the left child of its parent. The parent is where you can tell.
Recurse with a flag saying whether the node is a left child; add its value when it is a leaf and the flag is set.

cases.note: Different inner nodes, same leaves.

hints.text: Only the leaves, read left to right, matter.
Collect each tree's leaf sequence with a DFS that visits left before right, then compare the two lists.

cases.note: One tree is empty: the answer is the other tree.

hints.text: Walk both trees together. Where both have a node, add the values; where only one has a node, that whole subtree is reused as is.
Recurse: if either is empty return the other; otherwise add root2's value into root1 and merge the children pairwise.

merge(a, b):
  if a is empty: return b
  if b is empty: return a
  a.val = a.val + b.val
  a.left = merge(a.left, b.left)
  a.right = merge(a.right, b.right)
  return a

cases.note: Same depth, same parent: siblings, not cousins.

hints.text: Cousins sit at the same depth but have different parents. Find the depth and parent of x and of y.
One DFS (or BFS) records (depth, parent) for both values; compare.

find(node, parent, depth):
  if node is empty: return
  if node.val == x: dx, px = depth, parent
  if node.val == y: dy, py = depth, parent
  find(node.left, node, depth + 1)
  find(node.right, node, depth + 1)
return dx == dy and px != py

cases.note: Equal values count as good.

hints.text: A node is good when nothing on the path from the root to it is bigger. You only need the maximum seen so far on the way down.
DFS passing the running maximum; count the node if its value is at least that maximum.

cases.note: Inorder equals preorder: every node has only a right child.

hints.text: preorder[0] is the root. Its position in inorder splits the remaining values into the left and right subtrees.
Map each value to its inorder index. Recurse on an inorder range, taking roots from preorder with a moving pointer: build left before right.

pos = map value -> index in inorder; p = 0
build(lo, hi):
  if lo > hi: return empty
  root = node(preorder[p]); p += 1
  m = pos[root.val]
  root.left = build(lo, m - 1)
  root.right = build(m + 1, hi)
  return root
return build(0, n - 1)

cases.note: Every node has only a right child.

hints.text: The last value of postorder is the root, and its inorder position splits left from right.
Walk postorder from the end with a pointer. Because postorder ends ...left, right, root, build the right subtree before the left.

pos = map value -> index in inorder; p = n - 1
build(lo, hi):
  if lo > hi: return empty
  root = node(postorder[p]); p -= 1
  m = pos[root.val]
  root.right = build(m + 1, hi)
  root.left = build(lo, m - 1)
  return root
return build(0, n - 1)

cases.note: p is the root itself.
Both nodes are deep in the left subtree.

hints.text: p and q are nodes of the tree. The answer is the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree (a node counts as its own descendant).
Recurse: return the node itself if it is p or q; otherwise ask both children. If both sides found something, this node is the answer; else pass up whichever side did.

lca(node):
  if node is empty or node == p or node == q: return node
  l = lca(node.left)
  r = lca(node.right)
  if l and r: return node
  return l if l else r
It is the usual level order, just listed from the bottom level up.
BFS level by level collecting each level's values, then reverse the list of levels.

cases.note: Level 2 is read right to left, level 3 left to right.

hints.text: Level order, but every other level is read right to left.
BFS by level as usual, and reverse the values of odd-numbered levels (or insert at the front) before adding them.

levels = [], queue = [root] if root, depth = 0
while queue not empty:
  level = values in queue
  if depth is odd: reverse level
  levels.append(level)
  queue = children, left to right
  depth += 1
return levels

cases.note: Two different paths with the same values.

hints.text: Like Path Sum, but you must return every root-to-leaf path with the target sum, so carry the path itself. Any order of paths is accepted.
Backtracking DFS: push the node, recurse with the remaining sum, pop on the way back. At a leaf with remaining 0, save a copy of the path.

out = [], path = []
dfs(node, left):
  if node is empty: return
  path.append(node.val); left = left - node.val
  if node is a leaf and left == 0: out.append(copy of path)
  dfs(node.left, left); dfs(node.right, left)
  path.pop()
dfs(root, targetSum)
return out

cases.note: Every single node and both two-node paths sum to 0.

hints.text: A path can start and end anywhere, as long as it goes downward. That is a subarray-sum question on every root-to-node path.
DFS carrying the running prefix sum and a map of prefix sums seen on the current path. Paths ending here = count[sum - target]. Undo the map entry when you return.

count = {0: 1}
dfs(node, sum):
  if node is empty: return 0
  sum = sum + node.val
  found = count[sum - targetSum]
  count[sum] += 1
  found = found + dfs(node.left, sum) + dfs(node.right, sum)
  count[sum] -= 1
  return found
return dfs(root, 0)

cases.note: Leading digit 1, trailing zeros: 10 + 10.

hints.text: Each root-to-leaf path spells a number. Going down one level multiplies the number so far by 10 and adds the digit.
DFS carrying the number built so far; at a leaf return it, otherwise return the sum of both children.

cases.note: A left chain becomes a right chain.
Already flat: nothing moves.

hints.text: The result is the preorder sequence, linked through right pointers, with every left pointer null. Change the tree in place.
For each node with a left subtree: find the rightmost node of that left subtree, hang the node's right subtree there, move left to right, and set left to null. Then step right.

cur = root
while cur:
  if cur.left:
    tail = cur.left
    while tail.right: tail = tail.right
    tail.right = cur.right
    cur.right = cur.left
    cur.left = empty
  cur = cur.right

cases.note: The deepest node is a right child.
The last level has only one node, on the far right.

hints.text: You want the first node of the last level.
BFS that enqueues the right child before the left: the very last node dequeued is the bottom-left one.

queue = [root]
while queue not empty:
  node = dequeue
  enqueue node.right if present
  enqueue node.left if present
return node.val

cases.note: k = 0 is the target itself.
The target is the root.
The answer is up the chain.

hints.text: Distance can go up through parents as well as down. Once you can move to a parent, the tree is just an undirected graph.
Record every node's parent with one DFS, then BFS from target over left, right and parent, k steps, never revisiting. Any order is accepted.

cases.note: One node per level: width 1.
The gap between 4 and 5 counts.

hints.text: Number the nodes like a heap: the root is 0, the children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. A level's width is last index - first index + 1, gaps included.
BFS by level with these indexes. Subtract the level's first index from every index so the numbers stay small on deep trees.

queue = [(root, 0)], best = 0
while queue not empty:
  first = index of queue[0]
  best = max(best, index of last - first + 1)
  next = []
  for (node, i) in queue:
    i = i - first
    add (node.left, 2i + 1) and (node.right, 2i + 2) when present
  queue = next
return best

cases.note: A perfect tree: no recursion needed.

hints.text: Counting every node is O(n). In a complete tree, if the leftmost and rightmost depths match, the tree is perfect and has 2^h - 1 nodes.
Otherwise recurse into both children; one of them is always perfect, so the work is O(log^2 n).

count(node):
  if node is empty: return 0
  l = depth following left pointers
  r = depth following right pointers
  if l == r: return 2^l - 1
  return 1 + count(node.left) + count(node.right)

cases.note: Rob 4 and 3, two apart.

hints.text: You cannot rob a node and its parent together. For each node you want two numbers: the best with it robbed and the best with it skipped.
Return the pair from a post-order DFS: robbed = val + skipped(left) + skipped(right); skipped = best(left) + best(right).

cases.note: Increasing input: a left-leaning chain.

hints.text: The maximum is the root; everything left of it builds the left subtree, everything right of it the right subtree.
Recursion is O(n^2) on sorted input. A decreasing stack builds it in O(n): each new value adopts the last popped smaller node as its left child and becomes the right child of the stack top.

stack = []
for x in nums:
  node = new node(x), last = empty
  while stack not empty and top.val < x: last = pop
  node.left = last
  if stack not empty: top.right = node
  push node
return stack[0]

cases.note: Start at a leaf: the infection climbs first.

hints.text: Infection spreads to parents as well as children each minute. The answer is the farthest any node is from start.
Treat the tree as an undirected graph (record parents), then BFS from the start node and count the levels.

parent = map from one DFS; startNode = node with value start
queue = [startNode], seen = {startNode}, minutes = -1
while queue not empty:
  minutes += 1
  next = unseen neighbours (left, right, parent) of every node in queue
  mark them seen; queue = next
return minutes

cases.note: Levels 1 and 2 tie: the smaller level wins.

hints.text: Levels are numbered from 1. Sum each level and return the level with the largest sum (the smallest level on a tie).
BFS by level keeping the best sum and its level; only replace on a strictly larger sum.

queue = [root], level = 0, best = -infinity, ans = 1
while queue not empty:
  level += 1
  s = sum of values in queue
  if s > best: best = s, ans = level
  queue = children of queue
return ans

cases.note: Two left steps in a row do not zigzag.
Left, right, left: length 3.

hints.text: A zigzag alternates left and right. When you step left, the path continues only if the next step goes right.
DFS passing two lengths: the zigzag arriving here by a left step and by a right step. Going left extends the 'arrived by right' length; going right extends the 'arrived by left' length.

best = 0
dfs(node, viaLeft, viaRight):
  if node is empty: return
  best = max(best, viaLeft, viaRight)
  dfs(node.left, viaRight + 1, 0)
  dfs(node.right, 0, viaLeft + 1)
dfs(root, 0, 0)
return best

cases.note: A right child with no left sibling.
A new level started on the left: still complete.

hints.text: In a complete tree, a level-order walk never meets a real node after it has met a missing one.
BFS that also enqueues missing children. Once you dequeue an empty slot, every later slot must be empty too.

queue = [root], seenGap = false
while queue not empty:
  node = dequeue
  if node is empty: seenGap = true
  else:
    if seenGap: return false
    enqueue node.left, node.right (even if empty)
return true

cases.note: Every node already has one coin.

hints.text: Look at one edge: the coins that must cross it equal |coins in the subtree below - nodes in that subtree|.
Post-order DFS returning each subtree's excess (coins - nodes). Add |excess| of each child to the move count.

moves = 0
excess(node):
  if node is empty: return 0
  l = excess(node.left); r = excess(node.right)
  moves = moves + |l| + |r|
  return node.val + l + r - 1
excess(root)
return moves

cases.note: The greedy smaller child leads to a larger string.

hints.text: Values 0..25 are letters a..z, and each string is read from a leaf up to the root. Choosing the smaller child greedily fails, because a shorter string can win only at the very end.
DFS building the root-to-node string; at a leaf reverse it and keep the smallest. Compare complete strings only.

best = none
dfs(node, path):
  if node is empty: return
  path = letter(node.val) + path
  if node is a leaf: best = min(best, path)
  dfs(node.left, path); dfs(node.right, path)
dfs(root, "")
return best

cases.note: Two different digits cannot form a palindrome.

hints.text: Digits can be rearranged into a palindrome when at most one digit appears an odd number of times.
Carry a bitmask of digit parities down the path (toggle bit val). At a leaf the path counts if mask has at most one bit set: mask & (mask - 1) == 0.

cases.note: The best pair is the root and the deepest node.

hints.text: For a node, the best ancestor partner is the smallest or the largest value on its root path.
DFS carrying the min and max seen on the path; at each node compare against both, then update them for the children.

cases.note: A single negative node is still a path.
Every value is negative: take the largest one alone.

hints.text: Every path has one highest node where it bends. Through that node the best path is val + best downward gain on the left + on the right, ignoring negative gains.
Post-order DFS returning the best downward gain (val + max(0, left, right)) while updating a global best with val + max(0, left) + max(0, right).

best = -infinity
gain(node):
  if node is empty: return 0
  l = max(0, gain(node.left)); r = max(0, gain(node.right))
  best = max(best, node.val + l + r)
  return node.val + max(l, r)
gain(root)
return best

cases.note: Multi-digit and negative values.

hints.text: Any format works as long as deserialize(serialize(tree)) rebuilds the same tree. Mark empty children explicitly so the shape is not lost.
Preorder with a '#' for every empty child, joined by commas. To decode, read tokens with a pointer: '#' is empty; otherwise make a node and decode its left then right.

serialize(node):
  if node is empty: return "#"
  return node.val + "," + serialize(node.left) + "," + serialize(node.right)

  build():
    t = tokens[i]; i += 1
    if t == "#": return empty
    node = new node(t); node.left = build(); node.right = build()
    return node

cases.note: Same column and row: smaller value first.

hints.text: Give every node a (column, row): left child is (col - 1, row + 1), right child (col + 1, row + 1). Columns go left to right; inside a column, top to bottom, and equal positions by value.
Collect (col, row, val) for every node, sort by col, then row, then val, and group by column.

items = []
dfs(node, row, col): add (col, row, node.val); recurse into children
dfs(root, 0, 0)
sort items by (col, row, val)
group consecutive items with the same col
return the groups' values

cases.note: One node needs its own camera.
Cameras on both middle nodes cover everything.

hints.text: A camera watches its parent, itself and its children. Putting cameras on leaves wastes them; put them on leaves' parents instead.

cams = 0
state(node):

  l = state(node.left); r = state(node.right)
  if l == 0 or r == 0: cams += 1; return 1
  if l == 1 or r == 1: return 2
  return 0
if state(root) == 0: cams += 1
return cams

cases.note: Not in the tree: return null (an empty tree).
The root itself matches.

hints.text: In a BST everything smaller is on the left and everything larger on the right, so one comparison tells you which half to drop.
Walk down from the root: go left when val is smaller, right when larger, and return the node when it matches (or null when you fall off).

node = root
while node and node.val != val:
  node = node.left if val < node.val else node.right
return node

cases.note: Seven values: a perfect tree.

hints.text: The middle element as root splits the rest into two halves of nearly equal size, which keeps the tree balanced.
Recurse on index ranges: root = middle, left = build(left half), right = build(right half). Either middle works when the length is even; any height-balanced BST is accepted.

build(lo, hi):

  mid = (lo + hi) // 2

  node.left = build(lo, mid - 1)
  node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)

return build(0, n - 1)

cases.note: The closest pair is the root and a grandchild.

hints.text: An inorder walk of a BST visits values in sorted order, and the closest pair in a sorted list is always adjacent.

inorder(node):
  if node is empty: return
  inorder(node.left)
  if prev is set: best = min(best, node.val - prev)
  prev = node.val
  inorder(node.right)
inorder(root)
return best

stack = [], cur = root, prev = none, best = infinity
while cur or stack not empty:

  cur = pop
  if prev is set: best = min(best, cur.val - prev)
  prev = cur.val
  cur = cur.right

cases.note: One node cannot pair with itself.

hints.text: Two different nodes must add up to k. Classic Two Sum, but the numbers live in a tree.
DFS with a set of values seen so far: if k - val is in the set, done. (Or take the sorted inorder list and use two pointers.)

seen = empty set
dfs(node):

  if k - node.val in seen: return true
  add node.val to seen
  return dfs(node.left) or dfs(node.right)

cases.note: The answer is p's parent, not the root.
q is given before p in value order.

hints.text: In a BST, if both values are smaller than the node, the answer is on the left; if both are larger, on the right.
Walk down from the root. The first node whose value lies between p and q (inclusive) is where their paths split: that is the LCA.

node = root
loop:
  if p.val < node.val and q.val < node.val: node = node.left
  else if p.val > node.val and q.val > node.val: node = node.right
  else: return node

cases.note: An empty tree becomes a single node.
Smaller than everything: goes to the far left.

hints.text: val is not in the tree yet. Walk down as if searching for it; the empty spot you reach is a valid place for the new node. Any valid BST is accepted.
Iterate: at each node go left if val is smaller, right if larger, and attach a new node at the first missing child. An empty tree becomes just the new node.

cases.note: Deleting the only node leaves an empty tree.
Delete the root, which has two children.

hints.text: Find the node first. A leaf just disappears and a node with one child is replaced by that child. Any valid BST is accepted.
With two children, copy in the smallest value of the right subtree (the inorder successor), then delete that value from the right subtree.

delete(node, key):
  if node is empty: return empty
  if key < node.val: node.left = delete(node.left, key)
  else if key > node.val: node.right = delete(node.right, key)
  else:
    if node.left is empty: return node.right
    if node.right is empty: return node.left
    s = leftmost node of node.right
    node.val = s.val
    node.right = delete(node.right, s.val)
  return node

cases.note: A left chain: the stack starts full.
hasNext never advances.

hints.text: next() returns values in sorted order, which is an inorder traversal paused between calls.
Keep a stack of the left spine. next() pops a node, then pushes the left spine of its right child. Each node is pushed once, so next() is O(1) on average and memory is O(height).

constructor(root): stack = []; pushLeft(root)
pushLeft(node): while node: push node; node = node.left
next():
  node = pop
  pushLeft(node.right)
  return node.val
hasNext(): return stack not empty

cases.note: Two nodes swapped with each other.
The two swapped nodes are siblings.

hints.text: Exactly two values were swapped, so the inorder sequence is sorted except for one or two places where a value is bigger than the next.
Walk inorder with a prev pointer. At the first drop, first = prev; at every drop, second = current. Swap the values of first and second at the end.

first = second = prev = none
inorder(node):
  if node is empty: return
  inorder(node.left)
  if prev and prev.val > node.val:
    if first is none: first = prev
    second = node
  prev = node
  inorder(node.right)
inorder(root)
swap first.val and second.val
Pick the root i. The values below it form the left subtree and the values above it the right, independently.
Let g[k] be the number of BSTs on k values. g[k] = sum over the root position of g[left size] * g[right size], with g[0] = g[1] = 1 (the Catalan numbers).

cases.note: 14 trees.
42 trees.

hints.text: Every value can be the root; then every left subtree from the smaller values pairs with every right subtree from the larger ones. Any order of trees is accepted.
Recurse on a value range [lo, hi]: an empty range gives [null]. For each root, combine every left tree with every right tree.

cases.note: Everything is out of range.
The range covers every value: nothing changes.

hints.text: If a node is below low, it and its whole left subtree are gone, but its right subtree may still have keepers. Symmetrically above high.
Recurse: too small means return trim(right); too big means return trim(left); otherwise trim both children and keep the node.

trim(node):
  if node is empty: return empty
  if node.val < low: return trim(node.right)
  if node.val > high: return trim(node.left)

  node.right = trim(node.right)

cases.note: Decreasing preorder: a left chain.
Increasing preorder: a right chain.

hints.text: Inserting the values one by one works in O(n^2). Can you place each value with an upper bound instead?
Recurse with a bound: build a node from the next value only if it is below the bound; its left subtree gets the node's value as bound, its right subtree inherits the parent's bound.

i = 0
build(bound):
  if i == n or preorder[i] > bound: return empty
  node = new node(preorder[i]); i += 1
  node.left = build(node.val)
  node.right = build(bound)
  return node
return build(infinity)
Each node becomes itself plus every larger value. Visiting nodes from largest to smallest lets you keep a running sum.
Reverse inorder (right, node, left) with a running total; add the node's value to the total and write the total back.

total = 0
visit(node):
  if node is empty: return
  visit(node.right)
  total = total + node.val
  node.val = total
  visit(node.left)
visit(root)
return root

cases.note: Touching end and start do not overlap.
The third booking overlaps both neighbours.

hints.text: Two half-open intervals [s1, e1) and [s2, e2) overlap exactly when s1 < e2 and s2 < e1.
Keep the booked intervals sorted by start. Binary search for the insert position and check only the neighbours on each side (a balanced BST or sorted map does this in O(log n)).

book(s, e):
  i = first position whose start >= s
  if i > 0 and booked[i - 1].end > s: return false
  if i < len(booked) and booked[i].start < e: return false
  insert (s, e) at i

cases.note: Every BST has a negative sum: the empty BST (0) wins.
Equal values break the BST rule.

hints.text: A subtree is a BST when both children are BSTs and the node is above the left maximum and below the right minimum. The empty BST counts, so the answer is at least 0.
Post-order DFS returning (isBST, min, max, sum) for each subtree; when it is a BST, update the best sum.

cases.note: Increasing: nothing smaller to the right.
Only strictly smaller values count.

hints.text: For each value you need how many values to its right are strictly smaller. Scanning from the right, that is a rank query on everything seen so far.
Scan from the right inserting into a sorted structure (a BST with subtree sizes, a Fenwick tree over ranks, or merge sort counting how many right-half items jump ahead).

ranks = compress values to 1..m
fenwick = empty tree of size m
for i from n - 1 down to 0:
  ans[i] = fenwick.sum(rank[i] - 1)
  fenwick.add(rank[i], 1)
return ans

cases.note: Source and destination are the same node.
Edges work in both directions.

hints.text: Build an adjacency list from the undirected edges, then ask whether source can reach destination.
BFS or DFS from source with a visited array; stop as soon as you reach destination. (Union-find also works: same root means connected.)

adj = adjacency list from edges (both directions)
seen = {source}; queue = [source]
while queue not empty:
  u = pop front
  if u == destination: return true
  for v in adj[u]:
    if v not in seen: add v to seen; push v
return false

cases.note: Alone in town: person 1 is the judge.

hints.text: The judge is trusted by everyone else (n - 1 people) and trusts nobody.
Keep a score per person: +1 when trusted, -1 when trusting. The judge is the one whose score is exactly n - 1.

score = array of n + 1 zeros
for (a, b) in trust:
  score[a] -= 1
  score[b] += 1
for p in 1 .. n:
  if score[p] == n - 1: return p
return -1

cases.note: The new colour equals the old one: nothing changes.
Diagonal pixels are not connected.

hints.text: Repaint the start pixel and every pixel of the same original colour connected to it up, down, left or right.
DFS from (sr, sc) repainting as you go. If the new colour equals the old one, return immediately, or the search never ends.

old = image[sr][sc]
if old == color: return image
fill(r, c):

  image[r][c] = color
  fill each of the 4 neighbours
fill(sr, sc)
return image

cases.note: A solid block.
A strip touching the grid edges.

hints.text: Each land cell has 4 sides. A side counts toward the perimeter unless another land cell is on the other side.
Count land cells and shared edges (look only right and down so each pair is counted once). Perimeter = 4 * land - 2 * shared.

land = 0; shared = 0
for each cell (r, c) with grid[r][c] == 1:
  land += 1
  if the cell below is land: shared += 1
  if the cell to the right is land: shared += 1
return 4 * land - 2 * shared

cases.note: Connected only through a chain.

hints.text: A province is a connected component in a graph given as an adjacency matrix.
Loop over cities; each unvisited city starts a new DFS that marks its whole component. Count how many DFS starts you made.

count = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 1:

return count

hints.text: Room 0 is open. A key is an edge from the room it lies in to the room it opens. Can you reach every room?
DFS (or BFS) from room 0, collecting keys; at the end, check that every room was visited.

cases.note: Diagonal neighbours are separate islands.

hints.text: An island is a group of '1' cells connected up, down, left or right. Count the groups.

for each cell (r, c):

sink(r, c):

  grid[r][c] = '0'

return count

cases.note: Diagonal cells are separate islands.

hints.text: Same as counting islands, but measure each island's size and keep the largest.

for each cell (r, c) with grid[r][c] == 1:

area(r, c):

  grid[r][c] = 0

return best

Connected to the top edge: survives.

hints.text: An 'O' survives only if it is connected to an 'O' on the border. Finding the survivors is easier than finding the captured ones.
DFS from every border 'O', marking it safe (say '#'). Then flip every remaining 'O' to 'X' and every '#' back to 'O'.

for each border cell with board[r][c] == 'O': mark(r, c)
mark(r, c):
  if (r, c) is outside or board[r][c] != 'O': return
  board[r][c] = '#'

hints.text: A land cell is an enclave when you cannot walk off the grid from it. Land connected to the border is the opposite.

for each border cell with grid[r][c] == 1: sink(r, c)
sink(r, c):

  grid[r][c] = 0

All water.

hints.text: Careful: here 0 is land and 1 is water. A closed island is land surrounded by water on all four sides, so it cannot touch the border.

for each border cell with grid[r][c] == 0: sink(r, c)
sink(r, c):

  grid[r][c] = 1

One row touches both oceans.

hints.text: Checking every cell's downhill paths is slow. Turn it around: start from each ocean and walk uphill. Any order of cells is accepted.

atl = cells reachable uphill from the bottom row and right column
reach(starts):

cases.note: No fresh oranges: 0 minutes.
A fresh orange with nothing to rot it.
A long row.

hints.text: Rot spreads from every rotten orange at once, one step per minute. That is BFS starting from many sources together.

hints.text: Running a BFS from every 1 is too slow. Run one BFS from all the 0s at the same time instead.
Distance 0 for every 0 cell, infinity elsewhere; push all 0s, then BFS: a neighbour gets distance + 1 the first time it is reached.

No water at all.

hints.text: You want the water cell whose nearest land is farthest away (Manhattan distance). Return -1 when there is no land or no water.

if queue is empty or every cell is land: return -1
dist = -1

cases.note: Start is the end: path length 1.

Go around the blocked centre.

The start itself is a deadend.
The farthest state: 5 turns on every wheel.

BFS from '0000' over the 8 neighbours of each state, skipping deadends and visited states. If '0000' is itself a deadend, return -1.

cases.note: Two single cells with one gap.
Opposite corners.

cases.note: No middle word connects them.
beginWord is in the list but too far from endWord.

hints.text: Words are nodes; two words are joined when they differ in exactly one letter. You want the shortest path, counted in words, or 0 if there is none.
BFS from beginWord. To find neighbours fast, try changing each position to each letter a..z and look the result up in a set of unused words.

cases.note: An odd cycle can never be two-coloured.
A good component and a triangle.

hints.text: Bipartite means you can colour every node with one of two colours so that every edge joins different colours. The graph may be disconnected.

cases.note: A 5-cycle is odd.

hints.text: People are nodes and each dislike is an edge between two people who must end up in different groups. That is a two-colouring question.
Build the adjacency list (people are numbered from 1) and BFS-colour each component, failing on an edge whose ends share a colour.

cases.note: A self-loop is never safe.
A chain into a terminal node: all safe.

cases.note: A diamond shape is fine.

queue = courses with indeg 0; taken = 0

cases.note: Both nodes are centres.
A path: the middle node.

hints.text: The best roots sit in the middle of the longest path, so there are at most two of them. Any order is accepted.
Peel the tree like an onion: remove all current leaves (degree 1) at once, update degrees, and repeat until at most 2 nodes are left.

cases.note: No relations: the slowest course decides.
A chain: times add up.

hints.text: With unlimited parallel work, a course finishes at its own time plus the latest finish among its prerequisites. The answer is the latest finish overall.
Topological order (Kahn) over the DAG: finish[v] = time[v] + max finish of its prerequisites. Relax each edge as you pop nodes.

finish[v] = time[v - 1] for every course

cases.note: The indirect route is faster.

hints.text: The signal reaches each node along its shortest path from k, so the answer is the largest shortest-path distance (or -1 if a node is unreachable).
Dijkstra from k over the directed, non-negative weighted edges, then take the maximum distance.

cases.note: Going around beats the direct jump.

hints.text: A path's cost is its biggest single step, not the sum. You want the path from top-left to bottom-right whose biggest step is smallest.
Dijkstra where a path's 'distance' is the max absolute height difference along it: relax a neighbour with max(effort so far, step).

cases.note: The cheap route needs too many stops.

repeat k + 1 times:

cases.note: Already at the destination: one way.
Two equal shortest paths.
A direct road ties with the two-step route.

hints.text: Count how many different shortest paths go from 0 to n - 1 (modulo 1e9 + 7).
Dijkstra that also tracks ways[v]: a strictly shorter route resets ways[v] to ways[u]; an equally short one adds ways[u].

cases.note: Nobody is reachable: the larger index wins the tie.
Exactly at the threshold counts.

hints.text: You need shortest distances between every pair of cities, then count for each city how many others are within the threshold.
Floyd-Warshall (n is small) fills the all-pairs table. Pick the city with the fewest reachable neighbours, breaking ties by the larger index.

cases.note: The start is the highest cell.
The end is the highest cell.

hints.text: At time t you can stand on any cell with height <= t. The answer is the smallest t at which a path from top-left to bottom-right exists: a minimax path.
Dijkstra where the cost of a path is the highest cell on it (or binary search on t with a BFS).

Prim's algorithm on the dense graph in O(n^2): keep each outside point's cheapest link to the tree, add the cheapest point, and update the links.

repeat n times:

cases.note: The cycle closes in the middle of the list.
Every edge is on the cycle: return the last one.

hints.text: A tree plus one extra edge has exactly one cycle. Removing any edge of that cycle leaves a tree; return the one that appears last in the input.

parent[i] = i for 1 .. n
find(x): follow parent links to the root (compress the path)
for (a, b) in edges:
