  parent[find(a)] = find(b)

cases.note: Too few cables.
Already connected.

hints.text: Connecting n computers needs at least n - 1 cables. If you have that many, each move of a spare cable joins two components.
Return -1 when there are fewer than n - 1 cables; otherwise count components with union-find and return components - 1.

if len(connections) < n - 1: return -1
parent[i] = i
components = n
for (a, b) in connections:
  if find(a) != find(b): union them; components -= 1
return components - 1

cases.note: Emails must come back sorted.
The same account twice.
The third account links the first two.

hints.text: Two accounts belong to the same person when they share any email. Emails are the nodes; each account links its emails together.
Union-find over emails (union every email with the first email of its account). Group emails by root, sort each group, and put the owner's name in front. Accounts may come back in any order.

owner = map email -> name
for each account: union every email with the account's first email
groups = map root -> list of emails
for each email: append it to groups[find(email)]
return [owner[g[0]]] + sorted(g) for each group g

cases.note: No shared row or column.
Linked through a corner stone.
One row.

hints.text: Stones sharing a row or column are connected. Inside one connected group you can always remove every stone but one.
The answer is stones - components. Union-find on rows and columns: union row r with column c (offset the columns so they do not clash) for every stone.

parent = empty map
for (r, c) in stones: union(r, c + 10001)
components = number of distinct roots among the rows and columns used
return len(stones) - components

cases.note: Flip any cell: an island of 1.
The centre touches no island; an edge cell joins two.

hints.text: Flipping one 0 joins the islands around it. Re-running a search for every 0 is O(n^4); precompute each island's size once.
Label every island with an id and record its size. For each 0, add 1 plus the sizes of the distinct island ids among its 4 neighbours. If there is no 0, the answer is n * n.

id = 2; size = map
for each land cell not yet labelled: size[id] = flood(cell, id); id += 1
best = max of size values, or 0 if none
for each cell with grid[r][c] == 0:
  ids = distinct labels of the 4 neighbours
  best = max(best, 1 + sum of size[i] for i in ids)
return best

cases.note: Everything is on a cycle: no bridges.
Two triangles joined by one bridge.
A path: every edge is a bridge.

hints.text: A critical connection (bridge) is an edge on no cycle: removing it disconnects the graph. Any order of edges, and of the two ends of an edge, is accepted.
Tarjan's DFS: give each node a discovery time and a low value (the earliest time reachable using at most one back edge). Edge u-v is a bridge when low[v] > disc[u].

timer = 0; disc and low unset
dfs(u, parent):
  disc[u] = low[u] = timer; timer += 1
  for v in adj[u]:
    if v == parent: continue
    if disc[v] is unset:
      dfs(v, u)
      low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])
      if low[v] > disc[u]: record [u, v]
    else: low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])
dfs(0, none)
return the recorded edges

cases.note: Start on the cheaper step and jump to the top.

hints.text: You may start on step 0 or 1 and climb 1 or 2 steps, paying the cost of each step you stand on. The top is one past the last step.
Let best[i] be the cheapest way to stand past step i - 1: best[i] = min(best[i - 1] + cost[i - 1], best[i - 2] + cost[i - 2]). Two variables are enough.

a = 0; b = 0   (cheapest to reach steps i - 2 and i - 1)
for i in 2 .. n:
  c = min(b + cost[i - 1], a + cost[i - 2])
  a = b; b = c
return b

cases.note: The largest allowed n still fits in 32 bits.

hints.text: T0 = 0, T1 = 1, T2 = 1 and each later term is the sum of the three before it.
Plain recursion repeats work exponentially. Keep the last three values and slide them forward.

if n == 0: return 0
a = 0; b = 1; c = 1
repeat n - 2 times:
  a, b, c = b, c, a + b + c
return c

cases.note: First and last are both big, but they touch.

hints.text: The houses form a circle, so the first and last are neighbours. You can never rob both.
Run the straight-line House Robber twice: once without the last house and once without the first, and take the better result. One house is a special case.

cases.note: Each zero can take either sign.
Parity makes it impossible.

hints.text: Each number gets a + or a -. The plus group P and minus group M satisfy P - M = target and P + M = total.

So P = (total + target) / 2: count subsets with that sum (0/1 knapsack counting). If that is not a whole number or is negative, the answer is 0. Zeros double the count, which the DP handles naturally.

total = sum(nums)
if |target| > total or (total + target) is odd: return 0
want = (total + target) / 2
ways = array of want + 1 zeros; ways[0] = 1
for x in nums:
  for s from want down to x:
    ways[s] += ways[s - x]
return ways[want]

cases.note: Amount 0: one way, use nothing.

hints.text: Count combinations, not orders: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same way. Coins can be reused.
Unbounded knapsack counting with the coin loop on the outside, so each combination is built in one fixed coin order.

cases.note: Needs 4 squares: 4 + 1 + 1 + 1.

hints.text: The fewest perfect squares that add up to n. Greedy (take the biggest square) fails: 12 = 4 + 4 + 4, not 9 + 1 + 1 + 1.
best[i] = 1 + min over squares s <= i of best[i - s], built from 0 upward.

cases.note: Only one way: all ones.
Every arrangement counts.

hints.text: Despite the name, different orders count as different ways here (1+2 and 2+1 are two).
ways[t] = sum over nums x <= t of ways[t - x], with the target loop outside and the numbers loop inside.

cases.note: Two separate runs of values.

hints.text: Taking value v earns v for every copy of it but forbids v - 1 and v + 1. Group equal values first.
Make points[v] = v * count(v) and run House Robber over the values: adjacent values are adjacent houses.

cases.note: Prices only fall: do nothing.
The cooldown forbids buying right after a sale.

hints.text: After you sell, you must wait one day before buying again. Track what state you are in each day.
Three states: holding a share, just sold (cooldown next day), and resting with no share. Update all three from yesterday's values.

hold = -infinity; sold = 0; rest = 0
for p in prices:
  prevSold = sold
  sold = hold + p
  hold = max(hold, rest - p)
  rest = max(rest, prevSold)
return max(sold, rest)

cases.note: No fee: take every rise.
Each rise only pays the fee: profit 0.

hints.text: Unlimited trades, but each sale costs a fee, so tiny wiggles are no longer worth trading.
Two states per day: cash (no share) and hold (one share). cash = max(cash, hold + price - fee); hold = max(hold, cash - price).

cash = 0; hold = -prices[0]
for p in prices[1 ..]:
  cash = max(cash, hold + p - fee)
  hold = max(hold, cash - p)
return cash

cases.note: k = 1: nothing changes.
One piece covers everything.

hints.text: Cut the array into pieces of length at most k; every value in a piece becomes the piece's maximum. Maximise the total.
best[i] = the answer for the first i elements: try every last piece length L from 1 to k and take best[i - L] + L * max of that piece.

best = array of n + 1 zeros
for i in 1 .. n:
  m = 0
  for L in 1 .. min(k, i):
    m = max(m, arr[i - L])
    best[i] = max(best[i], best[i - L] + m * L)
return best[n]

cases.note: Every single element is a longest subsequence.
Strictly increasing: two ways through the 2s.

hints.text: Alongside the LIS length ending at each index, keep how many increasing subsequences reach that length there.
For j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]: a longer length resets count[i] to count[j]; an equal length adds count[j]. Finally sum the counts of indices with the maximum length.

len = n ones; cnt = n ones
for i in 0 .. n - 1:
  for j in 0 .. i - 1 with nums[j] < nums[i]:
    if len[j] + 1 > len[i]: len[i] = len[j] + 1; cnt[i] = cnt[j]
    else if len[j] + 1 == len[i]: cnt[i] += cnt[j]
best = max(len)
return sum of cnt[i] where len[i] == best

cases.note: Two routes to the same word.
Insertion can happen anywhere in the word.

hints.text: A word's predecessor is the word with exactly one letter removed. Chains only grow by one letter at a time, so process words from shortest to longest.
Sort by length; for each word, try deleting each letter and look up the best chain ending at that shorter word in a map.

cases.note: The start itself is blocked.
A full row of obstacles.

hints.text: Moving only right or down, the ways into a cell are the ways into the cell above plus the cell to the left, unless the cell is an obstacle (0 ways).
One row of DP is enough: ways[c] += ways[c - 1] for open cells, and ways[c] = 0 for obstacles.

cases.note: A single column: one path.

hints.text: Moving right or down, the cheapest way into a cell comes from the cheaper of its top and left neighbours.
Fill a DP row by row: best[c] = grid[r][c] + min(best[c] from the row above, best[c - 1] in this row). The first row and column have only one way in.

cases.note: Hugging the right edge is cheapest.

hints.text: From index i in a row you may step to index i or i + 1 in the next row. Find the cheapest top-to-bottom path.
Work bottom-up: start with the last row and replace each value by itself plus the smaller of the two values below it. The top then holds the answer.

cases.note: The diagonal moves matter.

hints.text: Start anywhere in the first row; each step goes to the cell directly below or diagonally below-left or below-right.
Row by row: best[c] = matrix[r][c] + min of the previous row's best at c - 1, c, c + 1 (where they exist). The answer is the smallest value in the last row.

cases.note: A strip only fits 1x1 squares.

hints.text: Let side[r][c] be the biggest all-'1' square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c). Return the area, side squared.
side[r][c] = 1 + min(side above, side to the left, side above-left) when the cell is '1', else 0.

cases.note: 9 + 4 + 1 squares.

hints.text: A cell that is the corner of a k x k all-ones square is also the corner of the 1 x 1 .. (k-1) x (k-1) ones, so it contributes k squares.
Same recurrence as Maximal Square: side = 1 + min(top, left, top-left) for 1 cells. Sum every side value.

cases.note: Two columns: the robots may swap sides.
Both want the middle; it counts once.

hints.text: Both robots move down one row at a time, each stepping to column c - 1, c or c + 1. Move them together so the state is (row, column of robot 1, column of robot 2).
dp over rows: for every pair of columns, take the best of the 9 combined moves from the previous row and add the cherries in this row (count once if both robots share a cell).

cases.note: No two letters match: 1.

hints.text: Look at the two ends of s[i..j]: equal ends can both be kept; otherwise drop one of them.
Interval DP: L[i][j] = L[i + 1][j - 1] + 2 when s[i] == s[j], else max(L[i + 1][j], L[i][j - 1]). Fill by increasing length (or i from the right).

cases.note: Already equal: 0.
Nothing in common: delete everything.

hints.text: Whatever survives the deletions is a common subsequence, and you want to keep as much as possible.
Find the longest common subsequence; the answer is len(word1) + len(word2) - 2 * LCS.

cases.note: All distinct: n - 1 insertions.

hints.text: Characters that already pair up into a palindrome need no help; every other character needs one inserted partner.
The answer is n minus the longest palindromic subsequence. Or directly: f(i, j) = f(i + 1, j - 1) if the ends match, else 1 + min(f(i + 1, j), f(i, j - 1)).

cases.note: t is longer than s.
Choose 2 of 4 positions: 6.

hints.text: Count how many ways you can pick positions in s that spell t. When s[i] == t[j] you may use it or skip it; otherwise you must skip it.
ways[j] = number of ways to build t[0..j) from the prefix of s seen so far. For each character of s, update j from right to left so each s character is used once.

cases.note: Stars can match nothing.

hints.text: '?' matches one character and '*' matches any sequence, including the empty one. The whole string must match.
dp[i][j]: does s[0..i) match p[0..j)? A '*' can match nothing (dp[i][j - 1]) or one more character (dp[i - 1][j]).

cases.note: Every starred part can be empty.
c* matches nothing.

hints.text: '.' matches any one character and 'x*' means zero or more copies of x. The whole string must match.
dp[i][j]: does s[0..i) match p[0..j)? For 'x*': use zero copies (dp[i][j - 2]) or, if x matches s[i - 1], one more copy (dp[i - 1][j]).

cases.note: Lengths do not add up.
Both strings offer an 'a' first.

hints.text: s3 must use every character of s1 and s2 exactly once, keeping each string's order. Greedy choices fail when both strings offer the same next letter.
dp[i][j]: can the first i letters of s1 and j letters of s2 form the first i + j letters of s3? Come from dp[i - 1][j] using s1[i - 1] or from dp[i][j - 1] using s2[j - 1].

if len(s1) + len(s2) != len(s3): return false
dp = (m + 1) x (n + 1) false; dp[0][0] = true
for i in 0 .. m:
  for j in 0 .. n:
    k = i + j - 1
    if i > 0 and dp[i - 1][j] and s1[i - 1] == s3[k]: dp[i][j] = true
    if j > 0 and dp[i][j - 1] and s2[j - 1] == s3[k]: dp[i][j] = true
return dp[m][n]

cases.note: Three rises, but only two trades.

hints.text: At most two complete trades, and they cannot overlap.
Track four running values: best after the first buy, first sell, second buy and second sell. Each day updates them in that order.

buy1 = -infinity; sell1 = 0; buy2 = -infinity; sell2 = 0
for p in prices:
  buy1 = max(buy1, -p)
  sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p)
  buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - p)
  sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p)
return sell2

cases.note: More trades than rises: take every rise.

hints.text: Generalise the two-trade version to k trades: keep a buy and a sell value for each trade number.
buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t - 1] - p); sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + p), for t = 1..k each day. (If k >= n / 2, it is the same as unlimited trades.)
Thinking about which balloon to burst first is messy because neighbours change. Think about which balloon in a range is burst last.
Pad with 1 on both ends. best(l, r) over the open interval: try each k as the last one burst between l and r: nums[l] * nums[k] * nums[r] + best(l, k) + best(k, r).

cases.note: One cut costs the whole length.

hints.text: Each cut costs the length of the piece being cut, so the order matters. A cut splits the problem into two independent pieces.
Sort the cuts and add 0 and n as ends. cost(i, j) for the piece between cut points i and j = (c[j] - c[i]) + min over k between them of cost(i, k) + cost(k, j).

cases.note: Already a palindrome: 0 cuts.
All distinct: n - 1 cuts.

hints.text: cuts[i] = fewest cuts for the prefix ending at i. The last piece is some palindrome s[j..i].

Precompute which substrings are palindromes (pal[j][i] = s[j] == s[i] and pal[j + 1][i - 1]). Then cuts[i] = 0 if s[0..i] is a palindrome, else min over j of cuts[j - 1] + 1 where s[j..i] is a palindrome.

cases.note: A perfect split exists: 0.

hints.text: Every smash subtracts one stone from another, so the final weight is a sum where each stone gets a + or a - sign. Make it as small as possible (and non-negative).
Split the stones into two groups as evenly as possible: find the largest reachable subset sum not above total / 2 (0/1 knapsack); the answer is total - 2 * that sum.

total = sum(stones); half = total // 2
can = array of half + 1 false; can[0] = true
for x in stones:
  for s from half down to x:
    if can[s - x]: can[s] = true
best = largest s with can[s]
return total - 2 * best

cases.note: The whole word is also a prefix of itself.

hints.text: Each node holds up to 26 children and a flag saying whether a word ends there. Words that share a prefix share a path.
insert walks down creating missing children and marks the last node; search walks down and checks the flag; startsWith only needs the walk to succeed.

insert(w): node = root; for ch in w: node = node.child[ch] (create if missing); node.end = true
walk(s): node = root; for ch in s: if ch not in node.child: return none; node = node.child[ch]; return node
search(w): n = walk(w); return n is not none and n.end
startsWith(p): return walk(p) is not none

cases.note: Dots must match exactly one letter each.

hints.text: A trie handles plain lookups. The '.' wildcard means 'any one letter', so at that position you must try every child.
search is a DFS over (node, index): a letter follows one child, a '.' tries all children; succeed when the index reaches the end at a word-ending node.

input: the cattle was rattled by the battery
cases.expected: the cat was rat by the bat

cases.note: The shortest root wins.
A word equal to a root.

input: ab cbbb bbaa acc aab aa
cases.expected: ab cbbb b acc aab aa

hints.text: Each word in the sentence is replaced by the shortest root that is a prefix of it, if any.
Put the roots in a trie. For each word, walk the trie letter by letter and stop at the first node that ends a root.

trie = all roots
for each word w in sentence.split(' '):
  node = root; out = w
  for i, ch in w:
    if ch not in node.child: break
    node = node.child[ch]
    if node.end: out = w[0 .. i]; break
  replace w by out
return the words joined by spaces

cases.note: No one-letter start: the answer is ''.
A tie goes to the alphabetically smaller word.

hints.text: A word counts only if every prefix of it (length 1, 2, ...) is also in the list. Return the longest such word, breaking ties by the smallest in alphabetical order.
Sort the words; then a word is buildable when its prefix without the last letter was already marked buildable (or it has one letter). Track the best as you go.

sort words
ok = set containing the empty string; best = ''
for w in words:
  if w without its last letter is in ok:
    add w to ok
    if len(w) > len(best): best = w
return best

cases.note: Only three suggestions even when four match.

hints.text: After each typed letter, return up to three products starting with the typed prefix, in alphabetical order.
Sort the products once. For each prefix, binary search the first product >= prefix and take up to three that still start with it. (A trie storing the three best words per node also works.)

sort products
out = []
for i in 1 .. len(searchWord):
  p = searchWord[0 .. i - 1]
  k = first index with products[k] >= p
  out.append(the products from k on that start with p, at most 3)
return out

cases.note: Re-inserting a key replaces its value.

hints.text: sum(prefix) adds the values of every key that starts with prefix. Inserting an existing key replaces its old value.
Store in each trie node the total of all values below it. On insert, add the difference between the new and old value of the key along its path.

vals = map key -> value
insert(key, val):
  delta = val - vals.get(key, 0); vals[key] = val
  node = root
  for ch in key: node = node.child[ch] (create if missing); node.total += delta
sum(prefix):
  walk prefix; return node.total, or 0 if the walk fails

cases.note: Nothing matches: every character is extra.

hints.text: Break s into dictionary words plus leftover characters, minimising the leftovers.
best[i] = fewest extras in s[i..]. Either s[i] is extra (1 + best[i + 1]) or some dictionary word starts at i (best[j] where the word ends at j). A trie from i finds all such words in one walk.

cases.note: A cell cannot be reused within one word.

hints.text: Running Word Search once per word repeats work. Put all words in a trie and search the board once, following the trie as you walk. Any order of words is accepted.
DFS from every cell carrying the current trie node; a cell may not be reused in one word. When a node ends a word, record it and clear the mark so it is reported once.

trie = all words, word stored at its end node
for each cell (r, c): dfs(r, c, root)
dfs(r, c, node):
  ch = board[r][c]
  if ch == '#' or ch not in node.child: return
  node = node.child[ch]
  if node.word: add node.word to found; node.word = none
  board[r][c] = '#'
  dfs each of the 4 neighbours inside the board with node
  board[r][c] = ch
return found

cases.note: The empty word pairs with every palindrome, both ways.

hints.text: Checking every ordered pair is O(n^2 * L). Split each word into a prefix and a suffix: if one part is a palindrome, you need the reverse of the other part to be a word. Any order of pairs is accepted.

Map each reversed word to its index. For word i and every split point k: if word[0..k) is a palindrome and reverse(word[k..]) is another word j, then [j, i] works; if word[k..] is a palindrome and reverse(word[0..k)) is word j, then [i, j] works. Skip k == len for the second case to avoid duplicates.

rev = map reverse(word) -> index
for i, w in words:
  for k in 0 .. len(w):
    left = w[0 .. k); right = w[k ..]
    if left is a palindrome and right in rev and rev[right] != i: add [rev[right], i]
    if k < len(w) and right is a palindrome and left in rev and rev[left] != i: add [i, rev[left]]
return pairs

cases.note: Two words end at the same letter.

hints.text: After each letter, ask whether some word is a suffix of everything typed so far. Checking every word every time is too slow.
Build a trie of the reversed words. Keep the stream; on each query, walk the trie from the newest letter backwards and stop at the first word end (or a missing child).

constructor(words): insert reverse(w) for every word into a trie
stream = []
query(ch):
  append ch to stream
  node = root
  for i from len(stream) - 1 down to 0:
    if stream[i] not in node.child: return false
    node = node.child[stream[i]]
    if node.end: return true
  return false

cases.note: Every number is above m.

hints.text: Each query [x, m] wants the largest x XOR num over nums with num <= m, or -1 if none qualifies.
Answer offline: sort nums and the queries by m. Insert nums into a binary trie (high bit first) while they are <= m, then walk the trie greedily choosing the opposite bit of x whenever possible.

sort nums; sort query indices by m
k = 0
for each query (x, m, idx) in that order:
  while k < n and nums[k] <= m: insert nums[k] bit by bit (bit 30 down to 0); k += 1
  if k == 0: ans[idx] = -1; continue
  node = root; best = 0
  for b from 30 down to 0:
    want = 1 - bit b of x
    if node has child want: best |= 1 << b; node = child want
    else: node = the other child
  ans[idx] = best
return ans

cases.note: One word alone is never concatenated.

hints.text: A concatenated word is made of at least two shorter words from the list. Any order of answers is accepted.
Process words from shortest to longest; a word is concatenated when Word Break succeeds using only the shorter words seen so far. Then add the word to the set.

cases.note: Nothing to add: the answer is 0, not undefined.
All negative: the total goes below zero.

hints.text: You only need one pass over the array. What single value do you carry from one element to the next?
Keep a running total that starts at 0 and add every element to it. The total after the last element is the answer, and an empty array never enters the loop.

total = 0
for each value in nums:
  total = total + value
return total

cases.note: All negative: starting the best at 0 returns 0, which isn't in the array.
The largest value is the last element.

hints.text: Imagine reading the numbers one at a time. What do you need to remember so far to know the largest at the end?
Track the best value seen so far. Start it at the first element (not 0, which breaks on all-negative input) and replace it whenever a bigger value appears.

cases.note: 0 is even.
-3 % 2 is -1, so a check for === 1 misses negative odd numbers.

hints.text: Each element either matches the rule or doesn't. What do you increase when it matches?
Loop once with a counter. A number is even when its remainder by 2 is 0; compare with 0 rather than with 1, because -3 % 2 is -1 in JavaScript.

cases.note: Absent target: return -1, not undefined.
The first match is index 1, not the last one.

hints.text: Scan from the left. The moment you find the target, do you need to look any further?
Return the index as soon as nums[i] equals target (an early return gives the first occurrence). If the loop finishes, the target isn't there, so return -1.

cases.note: The smallest value is the last element; starting from 0 would also be wrong here.

hints.text: This is the mirror image of finding the largest. Which single value do you keep while scanning?
Keep the smallest value seen so far, starting from the first element. Starting from 0 fails when every value is positive.

cases.note: Values equal to x are not greater than x.

hints.text: Turn the threshold into a yes/no question for each element. What do you do on a yes?
Count elements with nums[i] > x. Use strict comparison: an element equal to x does not count.

cases.note: Nothing is greater than x: the sum is 0.
Negative values above the threshold still add up to a negative sum.

hints.text: It's a running total, but not every element is allowed in. Where does the condition go?
Loop once and add nums[i] to the total only when nums[i] > x. Start the total at 0 so nothing qualifying still gives 0.
Which element of nums ends up first in the answer, and which ends up last?
Walk nums from the last index down to 0 and push each value onto a fresh result array.

result = empty list
for i from n - 1 down to 0:
  append nums[i] to result
return result

cases.note: Zero is not positive, so the answer is empty.

hints.text: You're building a second array as you scan the first. When does an element get copied?
Push nums[i] onto the result only when it is greater than 0. Zero is not positive.

cases.note: An empty array is sorted.
Equal neighbours are allowed in non-decreasing order.

hints.text: A global property like 'sorted' can be checked locally. Which pairs of elements do you need to compare?
Compare each element with its neighbour. One pair with nums[i] < nums[i-1] proves it isn't sorted; equal neighbours are fine.

cases.note: Only one distinct value: there is no second largest.
Initialising second to 0 or -1 is wrong when every value is negative.
The second largest distinct value is 4, not the duplicated 5.

hints.text: Keeping just the maximum isn't enough. What else do you need to remember while scanning?
Track the largest and second largest seen so far. A new maximum pushes the old one down to second place; a value strictly between them becomes the new second. Ignore values equal to the maximum.

cases.note: One element sits at index 0, which is even: the answer is 0.

hints.text: The condition is about where an element sits, not what it holds. What should the loop variable describe?
Either loop over every index and add nums[i] when i is odd, or start at index 1 and step by 2.

total = 0
for i from 1 to n - 1 in steps of 2:
  total = total + nums[i]
return total

cases.note: The last occurrence is the final element.

hints.text: With a first-occurrence search you stop at the first match. How can you make the first match you meet be the last one in the array?
Scan from the right end and return the first index that matches. (Scanning left to right and remembering the latest match also works.)

cases.note: No elements: every count is 0.

hints.text: Every element falls into exactly one of three buckets. How many counters do you need?
Keep three counters and, for each element, increase the one matching its sign with an if / else-if / else chain.

pos = 0, neg = 0, zero = 0
for each value in nums:
  if value > 0: pos += 1
  else if value < 0: neg += 1
  else: zero += 1
return [pos, neg, zero]

cases.note: One element is both the max and the min: the answer is 0.

hints.text: You already know how to find the largest and the smallest separately. Can one pass track both?
Keep both a running maximum and a running minimum, starting from the first element, and update both for every element.

hi = nums[0], lo = nums[0]
for each value in nums:
  if value > hi: hi = value
  if value < lo: lo = value
return hi - lo

cases.note: Index 0 is even, so a single element is the whole answer.

hints.text: Position decides whether an element counts. Which indexes are even, and where does the first one start?
Start at index 0 and step by 2, adding each element you land on.

total = 0
for i from 0 to n - 1 in steps of 2:
  total = total + nums[i]
return total

cases.note: Zeros are already non-negative and stay as they are.

hints.text: You may read and write the same array. When you look at nums[i], what decides whether you overwrite it?
Loop over the indexes (not a copy of the values) and assign nums[i] = 0 whenever nums[i] < 0.

cases.note: One element rotates onto itself.

hints.text: One element would be overwritten when you shift. Which one, and where can you keep it safe?
Save the last element in a temporary variable, shift elements right starting from the end (so you never overwrite something you still need), then put the saved value at index 0.

if n < 2: return
last = nums[n - 1]
for i from n - 1 down to 1:
  nums[i] = nums[i - 1]
nums[0] = last
Shifting left overwrites the first element. What should you save before you start?
Keep nums[0] in a temporary variable, move every element one step left starting from index 1, then write the saved value into the last slot.

if n < 2: return
first = nums[0]
for i from 1 to n - 1:
  nums[i - 1] = nums[i]
nums[n - 1] = first

cases.note: The first array is empty: the answer is just the second.

hints.text: The answer has a.length + b.length slots. In what order do the elements arrive?
Create an empty result, loop over a pushing each element, then loop over b doing the same.

result = empty list
for each value in a: append value to result
for each value in b: append value to result
return result

cases.note: Two empty arrays are equal.
Same prefix but different lengths.

hints.text: Before comparing elements, is there a quick check that can rule equality out?
If the lengths differ, return false. Otherwise walk both arrays with one index and return false at the first position where they differ. (a === b compares references, not contents.)

if length of a != length of b: return false
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  if a[i] != b[i]: return false
return true

cases.note: An empty array is a palindrome.

hints.text: Element i must match its mirror. Which index is the mirror of i in an array of length n?
Put one pointer at the start and one at the end. While they haven't crossed, compare the two values; any mismatch means false. Move both inward after each comparison.

left = 0, right = n - 1
while left < right:
  if nums[left] != nums[right]: return false
  left += 1
  right -= 1
return true
The first and last elements trade places. What happens next with the second and second-to-last?
Keep a left pointer at 0 and a right pointer at n - 1. Swap their values and move both inward until they meet.

left = 0, right = n - 1
while left < right:
  swap nums[left] and nums[right]
  left += 1
  right -= 1

cases.note: No elements: return an empty object.
0 is a real key: (counts[0] || 0) handles it, but if (counts[0]) checks would skip it.

hints.text: For each value you want a counter, but you don't know the values in advance. What structure creates counters on demand?
Use an object (or Map) keyed by the value. For each element, set count[value] = (count[value] or 0) + 1. Return a plain object.

counts = empty map
for each value in nums:
  counts[value] = counts[value] (or 0) + 1
return counts

cases.note: 7 appears once in the answer even though a repeats it.

hints.text: Checking each element of a against every element of b is O(n*m). What gives you O(1) membership tests?
Put the values of b in a Set. Walk a, and when a value is in that set and you haven't output it yet, add it to the result (a second set tracks what you've output).

inB = set of values in b
seen = empty set, result = empty list
for each value in a:
  if value in inB and value not in seen:
    add value to seen
    append value to result
return result

cases.note: 3 is shared twice: the smaller count wins.

hints.text: A set forgets how many copies there are. What do you need instead to respect multiplicity?
Count the values of a in a map. Walk b; whenever a value still has a positive count, output it and decrease that count.

count = frequency map of a
result = empty list
for each value in b:
  if count[value] > 0:
    append value to result
    count[value] -= 1
return result

cases.note: Every value repeats: return null.
0 is a valid answer; a truthiness check would skip it.

hints.text: Whether an element is unique depends on the whole array, not just what you've seen so far. How many passes does that suggest?
First pass: count every value. Second pass in the original order: return the first value whose count is 1.

count = frequency map of nums
for each value in nums:
  if count[value] == 1: return value
return null

cases.note: All negative: starting best at 0 would be wrong.
k = 1 is just the largest element.
k = n: the only window is the whole array.

hints.text: Recomputing each window from scratch is O(n*k). Two neighbouring windows share almost all their elements; what changes between them?
Sum the first k elements. Then slide: add the element entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left, updating the best sum each time.

window = sum of nums[0..k-1]
best = window
for i from k to n - 1:
  window = window + nums[i] - nums[i - k]
  best = max(best, window)
return best
Same window as the maximum version; only the comparison flips. What stays constant between neighbouring windows?
Build the first window's sum, then slide it one step at a time (add the new element, drop the old one) and keep the smallest sum seen.

window = sum of nums[0..k-1]
best = window
for i from k to n - 1:
  window = window + nums[i] - nums[i - k]
  best = min(best, window)
return best

cases.note: No even numbers at all: the answer is 0.
0 is even.

hints.text: Instead of a window sum, keep a window count. How does the count change when the window slides by one?
Count evens in the first k elements. When sliding, add 1 if the entering element is even and subtract 1 if the leaving element is even; track the best count.

count = evens among nums[0..k-1]
best = count
for i from k to n - 1:
  if nums[i] is even: count += 1
  if nums[i - k] is even: count -= 1
  best = max(best, count)
return best

cases.note: Every window matches, so every start index is returned.

hints.text: You need every window, not just the best one. What do you record when a window matches?
Slide a running window sum across the array. After each step, if the sum equals target, push the window's starting index (i - k + 1).

sum = 0, result = empty list
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  sum += nums[i]
  if i >= k: sum -= nums[i - k]
  if i >= k - 1 and sum == target:
    append i - k + 1 to result
return result

cases.note: Every element alone exceeds k: the answer is 0.
The whole array fits exactly.

hints.text: With only positive numbers, adding an element can only grow a sum and removing one can only shrink it. How does that let a window grow and shrink?
Expand the right end one step at a time and add its value. While the sum exceeds k, shrink from the left. After that, the window is valid; record its length.

left = 0, sum = 0, best = 0
for right from 0 to n - 1:
  sum += nums[right]
  while sum > k:
    sum -= nums[left]
    left += 1
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

cases.note: k = 0: the window may hold no odd numbers at all.
No odd numbers: the whole array qualifies.
-3 % 2 is -1 in JavaScript, so test oddness with !== 0.

hints.text: Only the odd elements are constrained. What do you need to count inside the window?
Grow the window to the right, counting odd numbers. When the count goes above k, move the left end forward (decreasing the count when an odd number leaves) until it's back to k.

left = 0, odd = 0, best = 0
for right from 0 to n - 1:
  if nums[right] is odd: odd += 1
  while odd > k:
    if nums[left] is odd: odd -= 1
    left += 1
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

cases.note: Ranges that start at 0 or end at n - 1 use the first and last prefix entries.

hints.text: Summing each range directly is O(n) per query. What could you precompute so every range sum becomes a subtraction?
Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i elements (prefix[0] = 0). Then the sum of nums[l..r] is prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l].

prefix = [0]
for each value in nums:
  append (last of prefix + value) to prefix
result = empty list
for each [l, r] in queries:
  append prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l] to result
return result

cases.note: Many equal values: [2, 2, 2] must appear only once.

hints.text: Fixing one value turns the rest into a pair-sum problem. What makes pair sums easy, and how do you avoid repeated triplets?
Sort the array. For each index i (skipping values equal to the previous one), run two pointers on the rest looking for target - nums[i]. After a match, move both pointers past duplicates.

sort nums
for i from 0 to n - 3:
  if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue
  l = i + 1, r = n - 1
  while l < r:
    s = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
    if s == target: record triplet, move l and r past duplicates
    else if s < target: l += 1
    else: r -= 1
return the recorded triplets

cases.note: Exactly one pair exists.
Every neighbouring gap ties at 2, so every pair is returned in ascending order.

hints.text: After sorting, where can the closest pair of values be? Do you need to compare every pair?
Sort the array. The minimum difference is between some pair of neighbours, so one scan finds it, and a second scan collects every neighbouring pair with that difference (already in ascending order).

sort arr
best = smallest arr[i + 1] - arr[i] over all i
result = empty list
for i from 0 to n - 2:
  if arr[i + 1] - arr[i] == best:
    append [arr[i], arr[i + 1]] to result
return result

cases.note: Nothing to add: the answer is 0, not undefined.
All negative: the total goes below zero.

hints.text: Describe the answer for an array in terms of the answer for a smaller array. What is the smallest array whose sum you know immediately?
Recurse on an index: sum(i) = nums[i] + sum(i + 1), with sum(n) = 0. Passing an index avoids copying the array with slice on every call.
Reversing a whole array is swapping its two ends and then reversing the inside. When does the recursion stop?
Copy nums, then recurse with two indexes l and r: swap copy[l] and copy[r], then recurse on l + 1 and r - 1, stopping when l >= r.

copy = a copy of nums
solve(l, r):
  if l >= r: return
  swap copy[l] and copy[r]
  solve(l + 1, r - 1)
solve(0, n - 1)
return copy

cases.note: 1 has no proper divisors other than itself, so it isn't perfect.
A large perfect number: a loop up to num would be too slow at the real limits.

hints.text: Divisors come in pairs: if i divides num, so does num / i. How far do you need to look?
Loop i from 2 while i * i <= num, adding both i and num / i when i divides num (once if they're equal). Start the sum at 1 and remember 1 itself is not perfect.

if num <= 1: return false
sum = 1
i = 2
while i * i <= num:
  if num % i == 0:
    sum += i
    if i != num / i: sum += num / i
  i += 1
return sum == num

cases.note: No odd digit at all: return the empty string.
Only the very last digit is odd: the whole string is the answer.

hints.text: A number is odd exactly when its last digit is odd. Which substring keeps the most digits and still ends on an odd one?
The best answer is always a prefix of num: scan from the right for the last odd digit and return everything up to it, or an empty string if there isn't one.

cases.note: Equal neighbours aren't drops.
Rotation by zero still counts as sorted and rotated.

hints.text: Walk around the array as a circle. In a sorted array rotated some amount, how many times can a value be smaller than the one before it?
Count positions i where nums[i] > nums[(i + 1) % n]. A sorted, rotated array has at most one such drop.

cases.note: All negatives come first: keep each sign's original order.

hints.text: In the answer, positives sit at even indexes and negatives at odd indexes, each in their original order.
Make a result array and two write indexes: 0 for the next positive, 1 for the next negative. Scan nums once and drop each value at its side's index, then advance that index by 2.

cases.note: Row 0 is just [1].
The largest row still fits in a safe integer.

hints.text: Each row is built from the row above. Can you update one array in place to get from one row to the next?
Start with [1]. For each new row, append 1 and update positions from right to left: row[j] += row[j - 1]. Going right to left keeps the old values you still need.

row = [1]
repeat rowIndex times:
  append 1 to row
  for j from length - 2 down to 1:
    row[j] = row[j] + row[j - 1]
return row

cases.note: Every missing number needed comes before the first element.
The answer is far past the end of the array.

hints.text: At index i of the sorted array, how many positive numbers are missing before arr[i]?
Missing before index i is arr[i] - (i + 1), which never decreases. Binary search for the first index where it reaches k; the answer is that index plus k.

lo = 0, hi = n
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2 rounded down
  if arr[mid] - (mid + 1) < k: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid
return lo + k

cases.note: Too large for a loop and for plain number multiplication.
The exact answer already exceeds 2^53 before the modulo.

hints.text: Even indexes have 5 choices (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) and odd indexes have 4 (2, 3, 5, 7). The answer is a product of powers, but n can be 10^15.
Compute 5^ceil(n/2) * 4^floor(n/2) mod 1e9+7 with fast exponentiation. Products exceed 2^53, so use BigInt (or split the multiplication) to stay exact.

MOD = 1000000007
power(b, e):
  result = 1
  while e > 0:
    if e is odd: result = result * b mod MOD
    b = b * b mod MOD
    e = e / 2 rounded down
  return result
return power(5, ceil(n / 2)) * power(4, floor(n / 2)) mod MOD

cases.note: The true answer 2^31 overflows: clamp to 2^31 - 1.
Both negative: the quotient is positive and rounds toward zero.

hints.text: Repeated subtraction is too slow for 2^31 / 1. Can you subtract the divisor doubled many times at once?
Work with absolute values. Repeatedly find the largest divisor * 2^k that fits, subtract it and add 2^k to the quotient. Apply the sign at the end and clamp to [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].

if dividend == -2^31 and divisor == -1: return 2^31 - 1
negative = signs differ
a = |dividend|, b = |divisor|, q = 0
while a >= b:
  chunk = b, times = 1
  while chunk + chunk <= a: chunk += chunk; times += times
  a -= chunk; q += times
return -q if negative else q

cases.note: One subarray with range 0.
Equal values must not be counted twice as max or min.

hints.text: The sum of (max - min) over all subarrays is (sum of maxes) - (sum of mins). Can you count how many subarrays each element is the maximum of?

For each index, find how far it extends left and right as the maximum using a monotonic stack (strict on one side, non-strict on the other to avoid double counting). Its contribution is value * left * right. Do the same for minimums and subtract.

cases.note: Already a palindrome: add nothing.

hints.text: You can only add characters in front. The part of s you keep untouched is its longest palindromic prefix.
Find the longest palindromic prefix in linear time with the KMP failure function of s + '#' + reverse(s). Prepend the reverse of the remaining suffix.

t = s + '#' + reverse(s)
lps = KMP failure table of t
keep = lps[last index of t]
return reverse(s[keep..]) + s

cases.note: A proper prefix can't be the whole string: the answer is empty.

hints.text: You want the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. That's exactly what the KMP prefix function stores.
Build lps where lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also its suffix. The answer is s[0..lps[n - 1]].

lps = array of n zeros
j = 0
for i from 1 to n - 1:
  while j > 0 and s[i] != s[j]: j = lps[j - 1]
  if s[i] == s[j]: j += 1
  lps[i] = j
return s[0 .. lps[n - 1]]

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Patterns are two nested loops: the outer loop picks the row, the inner loop builds that row. How many stars does each row need here?
The outer loop runs n times. For every row, the inner loop appends n stars to an empty string, then you push the string.

rows = empty list
for i from 1 to n:
  row = empty string
  for j from 1 to n: row += '*'
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: The row number tells you how many stars to print. How does the inner loop's bound depend on the outer loop?
Let the inner loop run up to i, the current row number, instead of up to n.

for i from 1 to n:
  row = '*' repeated i times
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Same shape as the star triangle, but each cell prints its column number instead of a star.
In row i, the inner loop variable j runs from 1 to i; append j itself.

for i from 1 to n:
  row = empty string
  for j from 1 to i: row += j
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Compare with the number triangle: which loop variable should you print now, the row or the column?
Print the row number i in every cell of row i, and row i has i cells.

for i from 1 to n:
  row = empty string
  repeat i times: row += i
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: The rows shrink by one star each time. Write the star count of row i as a formula in n and i.
Row i has n - i + 1 stars, so the inner loop bound is n - i + 1.

for i from 1 to n:
  row = '*' repeated (n - i + 1) times
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Combine two earlier ideas: the inverted triangle's row length and the number triangle's cell value.
Row i has n - i + 1 cells and cell j prints j.

for i from 1 to n:
  row = empty string
  for j from 1 to n - i + 1: row += j
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: A pyramid row is two parts: spaces to push the stars to the middle, then the stars. How do both counts change from row to row?
Spaces go down by one per row (n - i) while stars go up by two (2i - 1). Don't add spaces after the stars.

for i from 1 to n:
  row = ' ' repeated (n - i) times
  row += '*' repeated (2i - 1) times
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: This is the pyramid upside down. The spaces now grow and the stars shrink.
Row i (counting from 0) has i spaces and 2(n - i) - 1 stars.

for i from 0 to n - 1:
  row = ' ' repeated i times
  row += '*' repeated (2(n - i) - 1) times
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: You've already built both halves separately. Can you reuse them?
Print the pyramid rows, then the inverted pyramid rows. The inverted half is the pyramid read bottom to top.

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Use a single loop over all 2n - 1 rows. What's the star count before and after the middle row?
stars = i for i <= n, else 2n - i. The middle row (i = n) is printed once.

for i from 1 to 2n - 1:
  stars = i if i <= n else 2n - i
  add '*' repeated stars times
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Each row starts from a known digit and flips with every step. What decides the starting digit?
Start with 1 on even rows and 0 on odd rows, then toggle the digit after every cell (bit = 1 - bit).

for i from 0 to n - 1:
  bit = 1 if i is even else 0
  row = empty string
  repeat i + 1 times:
    row += bit
    bit = 1 - bit
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Split each row into three loops: numbers going up, a gap, numbers coming down.
The gap shrinks by two each row: 2(n - i) spaces. The right half is the left half reversed.

for i from 1 to n:
  row = 1..i joined
  row += ' ' repeated 2(n - i) times
  row += i..1 joined
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: The numbers don't restart on each row. What do you need to keep outside both loops?
Keep a counter that starts at 1 and increases after every printed number, across rows.

x = 1
for i from 1 to n:
  parts = empty list
  repeat i times: add x to parts; x += 1
  add parts joined by ' ' to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Letters are numbers in disguise: 'A' has code 65, 'B' 66 and so on.
Cell j (0-based) of every row is the letter with code 65 + j.

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: This is the letter triangle with the rows in the opposite order.
Let the outer loop count down from n to 1 and print that many letters from 'A'.

for i from n down to 1:
  row = first i letters
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: The letter depends only on the row, not on the column.
In row i (0-based), print letter 65 + i, i + 1 times.

for i from 0 to n - 1:
  row = letter(65 + i) repeated i + 1 times
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Each row is a pyramid row (leading spaces) whose middle is a palindrome of letters.
After the spaces, print letters A..(i-th) going up, then (i-1)-th..A going down, so the peak letter appears once.

hints.text: Every row ends with the n-th letter. Where does row i start?
Row i starts at letter index n - i and runs up to index n - 1; join the letters with spaces.

for i from 1 to n:
  parts = letters with index n - i to n - 1
  add parts joined by ' ' to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Each row is stars, a gap, stars. The bottom half is the top half mirrored.
In the top half the stars shrink by one on each side while the gap grows by two. Then print the same rows in reverse order.

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: This is the void pattern turned inside out: the star blocks grow toward the middle row and shrink after it.
Use one loop over 2n - 1 rows; compute s like in the half diamond, then print s stars, 2(n - s) spaces, s stars.

for i from 1 to 2n - 1:
  s = i if i <= n else 2n - i
  add (s stars + 2(n - s) spaces + s stars)
return rows

hints.text: Which cells are on the border? Think about the row and column indexes.
A cell is a star when it's in the first or last row or the first or last column; otherwise it's a space.

for i from 0 to n - 1:
  row = empty string
  for j from 0 to n - 1:
    if i is 0 or n - 1, or j is 0 or n - 1: row += '*'
    else: row += ' '
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: n = 1 is a single row.

hints.text: Look at one cell. How far is it from the top, left, bottom and right edges?
Cell (i, j) prints n - min(i, j, size - 1 - i, size - 1 - j), where size = 2n - 1.

size = 2n - 1
for i from 0 to size - 1:
  row = empty string
  for j from 0 to size - 1:
    row += n - min(i, j, size - 1 - i, size - 1 - j)
  add row to rows
return rows

cases.note: 0 has one digit even though the loop never runs.

hints.text: Dividing by 10 and dropping the remainder removes the last digit. How many times can you do that before n becomes 0?

if n == 0: return 1

return count

hints.text: If n has a divisor bigger than sqrt(n), it also has one smaller than sqrt(n). How far must you check?
Return false for n < 2. Then try every i from 2 while i * i <= n; any i that divides n proves it isn't prime.

i = 2
while i * i <= n:

lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b. Divide before multiplying so the intermediate value stays small.

count each value in a map

hints.text: Think of sorting a hand of cards: take the next card and slide it into place among the cards already sorted.
For i from 1, save key = a[i], shift larger elements of the prefix one step right, then drop key into the gap.

cases.note: Already sorted input must stay sorted.

hints.text: Merging two sorted arrays is easy with two pointers. How can you get two sorted halves?
Recursively sort the left and right halves (a single element is already sorted), then merge them by repeatedly taking the smaller front element.

mergeSort(a):
  if length <= 1: return a
  left = mergeSort(first half), right = mergeSort(second half)
  merged = empty; i = 0; j = 0
  while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
    take the smaller of left[i], right[j] and advance it
  append what remains of left and right
  return merged

cases.note: Already sorted input must stay sorted.

hints.text: After partitioning around a pivot, the pivot is in its final position. What's left to do?
Use Lomuto partitioning: pick the last element as the pivot, move everything smaller to the front, put the pivot after them, then recurse on both sides.

quickSort(lo, hi):
  if lo >= hi: return
  pivot = nums[hi]; p = lo
  for j from lo to hi - 1:
    if nums[j] < pivot: swap nums[p], nums[j]; p += 1
  swap nums[p], nums[hi]
  quickSort(lo, p - 1); quickSort(p + 1, hi)

hints.text: One bubble pass fixes the last position. What smaller problem remains?
Write bubble(n): if n <= 1 stop; do one pass over 0..n-2 swapping out-of-order neighbours; then call bubble(n - 1).

bubble(n):
  if n <= 1: return
  for j from 0 to n - 2:
    if nums[j] > nums[j + 1]: swap them

cases.note: Already sorted input must stay sorted.

hints.text: If the first n - 1 elements are already sorted, how do you place the n-th?
insertion(n): if n <= 1 stop; call insertion(n - 1); then shift the last element left past every larger value.

insertion(n):
  if n <= 1: return
  insertion(n - 1)
  key = nums[n - 1]; j = n - 2
  while j >= 0 and nums[j] > key:
    nums[j + 1] = nums[j]; j -= 1
  nums[j + 1] = key

return nums

hints.text: Both arrays are sorted, like two queues of numbers. Which one should give up its front value next?

while i < len(a) and j < len(b):

  else if a[i] > b[j]: j += 1
  else: append a[i]; i += 1; j += 1

hints.text: Compare the array with 1..n. Which two equations relate the repeating value r and the missing value m?

plus = q / s

m = r - s
return [r, m]

hints.text: Checking every pair is O(n^2). While merging two sorted halves, can you count many inversions at once?

  count = sortCount(left half) + sortCount(right half)
  merge: when right[j] < left[i]:

upper = first index with nums[i] > x (binary search)
