count(i, rem): if i == n return 1 when rem is 0 else 0. Otherwise count(i + 1, rem - nums[i]) + count(i + 1, rem). Since values are positive you can prune rem < 0.

cases.note: '11' is the only length-2 string left out.

hints.text: Build the string one character at a time. When is putting a '1' not allowed?
Recurse with the string so far: you can always append '0', and append '1' only if the last character isn't '1'. Trying '0' before '1' produces the strings already sorted.

build(s):
  if length of s == n: add s to out; return
  build(s + '0')
  if s is empty or last of s != '1': build(s + '1')
build('')
return out

cases.note: The start is blocked.
Diagonal moves aren't allowed: no path.

hints.text: This is a depth-first search that has to explore every path, not just find one. What must you undo when you return from a cell?
From each cell try the four moves; mark the cell visited before recursing and unmark it afterwards (backtracking). Trying D, L, R, U in that order produces the paths already sorted.

cases.note: A complete graph on 4 vertices needs 4 colours.
A path is always 2-colourable.

hints.text: Colour the vertices one by one. Which colours are allowed for the current vertex?
Backtrack: for vertex v, try each colour 1..m not used by an already-coloured neighbour, recurse to v + 1, and undo the colour if the recursion fails.

cases.note: The highest bit allowed.
An index past the highest set bit is 0.

hints.text: A number with only bit i set is 1 << i. How do you test one bit of n against it?
n & (1 << i) is non-zero exactly when bit i is set. (n >> i) & 1 works too.
return (n AND (1 shifted left by i)) != 0
Which bit decides whether a number is odd?
The lowest bit is 1 for every odd number, so test n & 1.
return (n AND 1) == 1

cases.note: All bits set: unchanged.
1000 becomes 1001.

hints.text: Adding 1 to n flips its trailing 1s to 0 and its rightmost 0 to 1. How can you combine that with n?
n | (n + 1) sets the rightmost unset bit. When n is all ones, n & (n + 1) is 0: return n then.

if (n AND (n + 1)) == 0: return n
return n OR (n + 1)

cases.note: Swapping equal values must not zero them out.

hints.text: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. What happens if you XOR a into b and then XOR again?
a = a ^ b; b = a ^ b (now the original a); a = a ^ b (now the original b).

a = a XOR b
b = a XOR b
a = a XOR b
return [a, b]
Write f(n) = 1 ^ 2 ^ ... ^ n. Then the range XOR is f(r) ^ f(l - 1). Is there a pattern in f(n)?
f(n) repeats every 4: it is n when n % 4 == 0, 1 when n % 4 == 1, n + 1 when n % 4 == 2 and 0 when n % 4 == 3.

f(n):
  if n mod 4 == 0: return n
  if n mod 4 == 1: return 1
  if n mod 4 == 2: return n + 1
  return 0
return f(r) XOR f(l - 1)

cases.note: Only part of the single item fits: 7.5.
Everything fits.

hints.text: Since fractions are allowed, which item gives you the most value for each unit of weight?
Sort items by value / weight, highest first. Take whole items while they fit, then a fraction of the next one to fill the rest.

sort items by val / wt descending
total = 0
for each item:
  if wt <= capacity: total += val; capacity -= wt
  else: total += val * capacity / wt; stop
return total rounded to 2 decimals

cases.note: One job never waits.

hints.text: Running short jobs first makes every later job wait less. In what order do the jobs run?
Sort the burst times. Each job waits for the sum of the jobs before it; add up those waits with a running total and divide by n.

sort bt ascending
elapsed = 0, waiting = 0
for t in bt:
  waiting += elapsed
  elapsed += t
return (waiting / n) rounded down

cases.note: Same deadline: only one job fits.
Every job fits.

hints.text: Do the most profitable jobs first. For each one, which time slot keeps the most options open for the others?
Sort by profit descending. Put each job in the latest free slot at or before its deadline; skip it if no slot is free.

cases.note: The second meeting starts exactly when the first ends: not allowed.

hints.text: To fit the most meetings, which meeting should go first so the room frees up as early as possible?
Sort meetings by end time. Take a meeting whenever its start is strictly greater than the end of the last meeting you took.

sort meetings by end time
count = 0, lastEnd = -1
for each meeting:
  if start > lastEnd:
    count += 1
    lastEnd = end
return count

cases.note: Arriving the minute the other train leaves still needs a second platform.

hints.text: The answer is the largest number of trains at the station at the same moment. Can you sweep through events in time order?
Sort arrivals and departures separately. Walk both with two pointers: an arrival at or before the next departure adds a platform, otherwise a departure frees one. Track the maximum.

cases.note: No characters allowed: 0.
k exceeds the distinct count: the whole string.

hints.text: A window that has too many distinct characters can only get better by dropping characters from its left.
Grow the right end, counting characters in a map. While the map has more than k keys, shrink from the left (deleting keys that reach 0). Record the window length each step.

left = 0, best = 0, freq = empty map
for right from 0 to n - 1:
  freq[s[right]] += 1
  while freq has more than k keys:
    freq[s[left]] -= 1; delete it at 0; left += 1
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

cases.note: Tightening the start gives 'ab', not 'aaab'.

hints.text: Once you find a window ending at some index that contains s2 as a subsequence, can you tighten its start?

Scan forward matching s2 greedily until all of it is matched at index end. Then walk backward from end matching s2 in reverse to find the latest possible start. Record the window and restart the forward scan from start + 1.

i = 0, best = none
while i < len(s1):
  match s2 forward from i; if it never completes: stop
  end = index where the last char of s2 matched
  walk back from end matching s2 in reverse to get start
  if best is none or end - start < best length: best = (start, end)
  i = start + 1
return s1[best] or ''

cases.note: An empty list has no values.

hints.text: A linked list has no indexes. How do you get from one node to the next?
Start a pointer at head and follow .next until it becomes null, pushing each node's val.

out = []
cur = head
while cur is not null:
  append cur.val
  cur = cur.next
return out

cases.note: The only node is the tail: return null.

hints.text: To remove the last node you have to change the pointer of the node before it. How do you stop one node early?
If head.next is null, return null. Otherwise walk while cur.next.next is not null, then set cur.next = null.

if head.next is null: return null
cur = head
while cur.next.next is not null:
  cur = cur.next
cur.next = null
return head

cases.note: Deleting the tail.
k is past the end: unchanged.

hints.text: Deleting the head is different from deleting any other node. Why?
If k == 1 return head.next. Otherwise walk to node k - 1 and, if it and its next exist, skip over the next: prev.next = prev.next.next.

if head is null: return null
if k == 1: return head.next
prev = head
repeat k - 2 times while prev is not null: prev = prev.next
if prev and prev.next exist: prev.next = prev.next.next
return head

cases.note: Only the first occurrence goes.
The tail holds x.

hints.text: You need the node before the one holding x. What if x is in the head itself?
Handle head.val == x by returning head.next. Otherwise walk with prev and stop when prev.next.val == x, then unlink prev.next.

if head is null: return null
if head.val == x: return head.next
prev = head
while prev.next is not null:
  if prev.next.val == x: prev.next = prev.next.next; return head
  prev = prev.next
return head

cases.note: The new node is the whole list.

hints.text: The new node becomes the head. What should its next pointer be?
Create the node with next = head and return it. This works for an empty list too.

node = new ListNode(x)
node.next = head
return node

cases.note: The new node becomes the head.

hints.text: Find the last node: it's the one whose next is null. What if there is no node at all?
If head is null, the new node is the head. Otherwise walk to the last node and set its next to the new node.

node = new ListNode(x)
if head is null: return node
cur = head
while cur.next is not null: cur = cur.next
cur.next = node
return head

cases.note: k = length + 1 appends at the tail.

hints.text: Inserting at position 1 changes the head. For any other position, which node's next pointer changes?
If k == 1 return a new node pointing at head. Otherwise walk to node k - 1, then splice: node.next = prev.next; prev.next = node.

if k == 1: return new ListNode(x, head)
prev = head
repeat k - 2 times: prev = prev.next
prev.next = new ListNode(x, prev.next)
return head

cases.note: x is at the head: the new node becomes the head.

hints.text: You must stop at the node before the one holding x. What if the head holds x?
If head.val == x, return a new node pointing at head. Otherwise walk until cur.next.val == x and splice the new node between cur and cur.next.

if head is null: return null
if head.val == x: return new ListNode(val, head)
cur = head
while cur.next is not null:
  if cur.next.val == x: cur.next = new ListNode(val, cur.next); return head
  cur = cur.next
return head
Walk the list once. What do you increment at every node?
Keep a counter starting at 0 and add 1 for every node until the pointer becomes null.

count = 0
cur = head
while cur is not null:
  count += 1
  cur = cur.next
return count

cases.note: The key is in the tail.

hints.text: This is linear search, but following next pointers instead of indexes.
Walk the list and return true as soon as a node's val equals key; return false after the loop.

cur = head
while cur is not null:
  if cur.val == key: return true
  cur = cur.next
return false

cases.note: No 1s: the 0s must link straight to the 2s.

hints.text: You could count the values and overwrite them, but relinking works in one pass. What if you built three separate lists?
Keep three dummy heads (for 0, 1, 2) with tails. Append every node to its list, then join zero-tail to the one-list (or two-list if empty), one-tail to the two-list, and end the two-list with null.

make dummy heads z, o, t with tails
for each node: append it to the tail of its value's list
zeroTail.next = o.next if o has nodes else t.next
oneTail.next = t.next
twoTail.next = null
return z.next if z has nodes else (o.next if o has nodes else t.next)

cases.note: Every digit carries: a new leading 1.

hints.text: Addition starts from the last digit, but the list only goes forward. How can you process digits from the end?

Recurse to the end and return a carry: carry = 1 at the tail; each node sets val = val + carry, keeps val % 10 and passes floor(val / 10) back. If a carry is left at the head, add a new node 1 in front.

carryFrom(node):
  if node is null: return 1
  sum = node.val + carryFrom(node.next)
  node.val = sum mod 10
  return sum / 10 rounded down
if carryFrom(head) == 1: head = new ListNode(1, head)
return head

cases.note: A single node pointing at itself: a loop of length 1.
The whole list is the loop.

hints.text: First detect whether a cycle exists. Once two pointers meet inside the loop, how do you measure it?
Use slow and fast pointers. When they meet, keep one fixed and move the other around until it returns, counting steps.

slow = head, fast = head
while fast and fast.next exist:
  slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next
  if slow is fast:
    count = 1; cur = slow.next
    while cur is not slow: count += 1; cur = cur.next
    return count
return 0

cases.note: No nodes: return null.
The single node's prev must be null.

hints.text: Build the list left to right, remembering the last node you created. Which two pointers connect it to the new node?
Create the head from arr[0] with prev = null. For each next value, create a node, set tail.next = node and node.prev = tail, then move tail forward.

if arr is empty: return null
head = node(arr[0]); head.prev = null; tail = head
for i from 1 to n - 1:
  node = node(arr[i])
  tail.next = node; node.prev = tail
  tail = node
return head
Walk to the tail. Which node becomes the new tail, and which pointer must be cleared?
If head.next is null return null. Otherwise walk to the tail, then set tail.prev.next = null (and tail.prev = null to detach it).

if head.next is null: return null
tail = head
while tail.next is not null: tail = tail.next
tail.prev.next = null
tail.prev = null
return head

cases.note: Deleting the head: the new head's prev must be null.

hints.text: Find the k-th node. Then there are four cases: it's the only node, the head, the tail, or in the middle.
Let p = node.prev and q = node.next. If p is null the head moves to q (set q.prev = null). Otherwise p.next = q, and if q exists q.prev = p.

node = head; repeat k - 1 times: node = node.next
p = node.prev; q = node.next
if q is not null: q.prev = p
if p is null: return q
p.next = q
return head

cases.note: Removing the tail.

hints.text: With prev pointers, a node can unlink itself once you've found it. Which neighbours need updating?
Find the node. Point its prev's next at its next and its next's prev at its prev, handling a missing prev (the head moves) or a missing next.

node = head; while node.val != x: node = node.next
if node.next is not null: node.next.prev = node.prev
if node.prev is null: return node.next
node.prev.next = node.next
return head
The new node becomes the head. Which pointers on it and on the old head change?
Create the node with next = head and prev = null; if head exists set head.prev to the new node.

node = new ListNode(x, head)
node.prev = null
if head is not null: head.prev = node
return node

cases.note: One node: the new node becomes the head.

hints.text: Find the tail; the new node goes between tail.prev and tail. What if tail.prev is null?
Walk to the tail. Create node with prev = tail.prev and next = tail. If tail.prev is null, the node is the new head; otherwise tail.prev.next = node. Finally tail.prev = node.

tail = head; while tail.next is not null: tail = tail.next
node = new ListNode(x, tail); node.prev = tail.prev
if tail.prev is null: tail.prev = node; return node
tail.prev.next = node
tail.prev = node
return head

cases.note: k = 1 inserts a new head.

hints.text: Walk to the k-th node. The new node sits between it and its prev.
node.next = kth, node.prev = kth.prev. If kth.prev is null the node is the new head; otherwise kth.prev.next = node. Then kth.prev = node.

kth = head; repeat k - 1 times: kth = kth.next
node = new ListNode(x, kth); node.prev = kth.prev
if kth.prev is null: kth.prev = node; return node
kth.prev.next = node
kth.prev = node
return head

cases.note: The target is the head.

hints.text: Once you hold the target node, its prev pointer tells you where the new node goes.
Find the target node t. Create node with next = t and prev = t.prev; link t.prev.next (or make it the head if t.prev is null) and set t.prev = node.

t = head; while t.val != target: t = t.next
node = new ListNode(x, t); node.prev = t.prev
if t.prev is null: t.prev = node; return node
t.prev.next = node
t.prev = node
return head

cases.note: The list becomes empty.
The remaining node's prev must be cleared.

hints.text: The second node becomes the head. What still points back at the old head?
Take next = head.next. If it exists, set next.prev = null. Detach head.next and return next.

next = head.next
if next is not null: next.prev = null
head.next = null
return next

cases.note: Everything goes: null.
Deletions at the head and the tail.

hints.text: Unlinking one node in a doubly linked list is O(1). Can you do it while walking, without losing your place?
Walk with cur. When cur.val == key, save next = cur.next, link cur.prev and next to each other (moving head if cur was the head), then continue from next.

cur = head
while cur is not null:
  next = cur.next
  if cur.val == key:
    if cur.prev is null: head = next else cur.prev.next = next
    if next is not null: next.prev = cur.prev
  cur = next
return head

cases.note: No duplicates: unchanged.

hints.text: In a sorted list, duplicates are adjacent. For each node, how far ahead is the next different value?
From each node cur, skip forward past nodes with the same value to nxt; set cur.next = nxt and, if nxt exists, nxt.prev = cur. Move cur to nxt.

cur = head
while cur is not null:
  nxt = cur.next
  while nxt is not null and nxt.val == cur.val: nxt = nxt.next
  cur.next = nxt
  if nxt is not null: nxt.prev = cur
  cur = nxt
return head
In a sorted array you'd use two pointers from both ends. The prev pointers let you walk backwards too.

Put left at the head and right at the tail. If their sum is the target, record the pair and move both inwards; if it's too small move left forward, otherwise move right back. Stop when they meet or cross.

left = head; right = tail
while left is not right and right.next is not left:
  s = left.val + right.val
  if s == target: record [left.val, right.val]; left = left.next; right = right.prev
  else if s < target: left = left.next
  else: right = right.prev
return pairs

cases.note: Popping or reading an empty stack returns -1.
Last in, first out.

hints.text: A stack only ever touches one end. What single number tells you where that end is?
Keep an array and an index t = -1. push stores at ++t; pop returns the value at t and decrements it; top reads index t; empty means t == -1.

push(x): t += 1; arr[t] = x
pop(): if t == -1: return -1; v = arr[t]; t -= 1; return v
top(): return -1 if t == -1 else arr[t]
isEmpty(): return t == -1

cases.note: Removing from or reading an empty queue returns -1.
First in, first out.

hints.text: Removing from the front of an array by shifting is slow. What if you just remember where the front is?
Keep indexes front and rear. push writes at rear and advances it; pop reads at front and advances it. The queue is empty when front == rear.

push(x): arr[rear] = x; rear += 1
pop(): if front == rear: return -1; v = arr[front]; front += 1; return v
peek(): return -1 if front == rear else arr[front]
isEmpty(): return front == rear

cases.note: Popping or reading an empty stack returns -1.
Last in, first out.

hints.text: Which end of a singly linked list can you add to and remove from in O(1)?
Use the head as the top. push makes a new node pointing at the old head; pop moves head to head.next and returns the old value.

push(x): head = node(x, next = head)
pop(): if head is null: return -1; v = head.val; head = head.next; return v
top(): return -1 if head is null else head.val
isEmpty(): return head is null

cases.note: Removing from or reading an empty queue returns -1.
First in, first out.

hints.text: You need O(1) work at both ends. Which two node references do you keep?
Keep head (front) and tail (back). push links a new node after tail (or sets both when empty); pop advances head and clears tail when the queue empties.

push(x): n = node(x); if tail is null: head = tail = n else tail.next = n; tail = n
pop(): if head is null: return -1; v = head.val; head = head.next; if head is null: tail = null; return v
peek(): return -1 if head is null else head.val
isEmpty(): return head is null

cases.note: ^ groups right to left: abc^^.
- groups left to right: ab-c-.

hints.text: Operands go straight to the output. Operators have to wait until you know nothing tighter follows. Where do they wait?

Use an operator stack (shunting-yard). On an operator, pop to the output while the stack top binds tighter, or equally tight and the new operator isn't '^'. '(' is pushed; ')' pops until the matching '('. Pop everything at the end.

for c in s:
  if c is an operand: output c
  else if c == '(': push c
  else if c == ')': pop to output until '('; discard '('
  else:
    while top is an operator and (prec(top) > prec(c) or (prec(top) == prec(c) and c != '^')): output pop
    push c
pop the rest to output

cases.note: ^ groups right to left: ^a^bc.
- groups left to right: --abc.

hints.text: Prefix is the mirror of postfix, but associativity flips when you mirror. Can you build the postfix tree first?

One clean way: convert to postfix with shunting-yard, rebuild the expression tree from the postfix with a stack, then print it root-first. (The reverse-the-string trick also works if you handle associativity carefully.)

post = infix to postfix (shunting-yard)
stack = empty
for c in post:
  if c is an operand: push c
  else: right = pop; left = pop; push c + left + right
return pop

cases.note: A lone operand needs no parentheses.

hints.text: In prefix the operator comes before its operands. Reading from the right, when you meet an operator, its operands are already complete.
Scan right to left with a stack of strings. Push operands; on an operator pop a (left) then b (right) and push '(' + a + op + b + ')'.

for c in s from right to left:
  if c is an operand: push c
  else: a = pop; b = pop; push '(' + a + c + b + ')'
return pop
As with prefix to infix, scan from the right so operands are ready when you meet an operator.
Scan right to left with a stack. Push operands; on an operator pop a then b and push a + b + op.

for c in s from right to left:
  if c is an operand: push c
  else: a = pop; b = pop; push a + b + c
return pop
In postfix an operator follows its two operands. Which data structure gives you the two most recent complete operands?
Scan left to right with a stack of strings. Push operands; on an operator pop b (right) then a (left) and push '(' + a + op + b + ')'.

for c in s:
  if c is an operand: push c
  else: b = pop; a = pop; push '(' + a + c + b + ')'
return pop
Read the postfix left to right; each operator combines the two latest complete operands.
Use a stack of strings. Push operands; on an operator pop b then a and push op + a + b.

for c in s:
  if c is an operand: push c
  else: b = pop; a = pop; push c + a + b
return pop

cases.note: Increasing: nothing smaller to the right.
Equal isn't smaller.

hints.text: Scanning from the right, which earlier-seen values can never be anyone's answer again?
Go right to left with a stack. Pop values that are >= nums[i] (they're hidden behind nums[i]). The stack top is then the answer (or -1). Push nums[i].

stack = empty; ans = array of n
for i from n - 1 down to 0:
  while stack not empty and top >= nums[i]: pop
  ans[i] = top if stack not empty else -1
  push nums[i]
return ans

cases.note: The last index has nothing to its right.

hints.text: With at most 100 queries, a direct scan per query is fast enough. What exactly do you count?
For each query index i, scan j from i + 1 to the end and count nums[j] > nums[i]. (For many queries, a Fenwick tree over values processed right to left answers every index.)

cases.note: Alone at the party: trivially the celebrity.
Nobody knows anybody.
Person 0 is the celebrity.

hints.text: One question "does a know b?" always rules someone out. Who?
If a knows b, a isn't the celebrity; otherwise b isn't. Eliminate with two pointers (or a stack) until one candidate is left, then verify that candidate's row and column.

a = 0; b = n - 1
while a < b:
  if M[a][b] == 1: a += 1
  else: b -= 1
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  if i != a and (M[a][i] == 1 or M[i][a] == 0): return -1
return a

cases.note: Same value: nothing moves.
Tie between children: swap with the left one.

hints.text: Changing one value can only break the heap order between that node and its parent, or between it and its children.
After writing val, if it's smaller than nums[parent], keep swapping upward. Otherwise keep swapping downward with the smaller child while that child is smaller.

nums[ind] = val
if ind > 0 and nums[ind] < nums[parent(ind)]:
  while ind > 0 and nums[ind] < nums[parent]: swap; ind = parent
else:
  loop: s = index of the smaller child (left on a tie)
    if no child or nums[s] >= nums[ind]: stop
    swap nums[ind], nums[s]; ind = s

cases.note: Already a heap: nothing moves.

hints.text: Leaves are already one-element heaps. Which nodes need fixing, and in what order?
Sift down every non-leaf, starting from the last one (index n/2 - 1) and moving to the root. This is O(n) overall.

siftDown(i):
  loop: s = smaller child of i (left on a tie)
    if no child or nums[s] >= nums[i]: stop
    swap nums[i], nums[s]; i = s
for i from n / 2 - 1 down to 0: siftDown(i)
return nums

cases.note: Reading an empty heap returns -1.

hints.text: Store the heap as an array where the children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. Which operations break the order, and where?
insert appends and sifts up while smaller than the parent. extractMin swaps the root with the last element, pops it, then sifts the new root down toward the smaller child.

insert(x): append x; sift it up
getMin(): return -1 if empty else a[0]
extractMin(): if empty return -1; m = a[0]; a[0] = last; remove last; sift a[0] down; return m
heapSize(): return length of a

cases.note: Reading an empty heap returns -1.

hints.text: It's the min-heap with every comparison flipped. Where does the largest value live?
insert appends and sifts up while larger than the parent. extractMax moves the last element to the root and sifts it down toward the larger child.

insert(x): append x; sift it up while a[i] > a[parent]
getMax(): return -1 if empty else a[0]
extractMax(): if empty return -1; m = a[0]; a[0] = last; remove last; sift down toward the larger child; return m
heapSize(): return length of a

cases.note: Equal values are allowed.

hints.text: Only parent-child pairs matter. Which indexes are parents?
Check every i from 0 to n/2 - 1 against its existing children; any child smaller than its parent breaks the heap.

for i from 0 to n / 2 - 1:
  if 2i + 1 < n and nums[2i + 1] < nums[i]: return false
  if 2i + 2 < n and nums[2i + 2] < nums[i]: return false
return true
The existing min-heap order doesn't help much. Treat the array as unordered and build a max-heap.
Run the bottom-up build with flipped comparisons: sift down every non-leaf from the last one to the root, swapping with the larger child.

siftDown(i):
  loop: b = larger child of i (left on a tie)
    if no child or nums[b] <= nums[i]: stop
    swap nums[i], nums[b]; i = b
for i from n / 2 - 1 down to 0: siftDown(i)
return nums

cases.note: Already sorted input must stay sorted.

hints.text: A max heap keeps the largest value at index 0. How can you use that to fill the array from the back?
Heapify the array bottom-up (sift down every index from n/2 - 1 to 0). Then for end from n - 1 down to 1: swap a[0] with a[end] and sift a[0] down within the first end elements.

cases.note: Equal values share rank 1.

hints.text: If you list the distinct values in increasing order, what is each value's rank?
Sort a copy (or pop from a min-heap), give each new distinct value the next rank in a map, then map every original element to its rank.

sorted = distinct values of nums in increasing order
rank = map value -> position in sorted + 1
return [rank[x] for x in nums]

cases.note: Nothing to join: cost 0.

hints.text: A stick joined early is paid for again in every later join. Which sticks should be joined first?
Always join the two shortest sticks (a min-heap does this efficiently) and push their sum back. Add every join's cost.

heap = min-heap of sticks
cost = 0
while heap has more than one stick:
  a = pop; b = pop
  cost += a + b
  push a + b
return cost

cases.note: Different index pairs with equal sums all count.

hints.text: After sorting both arrays descending, the largest sum is a[0] + b[0]. Which pairs can be the next largest?
Use a max-heap of (sum, i, j) seeded with (0, 0). Each time you pop (i, j), push (i + 1, j) and (i, j + 1) if you haven't seen them. Pop k times.

sort a and b descending
heap = max-heap with (a[0] + b[0], 0, 0); seen = {(0, 0)}
repeat k times:
  (s, i, j) = pop; append s
  for (x, y) in (i + 1, j), (i, j + 1):
    if inside and not seen: push (a[x] + b[y], x, y); mark seen
return answers

cases.note: No nodes: three empty lists.

hints.text: Each node is visited three times in a DFS: on the way down, between its children, and on the way up. Which traversal records which visit?

Push (node, 1). When you pop a pair: state 1 records preorder and goes left, state 2 records inorder and goes right, state 3 records postorder. Re-push the node with the next state before pushing a child.

cases.note: A leaf has no children to compare against.

hints.text: The rule is local: each node only needs its own children. What do you check per node?
Recurse. A null node or a leaf is fine. Otherwise compare node.val with (left ? left.val : 0) + (right ? right.val : 0) and require both subtrees to pass.

check(node):
  if node is null or a leaf: return true
  sum = value of left (or 0) + value of right (or 0)
  return node.val == sum and check(node.left) and check(node.right)

cases.note: The root is also the only leaf: it appears once.
A left-only chain: left boundary, then the single leaf.

hints.text: Split the boundary into three independent walks, being careful not to count a leaf twice.

Walk the left edge (skip leaves), collect leaves with a DFS (left before right), walk the right edge (skip leaves) and append it reversed. Add the root first unless it is itself a leaf (the leaf DFS adds it then).

if root is null: return []
res = [root] if root is not a leaf else []
walk n = root.left: while n: if n is not a leaf: res.add(n); n = n.left or n.right
add every leaf in DFS order (left first)
walk n = root.right collecting non-leaves into tmp; n = n.right or n.left
res += reverse(tmp)
return res

cases.note: Nodes 4 and 5 share column 0 with the root, which is on top.

hints.text: Give the root column 0, a left child column - 1 and a right child column + 1.
BFS visits nodes in level order, so the first node you meet in each column is the top one. Keep a map column -> value and only set it once.

queue = [(root, 0)]; top = map
while queue not empty:
  (node, col) = dequeue
  if col not in top: top[col] = node.val
  enqueue (node.left, col - 1), (node.right, col + 1) when present
return top values by increasing col

cases.note: Nodes 4 and 5 tie at depth 2 in column 0: the later one in level order wins.

hints.text: Give the root column 0, a left child column - 1 and a right child column + 1.
BFS in level order and overwrite map[column] every time: the last write per column is the deepest node, and among equal depths the rightmost in level order.

queue = [(root, 0)]; bottom = map
while queue not empty:
  (node, col) = dequeue
  bottom[col] = node.val
  enqueue (node.left, col - 1), (node.right, col + 1) when present
return bottom values by increasing col

cases.note: The root is a leaf: one path of length 1.

hints.text: A DFS that goes left before right reaches the leaves in left-to-right order. What do you carry along the way?
Keep the current path in a list. Push the node, record a copy at a leaf, recurse into children, then pop (backtrack).

cases.note: Only the start node: it burns at time 0.
Fire climbs the whole chain.

hints.text: Fire moves upward too, but tree nodes don't point to their parents. How can you make the tree an undirected graph?
Record each node's parent with one traversal, then BFS from the start node over left, right and parent, counting levels. The answer is the last level reached.

cases.note: Two inorder traversals can't split left from right.
Preorder and postorder alone are ambiguous.

hints.text: Preorder and postorder both tell you the root, but neither tells you which nodes go left and which go right.
Inorder splits the remaining nodes into left and right subtrees around the root. You need inorder plus one of the other two, and two copies of the same traversal add nothing.
return a != b and (a == 2 or b == 2)

cases.note: The key itself is both floor and ceil.
Nothing is <= 3: floor is -1.
Nothing is >= 20: ceil is -1.

hints.text: Walking down a BST is a binary search. Each node you pass is a candidate for one of the two answers.
Do two walks (or one). For the floor: when node.val <= key it's a candidate, go right; otherwise go left. For the ceil, mirror it.

floor = -1; n = root
while n: if n.val == key: floor = key; stop
  if n.val < key: floor = n.val; n = n.right else n = n.left
ceil = -1; n = root
while n: if n.val == key: ceil = key; stop
  if n.val > key: ceil = n.val; n = n.left else n = n.right
return [floor, ceil]

cases.note: One node is both the minimum and the maximum.

hints.text: In a BST every smaller value is to the left. Where is the smallest one?
Follow left pointers to the end for the minimum and right pointers to the end for the maximum. No need to visit the rest of the tree.

lo = root; while lo.left: lo = lo.left
hi = root; while hi.right: hi = hi.right
return [lo.val, hi.val]

cases.note: The key itself doesn't count: both are -1.
Nothing smaller than 1.
15 is the largest value: no successor.

hints.text: This is floor and ceil with strict comparisons. What changes when node.val == key?
For the successor: when node.val > key record it and go left, otherwise go right. For the predecessor: when node.val < key record it and go right, otherwise go left.

pred = -1; n = root
while n: if n.val < key: pred = n.val; n = n.right else n = n.left
succ = -1; n = root
while n: if n.val > key: succ = n.val; n = n.left else n = n.right
return [pred, succ]

cases.note: A single node is a BST of size 1.
Equal values break the strict order: only the leaves count.

hints.text: Checking every subtree from scratch is O(n^2). What could each child report upward so the parent decides in O(1)?
Postorder: each subtree returns (size, min, max, isBST). A node is a BST root when both children are BSTs and left.max < node.val < right.min. Track the best size seen.

cases.note: Vertices 1 and 2 aren't reachable from 0.

hints.text: Both traversals mark vertices as visited so nothing is processed twice. What differs is the order in which pending vertices are taken.
BFS uses a queue and marks a vertex when it's enqueued. DFS recurses into each unvisited neighbour in adjacency order, recording a vertex when it's first entered.

bfs: seen = {0}; queue = [0]
  while queue: u = dequeue; record u
    for v in adj[u]: if v not seen: mark; enqueue v
dfs(u): mark u; record u
  for v in adj[u]: if v not seen: dfs(v)
return [bfs order, dfs order from 0]

cases.note: No edges: every vertex is its own component.

hints.text: Each traversal started from an unvisited vertex covers exactly one component.
Either run DFS/BFS from every unvisited vertex and count the starts, or union the endpoints of every edge in a disjoint set and count the roots.

parent[i] = i for all i; count = V
for (u, v) in edges:
  a = find(u); b = find(v)
  if a != b: parent[a] = b; count -= 1
return count

cases.note: All water: zero islands.
An L and a mirrored L are different shapes.

hints.text: Translation doesn't change the offsets of an island's cells from its first cell. How can that become a key?
Flood-fill each island from its first cell (in row-major order), record every cell as (row - r0, col - c0), turn the list into a string and add it to a set.

shapes = set
for each land cell (r0, c0) not yet seen:
  cells = flood fill from it, marking seen
  key = sorted list of (r - r0, c - c0) as a string
  shapes.add(key)
return size of shapes

cases.note: No edges: 0, 1, 2.
A chain forces the only order.

hints.text: A vertex can be placed once every edge into it has been satisfied. Which vertices can start?
Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degrees, keep the vertices with in-degree 0 in a min-heap, repeatedly take the smallest, output it and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees.

indeg = in-degree of every vertex
ready = min-heap of vertices with indeg 0
while ready not empty:
  u = pop smallest; output u
  for v in out[u]: indeg[v] -= 1; if indeg[v] == 0: push v
return output

cases.note: No pair differs: every letter is free, so alphabetical order.

hints.text: Two adjacent words tell you exactly one thing: the order of the first letters where they differ.
Build a graph on the k letters with an edge from a[i] to b[i] at the first difference of every adjacent pair, then run Kahn's algorithm, always taking the smallest ready letter.

for each adjacent pair (a, b):
  i = first index where a[i] != b[i]; if found: add edge a[i] -> b[i]
ready = min-heap of letters with in-degree 0
while ready not empty:
  c = pop smallest; append c
  for d in out[c]: indeg[d] -= 1; if 0: push d
return the string

cases.note: Vertices 1 and 2 aren't reachable from 0.
Edges into 0 never help.

hints.text: In a DAG you can process vertices so that every edge into a vertex is handled before you leave it.
Get a topological order, set dist[0] = 0, and relax every outgoing edge of each vertex in that order. Each edge is relaxed once.

cases.note: Vertex 2 is isolated.

hints.text: When every edge costs the same, which traversal reaches vertices in order of distance?
BFS from src: the first time you reach a vertex, its distance is its parent's distance + 1.

cases.note: Zero-weight edges are allowed.

hints.text: With non-negative weights, the closest unfinished vertex can't get any closer. Why?
Keep a min-heap of (distance, vertex). Pop the smallest, skip it if stale, and relax its edges, pushing improved distances.

cases.note: Vertex 3 is unreachable.
The direct edge loses to the cheaper detour.

hints.text: Dijkstra gives distances. What extra bit of information per vertex lets you rebuild the path?
Whenever you improve dist[v] through u, set parent[v] = u. After Dijkstra, walk parent pointers back from n to 1 and reverse.

run Dijkstra from 1, setting parent[v] = u on every improvement
if dist[n] is infinite: return [-1]
path = []; x = n
while x != 1: path.add(x); x = parent[x]
path.add(1)
return reverse(path)

cases.note: Already there: 0 steps.
Powers of two never give 3.
Multiplying 7 by 10 five times wraps to 0.

hints.text: There are only 100000 possible values. Think of each value as a vertex and each multiplication as an edge of cost 1.
BFS from start over values 0..99999, with neighbours (x * a) % 100000 for every a in arr. The level at which you first reach end is the answer.

if start == end: return 0
dist = -1 for all 100000 values; dist[start] = 0; queue = [start]
while queue not empty:
  x = dequeue
  for a in arr:
    y = (x * a) % 100000
    if dist[y] == -1: dist[y] = dist[x] + 1; if y == end: return dist[y]; enqueue y
return -1

cases.note: 1 -> 2 -> 1 has weight -1: a negative cycle.
The negative cycle isn't reachable from 0, so distances are returned.

hints.text: A shortest path without cycles uses at most V - 1 edges. How many rounds of relaxing every edge does that need?
Relax all edges V - 1 times (skipping edges out of unreached vertices). If one more round still improves a distance, a reachable negative cycle exists.

dist = INF everywhere; dist[src] = 0
repeat V - 1 times:
  for (u, v, w) in edges:
    if dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]: dist[v] = dist[u] + w
for (u, v, w) in edges:
  if dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]: return [-1]
return dist

cases.note: No edges at all.
Going through vertex 2 beats the direct edge.

hints.text: Build shortest paths by gradually allowing more intermediate vertices.
Replace -1 with infinity. For each k, for each pair (i, j), dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). Convert infinity back to -1.

cases.note: Every element is in its own set.

hints.text: Represent each set as a tree whose root is the set's name. When are two elements in the same set?
find(x) follows parents to the root, pointing every visited node straight at the root. unionSets links the smaller tree's root under the larger one. connected compares roots.

find(x): if parent[x] is unset: parent[x] = x; size[x] = 1
  if parent[x] != x: parent[x] = find(parent[x])
  return parent[x]
unionSets(u, v): a = find(u); b = find(v); if a == b: return
  attach the smaller of a, b under the larger; add sizes
connected(u, v): return find(u) == find(v)

cases.note: One vertex: an empty tree of weight 0.
Parallel edges: take the cheaper.

hints.text: The cheapest edge that joins two separate pieces is always safe to take. Why?
Kruskal: sort edges by weight and add each edge whose endpoints are in different disjoint sets. (Prim's algorithm with a min-heap also works.)

cases.note: Re-adding land changes nothing.
The middle cell joins two islands into one.

hints.text: Recounting the whole grid after every operation is too slow. How does one new land cell change the count?
Use a disjoint set over cells. A new land cell adds one island, then every union with a different neighbouring island removes one. Re-adding an existing land cell changes nothing.

cases.note: A lone vertex: removing it leaves zero components, fewer than before.
A cycle has no articulation point.

hints.text: In a DFS tree, a vertex is critical if some child's subtree has no back edge climbing above that vertex.

Tarjan: record discovery time tin and low (smallest tin reachable via the subtree plus one back edge). A non-root u is an articulation point if some child v has low[v] >= tin[u]; the root is one if it has two or more DFS children.

dfs(u, parent):
  tin[u] = low[u] = timer++; children = 0
  for v in adj[u]: if v == parent: continue
    if v visited: low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v])
    else: dfs(v, u); low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]); children += 1
      if parent != -1 and low[v] >= tin[u]: mark u
  if parent == -1 and children > 1: mark u
run dfs from every unvisited vertex; return marked vertices sorted, or [-1]

cases.note: Already on the last stair.

hints.text: The cheapest way to reach stair i only depends on the cheapest ways to reach i - 1 and i - 2.
dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + |h[i]-h[i-1]|, dp[i-2] + |h[i]-h[i-2]|). Two variables are enough instead of an array.

prev2 = 0; prev = 0
for i from 1 to n - 1:
  one = prev + |h[i] - h[i-1]|
  two = prev2 + |h[i] - h[i-2]| if i > 1 else infinity
  prev2 = prev; prev = min(one, two)
return prev

cases.note: k reaches the last stair directly.
k = 1 means stepping on every stair.

hints.text: Stair i can be reached from any of the k stairs before it.
dp[0] = 0 and dp[i] = min over j in 1..k (j <= i) of dp[i-j] + |h[i] - h[i-j]|.
The only thing day i needs to know about the past is which activity was done yesterday.
Let best[j] be the max merit up to today ending with activity j. Then newBest[j] = points[i][j] + max of best over the other two activities.

cases.note: The empty subset sums to 0.
All even: an odd target is impossible.

hints.text: Each element is either taken or skipped. What do you need to remember after deciding the first i elements?
Keep a boolean array can[s] of reachable sums. For each element x, update s from target down to x: can[s] = can[s] or can[s - x].

cases.note: Each zero can be in or out: 4 ways.

hints.text: It's subset sum, but you count ways instead of asking whether any exists.
ways[s] starts as [1, 0, 0, ...]. For each element x, for s from k down to x: ways[s] += ways[s - x]. Zeros double every count, which this handles automatically.

cases.note: The difference is bigger than the total.

hints.text: If S1 - S2 = diff and S1 + S2 = total, what must S2 add up to?
S2 = (total - diff) / 2. If that's negative or not an integer there are no ways; otherwise count the subsets that sum to it.

total = sum(arr)
if total < diff or (total - diff) is odd: return 0
t = (total - diff) / 2
ways = [0] * (t + 1); ways[0] = 1
for x in arr: for s from t down to x: ways[s] += ways[s - x] (mod M)
return ways[t]

cases.note: Nothing fits.
Each item can be used only once.

hints.text: For each item you either take it or not. Which smaller problem does each choice leave?
best[c] = best value with capacity c using the items so far. For each item go c from W down to wt[i] (so it's used once): best[c] = max(best[c], best[c - wt[i]] + val[i]).

cases.note: Five copies of the same item.

hints.text: Compared with 0/1 knapsack, taking an item doesn't remove it. How does that change the loop direction?
Go c upward from wt[i] to W: best[c] = max(best[c], best[c - wt[i]] + val[i]). best[c - wt[i]] may already include item i, which is exactly what's allowed.

cases.note: Equal prices: cut into unit pieces.

hints.text: Piece lengths can repeat. Which knapsack variant is this?
It's unbounded knapsack with item weights 1..n, values price, and capacity n: best[L] = max over piece lengths p <= L of price[p-1] + best[L-p].

cases.note: Strictly increasing: only one element fits.
Every element is an LIS of length 1; the earliest index wins.

hints.text: To choose the earliest possible first index, you need to know how long an increasing subsequence can be when it *starts* at each index.

Compute from[i] = length of the LIS starting at i (right to left, O(n^2)). Then build the answer greedily: take the first index with from = L, then the first later index with a bigger value and from = L - 1, and so on.

cases.note: Equal neighbours aren't strictly up or down.
Purely increasing counts.

hints.text: Every bitonic subsequence has a peak. What do you need to know on each side of a peak?
inc[i] = LIS ending at i (from the left); dec[i] = longest strictly decreasing subsequence starting at i (an LIS from the right). The answer is max of inc[i] + dec[i] - 1.

cases.note: No shared character.

hints.text: Unlike the longest common subsequence, a mismatch breaks the run completely.
dp[i][j] = length of the common substring ending exactly at s1[i-1] and s2[j-1]: dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 when the characters match, else 0. The answer is the largest dp value.

cases.note: Every non-empty subset is a palindrome: 15.

hints.text: Count by interval: how many palindromic subsequences live inside s[i..j]?
dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j] + dp[i][j-1] - dp[i+1][j-1] (inclusion-exclusion). When s[i] == s[j], add dp[i+1][j-1] + 1 for the palindromes wrapped by that pair.

dp[i][i] = 1
for len from 2 to n:
  for each window i..j of that length:
    dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j] + dp[i][j-1] - dp[i+1][j-1]
    if s[i] == s[j]: dp[i][j] += dp[i+1][j-1] + 1
    (empty windows count 0; keep everything mod M)
return dp[0][n-1]

cases.note: A single matrix: nothing to multiply.

hints.text: The last multiplication splits the chain into a left part and a right part. Try every split point.
cost(i, j) for matrices i..j = min over k in [i, j) of cost(i, k) + cost(k+1, j) + dims[i-1] * dims[k] * dims[j]. Fill it by increasing chain length.

cases.note: A lone F can't be true.

hints.text: The last operator evaluated splits the expression in two. To combine sides you need, for each side, the number of ways to get true and to get false.
For every interval of operands keep [ways true, ways false]. For each operator k inside it, combine the left and right pairs using the operator's truth table and add up.

cases.note: Erasing a missing word does nothing.
A longer prefix than the word, and a proper prefix that isn't a word.

hints.text: A plain trie marks where words end. What two counters per node answer both count queries?

Each node keeps pass (words going through it) and end (words ending at it). insert increments pass along the path and end at the last node; erase decrements them (only if the word is present); the queries read end or pass at the last node.

insert(w): n = root; for c in w: n = child(n, c) creating it; n.pass += 1
  n.end += 1
countWordsEqualTo(w): walk w; return 0 if missing else node.end
countWordsStartingWith(p): walk p; return 0 if missing else node.pass
erase(w): if countWordsEqualTo(w) == 0: return
  n = root; for c in w: n = n.child[c]; n.pass -= 1
  n.end -= 1

cases.note: Equal lengths: the lexicographically smaller one wins.
No word has its first letter as a word.

hints.text: Put every word in a trie with an end marker. What must be true along the path of a qualifying word?
A word qualifies when every node on its path is marked as the end of some word. Check each word, keeping the longest (then lexicographically smallest).

cases.note: Only a, aa, aaa, aaaa.
Upper and lower case are different characters.

hints.text: Every substring is a prefix of some suffix. Which structure stores many prefixes while sharing the common ones?
Insert every suffix of s into a trie, character by character. Every newly created node is a new distinct substring, so count node creations.

root = empty trie node; count = 0
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  node = root
  for j from i to n - 1:
    if s[j] is not a child of node: create it; count += 1
    node = child s[j]
return count

cases.note: Overlapping matches all count.
Pattern as long as the text.

hints.text: Comparing the pattern at every position is O(n * m). Can a number summarise each window so most comparisons are a single check?

Hash the pattern and the first window with a polynomial hash mod a prime. Slide the window: remove the leading character's term, multiply by the base, add the new character. When hashes match, confirm with a direct comparison.

cases.note: No later position starts with 'a'.

hints.text: Comparing from scratch at every i is O(n^2). Once you have matched a window [l, r) against the prefix, what do you already know about positions inside it?
Keep the rightmost window [l, r) that matches a prefix. For i < r, start z[i] at min(r - i, z[i - l]); then extend by direct comparison and move the window if you pass r.
If the border of s[0..i-1] has length k and s[i] == s[k], the border grows to k + 1. What if they differ?
On a mismatch, fall back to the next shorter border, k = lps[k - 1], and try again; stop at k = 0. Each step either extends or shrinks k, so the total work is linear.

lps = [0] * n; k = 0
for i from 1 to n - 1:
  while k > 0 and s[i] != s[k]: k = lps[k - 1]
  if s[i] == s[k]: k += 1
  lps[i] = k
return lps

cases.note: No primes up to 1.

hints.text: Testing each number by trial division repeats a lot of work. What if each prime crossed out its own multiples?
Sieve: mark all numbers from 2 as prime; for each p with p * p <= n that's still marked, cross out p * p, p * p + p, ... Collect what stays marked.

cases.note: 1 has no prime factors.
2 repeated ten times.

hints.text: If you divide out each factor as soon as you find it, which divisors can still divide what's left?
Try d = 2, 3, 4, ... while d * d <= n, dividing n by d as long as it divides (composite d never divide by then). Whatever is left above 1 is one last prime.

cases.note: No characters: the count is 0.
Uppercase vowels count too.
No vowels at all.

hints.text: Look at one character at a time. What question do you ask about each one?
Keep a counter. For each character, check whether it is one of aeiou or AEIOU (a small set or string of vowels makes the check easy) and add 1 when it is.

cases.note: A string of one repeated character reads the same reversed.

hints.text: Which character of s comes first in the answer?
Walk s from the last index down to 0 and append each character to a result string.

out = ""
for i from n - 1 down to 0:
  out = out + s[i]
return out

cases.note: The empty string is a palindrome.
Case matters: 'A' and 'a' are different characters.

hints.text: If s is a palindrome, how does its first character relate to its last?
Compare s[i] with s[n - 1 - i] for every i in the first half. Any mismatch means false; reaching the middle means true.

cases.note: Uppercase 'A' is a different character.

hints.text: This is the counting pattern from arrays, applied to characters.
Start a counter at 0 and add 1 for every index where s[i] equals c exactly.

cases.note: '{' and '`' sit right next to the letters in ASCII: only a-z change.
Already uppercase: nothing changes.

hints.text: Lowercase and uppercase letters sit in two runs of the ASCII table. How far apart are 'a' and 'A'?
'a' is 97 and 'A' is 65, so subtract 32 from the code of any character between 97 and 122. Leave everything else untouched.

cases.note: Only spaces: there are no words.
Trailing spaces don't start a word.

input: b   a ab bb b  a

hints.text: Splitting on a single space breaks on double spaces. What marks the start of a new word instead?
A word starts at a non-space character whose previous character is a space (or that is the first character). Count those starts.

cases.note: Every character repeats: return -1.
The only unique character is the last one.

hints.text: To know a character is unique you need to have seen the whole string. How many passes does that suggest?
Pass one counts every character. Pass two walks s again and returns the first index whose count is 1, or -1 if none is.

count = empty map
for each ch in s: count[ch] += 1
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  if count[s[i]] == 1: return i
return -1

cases.note: Everything is the same value: 1 distinct.
0 is a value like any other; truthiness checks skip it.

hints.text: Comparing every pair is O(n^2). What structure answers 'have I seen this value before?' in O(1)?
Put every value into a Set; duplicates collapse automatically. The Set's size is the answer.

seen = empty set
for each value in nums:
  add value to seen
return size of seen

cases.note: Tie between -2 and 5: the smaller value wins.

hints.text: First learn how often every value appears. Then the question is a simple 'best so far' scan.
Build a value -> count map. Walk its entries and keep the value with the larger count, breaking ties by the smaller value.

count = empty map
for each v in nums: count[v] += 1
best = none
for each (v, c) in count:
  if best is none or c > count[best] or (c == count[best] and v < best):
    best = v
return best

cases.note: Same set of values, different counts: false.
Different lengths never match.

hints.text: Order doesn't matter, but counts do. What could you compare instead of the arrays themselves?
Count a into a map, then subtract every value of b. The arrays match when the lengths are equal and no count goes below zero.

if len(a) != len(b): return false
count = counts of a
for each v in b:

  count[v] -= 1
return true

cases.note: One element can't pair with itself.
Three zeros make three pairs.

hints.text: For each element, the partner it needs is k - nums[j]. How many such partners appeared before it?
Scan left to right with a count map of values seen so far. For each value add count[k - value] to the answer, then record the value itself.

seen = empty map
pairs = 0
for each v in nums:
  pairs += seen[k - v] (0 if missing)
  seen[v] += 1
return pairs

cases.note: The base case on its own.
1000 nested calls: fine for recursion depth here.

hints.text: If you already had the list for n - 1, what single step turns it into the list for n?
Base case: n == 1 gives [1]. Otherwise recurse on n - 1 and append n to the result.

printOneToN(n):
  if n == 1: return [1]
  rest = printOneToN(n - 1)
  append n to rest
  return rest

cases.note: The base case on its own.

hints.text: Same idea as 1 to N, but where does n go relative to the smaller answer?
Base case: n == 1 gives [1]. Otherwise put n in front of printNToOne(n - 1).

cases.note: Equal values stay next to each other.

hints.text: If the rest of the stack (without the top) were already sorted, where would the popped top have to go?
Pop the top, sort the rest recursively, then insert the value back with a second recursion: while the top is bigger, pop it, insert below, and push it back.

sortStack(st):
  if st is empty: return st
  x = pop st
  sortStack(st)
  insert(st, x)
insert(st, x):
  if st empty or top <= x: push x; return
  y = pop st
  insert(st, x)
  push y

cases.note: The last symbol of row 30: 2^29 positions.
The first position of the second half.

hints.text: Row n is row n - 1 followed by its complement. Which half of row n does position k fall in?
If k is in the first half, the answer is the same as kthGrammar(n - 1, k). In the second half, it's the flip of kthGrammar(n - 1, k - half).

cases.note: k = 1 removes in order: the last friend wins.

hints.text: After the first friend leaves, the game is the same game with n - 1 friends, just starting from a shifted position.
Josephus: with 0-based seats, J(1) = 0 and J(n) = (J(n - 1) + k) mod n. Add 1 at the end.

winner(n, k):
  if n == 1: return 0
  return (winner(n - 1, k) + k) mod n
answer = winner(n, k) + 1

cases.note: One node: its prev and next both stay null.

hints.text: In a doubly linked list every node already knows its neighbour on both sides. What changes for one node when the list is reversed?
Walk the list and swap each node's next and prev. The last node you touch becomes the new head.

cur = head, newHead = null
while cur is not null:
  swap cur.next and cur.prev
  newHead = cur
  cur = cur.prev
return newHead

cases.note: A single node pointing at itself: the loop starts at 0.
The tail points at itself.

hints.text: A set of visited nodes finds the first repeated node in O(n) memory. Can fast and slow pointers find it in O(1)?
After slow and fast meet inside the loop, move one pointer back to head and advance both one step at a time: they meet at the loop's start. Count the steps from head.

slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
  slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next
  if slow is fast:
    p = head, i = 0
    while p is not slow: p = p.next; slow = slow.next; i += 1
    return i
return -1

cases.note: The list becomes empty.

hints.text: Which node becomes the first one once the head is gone?
Return head.next. Detaching the old head (head.next = null) is tidy but not required.

newHead = head.next
head.next = null
return newHead

cases.note: A power of two: every lower bit turns on.
All 31 bits set: the complement is 0.

hints.text: Only the bits up to num's highest set bit flip; leading zeros stay zero.
Build a mask of all 1s as wide as num (the smallest 2^k - 1 that is >= num) and return mask - num, which equals mask ^ num.

mask = 1
while mask <= num: mask = mask * 2
return mask - 1 - num

cases.note: 0x55555555: 31 alternating bits.

hints.text: If the bits alternate, n and n >> 1 differ in every position up to the top bit.
x = n ^ (n >> 1) is then all 1s, and a number of all 1s satisfies x & (x + 1) == 0.

x = n XOR (n >> 1)
return (x AND (x + 1)) == 0
The array is start, start + 2, start + 4, ... You don't need to store it.
Loop i from 0 to n - 1 and XOR start + 2 * i into the answer.

x = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 1:

return x

arr[i + 1] = encoded[i] ^ arr[i]. Start from first and walk forward.

arr = [first]
for e in encoded:

return arr

arr[0] = pref[0] and arr[i] = pref[i] ^ pref[i - 1].

arr[0] = pref[0]
for i in 1 .. n - 1:

return arr

cases.note: 1 ^ 2 ^ 3 = 0: both split points work.

hints.text: a == b means a ^ b == 0, i.e. the XOR of arr[i..k] is 0. Then every j in (i, k] works.
For each pair i < k whose range XOR is 0 (use prefix XORs or a running XOR), add k - i.
Comparing all pairs is O(n^2). Count one bit position at a time instead.
If c numbers have bit b set and n - c don't, that bit contributes c * (n - c) to the total.

total = 0
for b in 0 .. 30:
  c = count of x in nums with bit b set
  total = total + c * (n - c)
return total

cases.note: Every pair shares a letter: 0.

hints.text: Two words share no letters when their sets of letters don't intersect. A 26-bit mask per word turns that into one AND.
Build mask[i] with bit (c - 'a') set for each letter. For each pair with mask[i] & mask[j] == 0, take the product of lengths.

cases.note: No bit is shared: the best is one number.

hints.text: An AND is non-zero exactly when some single bit is set in every chosen number.
For each bit position, count how many candidates have it. The best combination takes all of them for the most common bit.

best = 0
for b in 0 .. 30:
  best = max(best, count of x in candidates with bit b set)
return best

cases.note: num1 has fewer bits than needed: fill from the bottom.
Only one bit allowed: keep num1's highest.

hints.text: x must have as many set bits as num2. To make x ^ num1 small, x should copy num1's set bits, highest first.
Let c = popcount(num2). Take num1's set bits from the top while c > 0. If bits remain, fill num1's unset bits from the bottom.
Each nums1[i] appears in len(nums2) pairs. XORing a value an even number of times cancels it.
If len(nums2) is odd, nums1's XOR survives; if len(nums1) is odd, nums2's XOR survives. Combine them.

cases.note: A continuation byte with no leading byte.
11111111 is never a valid leading byte.
A full 4-byte character.

hints.text: The leading byte's high bits say how long the character is: 0xxxxxxx is 1 byte, 110xxxxx is 2, 1110xxxx is 3, 11110xxx is 4. Continuation bytes are 10xxxxxx.
Walk the bytes keeping a count of continuation bytes still owed. A leading 10 with nothing owed, or a non-10 byte while something is owed, is invalid.

need = 0
for b in data:
  if need == 0:
    if b >> 7 == 0: continue
    else if b >> 5 == 6: need = 1
    else if b >> 4 == 14: need = 2
    else if b >> 3 == 30: need = 3
    else: return false
  else if b >> 6 == 2: need = need - 1
  else: return false
return need == 0

k = x ^ (2^maximumBit - 1). Keep a running XOR, answer, then XOR out the last element for the next query.

x = XOR of nums, mask = 2^maximumBit - 1, out = []
for i from n - 1 down to 0:
  append x XOR mask to out
  x = x XOR nums[i]
return out

cases.note: OR stays 0: one element is enough.
Every bit lives in a different element.

hints.text: The best OR starting at i is the OR of the whole suffix. You need to reach, for every bit in it, the nearest index at or after i that has that bit.
Scan from the right, keeping last[b] = the nearest index with bit b. For each i, the answer is max(last[b]) - i + 1 over known bits (at least 1).

last[b] = -1 for every bit
for i from n - 1 down to 0:
  for each bit b set in nums[i]: last[b] = i
  far = i
  for each bit b with last[b] != -1: far = max(far, last[b])
  ans[i] = far - i + 1
return ans

cases.note: Even the whole array's OR is too small.
k = 0: any single element is enough.

hints.text: OR only grows as a window widens, so a sliding window works, but you can't 'un-OR' a value directly.
Keep a count of how many window elements have each bit. Removing nums[left] decrements its bits; a bit is in the OR while its count is positive.

cnt[b] = 0 for every bit, left = 0, best = infinity
for right in 0 .. n - 1:
  add the bits of nums[right] to cnt
  while left <= right and OR(cnt) >= k:
    best = min(best, right - left + 1)
    remove the bits of nums[left] from cnt, left = left + 1
return -1 if best is infinity else best

cases.note: 4 adds a new bit length: 11011100.

hints.text: Appending i's binary digits to x is x * 2^len(i) + i. Take the modulus after every step.
The bit length grows by one exactly when i is a power of two (i & (i - 1) == 0).

MOD = 1e9 + 7, x = 0, len = 0
for i in 1 .. n:
  if i AND (i - 1) == 0: len = len + 1
  x = (x * 2^len + i) mod MOD
return x
Clearing just the top bit 2^k takes 2^(k+1) - 1 steps. The allowed moves are exactly the steps of a Gray code.
f(n) = (2^(k+1) - 1) - f(n without its top bit), where 2^k is n's top bit. Equivalently the answer is the inverse Gray code: n ^ (n >> 1) ^ (n >> 2) ^ ...

ans = 0
while n > 0:
  ans = ans XOR n
  n = n >> 1
return ans
Each pair contributes its smaller value. Pairing a small number with a much bigger one wastes the big one.
Sort and pair neighbours: the answer is the sum of the values at even indexes.

sort nums
sum = 0
for i in 0, 2, 4, ...: sum = sum + nums[i]
return sum

cases.note: 1 + 2 = 3 is degenerate, not a triangle.

hints.text: Three sides a <= b <= c form a triangle exactly when a + b > c.
Sort descending and check consecutive triples: for the largest c, the best partners are the next two largest values.

sort nums descending
for i in 0 .. n - 3:
  if nums[i + 1] + nums[i + 2] > nums[i]: return nums[i] + nums[i + 1] + nums[i + 2]
return 0

cases.note: The only 6 is the last digit.

hints.text: Turning a 6 into a 9 helps more the further left it is.
Change the leftmost 6 to a 9 (if there is one).

cases.note: Balanced only at the very end.

hints.text: Cut as soon as a piece is balanced: waiting can only merge pieces.
Keep a counter (+1 for R, -1 for L). Every time it returns to 0, count a piece.

bal = 0, pieces = 0
for c in s:
  bal = bal + (1 if c == 'R' else -1)
  if bal == 0: pieces = pieces + 1
return pieces

cases.note: Only one odd chip has to pay.

hints.text: Moving by 2 is free, so every chip can reach any position of the same parity for nothing.
Gather all chips on one even and one odd spot for free; then move the smaller group across at cost 1 each.

cases.note: Patch 1, 2, 4.
Patch 1, 2, 4, ..., 512: ten patches.

hints.text: Suppose every sum in [1, miss) can be formed. A number x <= miss extends that to [1, miss + x).
Walk the sorted nums. If the next number is <= miss, use it; otherwise patch with miss itself (the largest number that keeps the range gap-free), doubling the range.

cases.note: Ascending scores: the last athlete wins.

hints.text: You need each athlete's place, so you need the scores in descending order but the answers in the original order.
Push (score, index) into a max-heap and pop: the i-th pop is place i + 1. The top three get medals, the rest their place as a string.

heap = max-heap of (score[i], i)
names = ["Gold Medal", "Silver Medal", "Bronze Medal"]
for place in 1 .. n:
  (s, i) = pop
  ans[i] = names[place - 1] if place <= 3 else str(place)
return ans
Every second you need the current largest pile, and that pile then shrinks.
Max-heap: pop the largest, push back floor(sqrt(x)), k times. Sum what remains.

heap = max-heap of gifts
repeat k times:
  x = pop
  push floor(sqrt(x))
return sum of heap

cases.note: A pile of 1 never shrinks.

hints.text: Halving a big pile removes more stones than halving a small one, so always pick the current largest.
Max-heap: k times, pop x and push x - floor(x / 2). Return the heap's sum.

heap = max-heap of piles
repeat k times:
  x = pop
  push x - floor(x / 2)
return sum of heap

cases.note: Once everything is 1, each pick adds 1.

hints.text: Take the largest value every time; shrinking it to ceil(x / 3) can never make a smaller pick better.
Max-heap: k times, pop x, add it to the score, push ceil(x / 3).

heap = max-heap of nums, score = 0
repeat k times:
  x = pop
  score = score + x
  push ceil(x / 3)
return score

cases.note: The largest fraction is the last one.
The smallest fraction is 1 over the largest prime.

hints.text: For a fixed denominator arr[j], the fractions arr[0]/arr[j], arr[1]/arr[j], ... increase. That is a set of sorted lists.
Merge them with a min-heap: start with arr[0]/arr[j] for every j, pop k - 1 times, and after popping i/j push (i + 1)/j if i + 1 < j. Compare a/b < c/d as a*d < c*b.

heap = min-heap of (0, j) for j in 1 .. n - 1, ordered by arr[i] / arr[j]
repeat k - 1 times:
  (i, j) = pop
  if i + 1 < j: push (i + 1, j)
(i, j) = heap top
return [arr[i], arr[j]]

cases.note: The most frequent code fills every other slot.

hints.text: An answer always exists. Any arrangement with no two equal neighbours is accepted.
Max-heap by count: place the most frequent code that differs from the last one placed, holding back the one you just used for one step.

heap = max-heap of (count, code)
out = [], held = none
while heap not empty:
  (c, x) = pop; out.append(x)
  if held has count > 0: push held
  held = (c - 1, x)
return out

cases.note: Both ends of the range are included.

hints.text: Summing every node in range works, but the BST order tells you when a whole subtree is out of range.
If a node is below low, only its right subtree can contribute; if above high, only its left. Otherwise count it and go both ways.

cases.note: A left chain flips into a right chain.
Already a right chain: unchanged.

hints.text: The result is the inorder sequence laid out as a right-only chain.
Inorder walk with a tail pointer starting at a dummy node: for each node, clear its left child, hang it on tail.right and move tail.

dummy = new node(0); tail = dummy
inorder(node):
  if node is empty: return
  inorder(node.left)
  node.left = empty
  tail.right = node
  tail = node
  inorder(node.right)
inorder(root)
return dummy.right

cases.note: Every value appears once: all are modes.
Two modes tie.

hints.text: Here a BST allows duplicates (left <= node <= right), so equal values sit next to each other in inorder. Any order of modes is accepted.
Inorder walk counting the current run of equal values. A longer run replaces the answer list; an equal-length run is appended. No extra map needed.

prev = none, run = 0, best = 0, modes = []
inorder(node):
  if node is empty: return
  inorder(node.left)
  run = run + 1 if node.val == prev else 1
  prev = node.val
  if run > best: best = run; modes = [node.val]
  else if run == best: modes.append(node.val)
  inorder(node.right)
inorder(root)
return modes

cases.note: One tree is empty.

hints.text: Each tree's inorder is already sorted, so this is the merge step of merge sort.
Collect both inorder lists (or walk both trees with two stacks at once) and merge them with two pointers.

cases.note: A left chain.
Two nodes are already balanced.

hints.text: Inorder gives the values sorted, and a sorted list turns into a balanced BST by always picking the middle as root. Any balanced answer is accepted.
Two passes: collect the inorder values, then build recursively from index ranges using the middle element.

cases.note: Buckets must floor negative values correctly.
The equal pair is just outside the index window.

hints.text: Keep a window of the last indexDiff values and ask: is any value within valueDiff of the new one? A sorted set (BST) answers with floor/ceiling.

Without a sorted set, use buckets of width valueDiff + 1: two values in the same bucket are close enough, and otherwise only the two neighbouring buckets can hold a match. Evict the value that slides out of the window.

w = valueDiff + 1; buckets = empty map
for i, x in nums:
  b = floor(x / w)
  if b in buckets: return true
  if b - 1 in buckets and x - buckets[b - 1] <= valueDiff: return true
  if b + 1 in buckets and buckets[b + 1] - x <= valueDiff: return true
  buckets[b] = x
  if i >= indexDiff: remove bucket of nums[i - indexDiff]

cases.note: Only the given order: 0 other ways.
A chain has exactly one insertion order.
A perfect tree: many interleavings.

hints.text: The first value is always the root. After it, the left-subtree values and right-subtree values may interleave freely as long as each side keeps its own relative order.
ways(a) = C(len(a) - 1, len(left)) * ways(left) * ways(right), where left and right keep their original order. Subtract 1 for the given order and work modulo 1e9 + 7 (Pascal's triangle for C).

C = Pascal's triangle up to n, mod M
ways(a):
  if len(a) <= 2: return 1
  left = values in a smaller than a[0], in order
  right = values in a larger than a[0], in order
  return C[len(a) - 1][len(left)] * ways(left) * ways(right) mod M
return (ways(nums) - 1) mod M

cases.note: The prefix is longer than the word.

cases.note: Every pair counts: 3.

Small inputs: check every pair with startsWith and endsWith. (The hard version stores pairs (word[k], word[len - 1 - k]) in a trie so both ends are checked in one walk.)

cases.note: Equal words: the larger index wins.
